POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Fri, 06 Nov 2026 17:59:53 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 Jared Kushner’s European security plan isn’t convincing Europe https://www.politico.eu/article/jared-kushner-european-security-plan-is-not-convincing-europe/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 06 Nov 2026 17:58:32 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9287796 BRUSSELS — Europe is once again watching the White House through gritted teeth.

An opaque Trump administration proposal for a new European-wide security arrangement with Russia has met skepticism from European capitals that fear it risks sidelining the continent and emboldening Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin.

“We already have a European security architecture in place — NATO and European Union both have their respective roles,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Friday in reaction to the U.S. proposal. “We must make sure Ukraine is integrated into this architecture. The problem remains that Russia keeps breaking the treaties that underpin it … Putin does not have a veto over European security.”

The latest U.S. proposal underscores growing anxiety around Trump’s fresh rapprochement with Russia as he ramps up pressure on Ukraine and his administration attempts to revive long-stalled talks to end Moscow’s full-scale war against Kyiv.

POLITICO spoke to 12 NATO diplomats, EU envoys and European government officials, all of whom were granted anonymity to speak freely on the sensitive issue. NATO allies were not briefed about the American plans in advance, according to three alliance diplomats, and many remain skeptical of the idea.

U.S. President Donald Trump late Thursday talked of a “big, beautiful agreement,” after meeting with Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev, adding: “It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe.”

“Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment,” Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner added soon after.

Kushner said the arrangement would have five goals: “Permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.” 

“It is a bit obscure what Kushner meant,” said one NATO diplomat. “The general sentiment in Europe is that any discussion with Russia on the future architecture at the moment will just be used by Moscow to legitimize their arguments … it will not fly with the European allies.”

A senior European official added: “Literally, there’s nothing to find fault with, but we know there’s something else going on.”

‘The elephant in the room’

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s top adviser, Björn Seibert, briefed EU ambassadors on Friday, according to two EU diplomats, following a discussion between national security advisers on the issue.

“There’s willingness to engage in Kyiv and in the rest of Europe although there’s little confidence in the Russians — but the EU is not blocking it,” one of the EU diplomats said after the meeting. But “the group around Trump underestimated how important the conflict is for Europe and how a bad outcome for Ukraine is very dangerous for Europe.”

“It’s a long-standing position for us and many others that European security architecture should not be discussed while there is a war,” said a senior European security official. “And obviously not without Europeans.”

“Europe must have a seat at the table in negotiations on peace in Ukraine and the future European security architecture,” Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda added Friday, after a meeting of the eight Nordic and Baltic countries.

This week saw two rounds of working-level meetings in Brussels on a Ukraine peace deal, ahead of U.S.-brokered working-level talks with Ukraine and Russia on Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi.

“We must be realistic about the peace talks and we must be very careful when it comes to the real intentions of Russia,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told a group of reporters, including from POLITICO, earlier this week. “In winter, Putin might have less incentives to get a deal.”

Stefan Kornelius, spokesperson for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — who talked to Trump on Thursday night — said: “A new sense of urgency has … emerged” on negotiations after this week’s U.S. midterm elections, adding the issue would resurface at an informal gathering of EU leaders in Dublin next week.

The meeting had been intended to focus on AI, but developments in Ukraine could overshadow the talks, a third EU diplomat said. “Things are moving pretty fast,” they said.

Still, some allies fear the U.S. may tie its new initiative to an upcoming review of American troops in Europe, expected in December. 

“That’s the elephant in the room,” said a second NATO diplomat. “One thing is talking about European security architecture … with an ‘ordinary’ U.S. posture; another thing is to talk about a European security architecture ‘as things will be,’ and nobody knows how that’ll be.”

Three of the newsrooms were evacuated, disrupting RTÉ and Newstalk programs, while Virgin staff kept broadcasts running. Police confirmed they found no suspicious devices.

“We have expected a rise in hybrid threats to Ireland because of our hosting of the EU presidency, and the EPC meeting will be by far the biggest set-piece event of that presidency, so one must presume it’s no coincidence that we’re experiencing this spike in hybrid activity now,” the Irish official said.

The Irish government said the threats against media outlets were probably part of a European-wide pattern of threats that have targeted dozens of airlines this week, including Irish carriers Ryanair and Aer Lingus. Hackers also targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in at least seven European countries.

“It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralized or coordinated effort,” the Irish government said in a statement. “However, these threats come on the heels of the ongoing disruption to aviation around Europe caused by similar threats, and it seems likely that this is a coordinated campaign of disruption.”

Bomb threats also targeted at least 18 European flights Friday, after at least 22 the day before, raising concerns that the hoaxes may be part of a coordinated campaign to disrupt air traffic.

Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares told Spanish public broadcaster TVE on Friday that the bomb threats affecting flights could be “an attempt at hybrid aggression and war in some psychological way.” He added that “it cannot be a coincidence that so many identical events occur with the same modus operandi throughout Europe.”

Luis Gallego, CEO of airline group IAG, said: “It is clear that what they [the perpetrators] are looking for is to create chaos and disruption in the different airports.”

Fighter jets were scrambled in Hungary on Friday “in response to bomb threats involving three civilian passenger aircraft,” said Hungary’s Defense Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi.

Prague Airport said nine flights were targeted by bomb threats Friday alone, while France reported another four threats against aircraft flying over its territory that day. The Bulgarian government told AFP that two flights bound for Sofia were targeted by bomb threats on Friday.

Aviation professionals have said no threat should be underestimated. “No matter how remote the real possibility after a call that there is a bomb on board, we will treat it as if there is a bomb on board,” said Paul Reuter, an airline captain and vice president of the European Cockpit Association.

The Irish government official told POLITICO that the sudden increase in anonymous disruptions to airlines, supermarkets and now news outlets appeared to be timed to increase tensions ahead of Dublin’s hosting next Thursday of the EPC summit.

Created in 2022 following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EPC brings together the leaders of 47 countries and representatives of several bodies, including NATO, to discuss strategic issues. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is also attending.

The Irish official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss Friday’s threats freely, declined to identify Russia as the likely culprit. But he noted that EU partners — including Denmark, which faced a similar wave of so-called hybrid attacks in the run-up to its own 2025 hosting of the EPC — had drawn such links in the past.

Irish police Superintendent Liam Geraghty said the event posed an even tougher security challenge than hosting a U.S. presidential visit. “We have not seen a policing and security operation of this scale ever before in Ireland,” Geraghty told reporters.

Pablo Hernández de Cos, a former governor of Spain’s central bank, and the Netherlands’ Klaas Knot, a former president of the Dutch central bank, were the only candidates to emerge after the 5 p.m. deadline, as expected.

Their candidacies are part of a larger game of musical chairs that includes France and Germany, as Europe’s four economic powerhouses negotiate how to secure their seats on the ECB’s executive board.

The ECB is one of the most powerful institutions in Europe, responsible for setting interest rates to keep prices stable at 2% over the medium-term. The six-person executive board oversees the central bank’s day-to-day activities and an army of economists who scrutinize financial markets and the economy at large.

Berlin is determined to hold onto the seat that German economist Isabel Schnabel will vacate on Jan. 3, when she leaves the ECB for a job at the International Monetary Fund. Paris, meanwhile, is targeting the ECB’s chief economist role once the Irish incumbent Philip Lane concludes his eight-year term on May 31.

Eurozone finance ministers will take stock of the ECB shuffling at Monday’s Eurogroup meeting in Brussels. Neither Hernández de Cos nor Knot are scheduled to attend the closed-door meeting. But their national ministers will talk up their respective compatriots.

Diplomats expect EU leaders to engage in horse trading at an informal summit in Dublin at the end of next week. The deadline for candidates to replace Schnabel is on Nov. 27.

Two senior Spanish officials have already stepped down following the Urda crash. Puente resigned Tuesday, calling his decision “a matter of political dignity,” while Adif President Luis Pedro Marco de la Peña quit Wednesday, less than 24 hours later.

Mélenchon also said he would disobey current EU rules that would prevent him from implementing his platform if elected.

Proposing a “new deal” for Europe, Mélenchon wants to redraft the treaties, ditch core parts of the EU’s rulebook — including debt and deficit limits — suspend competition rules for public services such as energy, transport and telecoms, and loosen state aid laws.

“We will immediately implement our program at the national level. This will therefore require a confrontation with European institutions,” according to the manifesto from Mélenchon’s France Unbowed. “This also means disobeying rules blocking [us] whenever necessary.”

“Our logic is simple. As long as a deal on changing the treaties is not done, we negotiate with our partners and disobey […] blocking rules in parallel. If we get to an agreement, it will be put to a referendum,” the manifesto added.

The proposals, which echo Mélenchon’s earlier statements, would likely face tough opposition from France’s partners in the European Council, which is currently dominated by more conservative leaders.

The manifesto also said the European Central Bank should be “placed under democratic control and mobilized to fund the ecological and social transition.” Mélenchon triggered a flurry of criticism earlier this year when he said he would “set fire” to a large chunk of France’s public debt held by the ECB, setting off a nationwide debate on the subject.

France is among the countries hardest hit by a global surge in borrowing costs, with its fiscal situation also limiting the government’s ability to soften the impact of higher fuel and food prices, part of a larger cost-of-living crisis on the continent.

With public debt amounting to 117.5% of GDP and a public deficit above 5%, fiscal issues have become a central concern for voters. Presidential candidates are pitching radically different solutions to the problem.

Le Pen has tried to rebrand herself as a responsible steward of the economy unafraid of cuts — despite critics saying her plan is “overly optimistic” and her flagship promises are yet to be funded. Centrist candidates, such as former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, are pitching themselves as the voice of reason on economic and fiscal issues but are struggling to gain traction.

However, France under Mélenchon would still provide assistance to European Union countries under EU treaties, the document added, echoing what the far-left leader previously told POLITICO.

An increasing number of polls place Mélenchon in second place in next year’s high-stakes election to replace President Emmanuel Macron. The top two vote-getters go on to a second round, which could see Mélenchon facing off against far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who also pledges to take France out of NATO’s integrated command.

Unlike Le Pen’s far-right party, France Unbowed does not explicitly say it would stop providing assistance to Ukraine — but it does insist on the need for a diplomatic solution. Any peace agreement would need to lean on “collective security guarantees, between the belligerents and with the rest of Europe.”

France Unbowed wants more arms regulation, including of lethal autonomous weapons systems and nuclear weapons.

The far-left party is also pushing back against the “space arms race,” including by pledging to close NATO’s space center in Toulouse, but says France should have the means to guarantee its sovereignty. Unlike most other political parties, France Unbowed has strong interest in space policy, and argues in its presidential platform that France should acquire a space shuttle.

France Unbowed lawmakers have previously pushed for France to procure Dassault Aviation’s Vortex, a European reusable orbital spaceplane program spearheaded by the French aerospace manufacturer.

Overall, France should invest more in so-called critical enablers, meaning military equipment in areas such as communications, intelligence and logistics that are currently mostly provided by the U.S. via NATO. “They must be produced as a matter of priority,” the party wrote.

It also wants to nationalize some of the country’s main defense companies including ArianeGroup.

A more detailed platform specifically on defense will be released later, a France Unbowed lawmaker told POLITICO.

“The King has decided to decline the Prime Minister’s resignation and has asked him to resume the budget negotiations immediately,” Belgium’s royal palace said in an official statement Friday.

De Wever offered his resignation to the king earlier this week after weekslong budget talks hit a deadlock.

Since then, Philippe has met with the five party leaders who make up Belgium’s coalition government and concluded that there is still a possible path for them to agree under a De Wever premiership.

“Following his discussions with the leaders of the five majority parties, the King noted that each of them wishes to conclude the budget negotiations as quickly as possible … The King also received a formal commitment from the five party leaders that their respective parties are prepared to make concessions in order to reach an agreement within the government,” the palace’s statement said.

While the government is seeking to plug a €10 billion budget gap by 2029, coalition partners are at loggerheads over where to find the cash.

Flemish Socialist party Vooruit is pushing for the highest earners to contribute more, but French-speaking center-right Reformist Movement has ruled that out, and also opposed reforming the value-added tax.

De Wever, who had previously ruled out starting the new year with an emergency budget, this week confirmed that the country would have no choice but to fall back on it again.

Under that system, the government can spend one-twelfth of the preceding year’s budget per month. “This is a terrible failure on the part of the government,” De Wever told members of parliament while announcing he would submit his resignation.

The prime minister will meet the king again in 10 days on Nov. 16 to report on progress, the palace said.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:21:07 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Italy still obstructing asylum returns from other EU states amid simmering dispute that threatens Schengen https://euobserver.com/247568/italy-still-obstructing-asylum-returns-from-other-eu-states-amid-simmering-dispute-that-threatens-schengen/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:21:07 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247568 Italy's foot-dragging on taking back asylum seekers from other EU states is contributing to a simmering dispute that risks shattering whatever trust has been restored among member states on the Schengen border-free travel zone.]]> Rome is still not fully accepting the return of prospective asylum seekers from countries such as Germany even though they first entered Europe on Italian territory, in a simmering dispute that could potentially erupt and place further pressure on the EU’s border-free travel zone.

A document released on Friday (6 November) by the European Commission says transfer requests were still being rejected as of the end of September.

“Based on the information provided by the member states between 12 June and 30 September 2026, transfers requested by other member states continued to be rejected by the Italian authorities,” says the document.

“Furthermore, according to information received, there have been cases in which the Italian authorities returned persons to the transferring member states, despite Italy having been determined as the member state responsible,” it added.

Even though it says Italy, as of 29 October, has resumed transfers, according to an administrative letter, the European Commission couldn’t determine if anyone had actually departed for Italy.

The findings highlight a politically-explosive scenario whereby arriving asylum seekers fan out through the rest of Europe, triggering knee-jerk reactions by member states to impose internal border controls on the Schengen area.

It also echoes the scenario whereby Italy slapped border controls on Spain over the summer over unfounded fears that the tens of thousands of people that entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta would somehow end up on continental Europe.

Italy has for years allowed people to leave without first registering them, in a process of self-relocation that has angered other EU states. Many travel through France to reach northern Europe.

]]> Russians repel attack by Ukrainian ground-robots armed with RPGs, in futuristic assault (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,716) https://euobserver.com/247493/russians-repel-attack-by-ukrainian-ground-robots-armed-with-rpgs-in-futuristic-assault-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1716/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 14:29:51 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247493 Ukrainian commander Andriy Biletsky is gambling on mass robot assaults to spare his soldiers’ lives, as Russian troops rush to prove on camera that they can still swat the machines from the sky and fields around Lyman. ]]>
  • Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps is saving lives by sending robots into attacks.
  • In Orikhiv and Mala Tokmachka, Russians are being pushed out of built-up areas.
  • Even after more than half a year, Z-patriots cannot fully admit defeat in Dnipropetrovsk region, but fear the situation in Komar.

    ]]>         From India to Africa, renewables race ahead but Europe is lagging, IEA report shows https://euobserver.com/247441/from-india-to-africa-renewables-race-ahead-but-europe-is-lagging-iea-report-shows/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 14:05:51 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247441 The Iran war has pushed governments from India to sub-Saharan Africa to build more solar and wind, with some regions almost tripling new capacity. But in Europe, that rollout is stalling. ]]> The oil and gas shock from the Strait of Hormuz is speeding up the transition to renewables almost everywhere in the world, but not in Europe, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its annual renewables report on Friday (6 November).

    The Paris-based agency expects global renewable power capacity to grow by almost 4,800 GW between 2026 and 2031, which is 57 percent more than in the previous six years. 

    But it cut its expected growth forecast for Europe by six percent compared to estimates made last year, although Europe will still add around 100 gigawatts (GW) a year until 2031.

    “Higher electricity prices associated with the current conflict in the Middle East have not yet translated into major policy revisions or a measurable acceleration in installations,” the report says about the situation in Europe. 

    In most places, the adoption of renewables is speeding up, driven by high costs of fuels and energy security worries. 

    “Previously, environmental concerns were the policy priority behind the growth of renewables,” said IEA executive director Fatih Birol on Friday. 

    “Today, it’s mainly energy security that is driving renewables’ expansion as more and more countries seek to reduce their exposure to imported fuels,” he also said. 

    The IEA raised its forecast for the United States by almost 40 percent compared with last year, and for sub-Saharan Africa by 54 percent.

    For the first time, poorer countries outside China will add renewables as fast as rich ones.

    ]]>         Hungary’s communist secret‑police files go online – and a Fidesz MP is named by mistake (Day 178 of the Tisza government) https://euobserver.com/247289/hungarys-communist-secretpolice-files-go-online-and-a-fidesz-mp-is-named-by-mistake-day-178-of-the-tisza-government/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 13:42:10 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247289 Budapest finally opens its communist-era files and trims money for cultural and diaspora projects. Prime minister Péter Magyar navigates a minefield where each disclosure risks empowering Fidesz loyalists and unsettling Hungary’s neighbours alike. ]]> The series continues as we report on developments following April’s historic election and on the steps taken since then by the Tisza government. This week, we cover the following topics:

    • Secret-police files: familiar names and an embarrassing error.
    • Director of the Institute of International Affairs dismissed – he had also worked for the Fidesz government.
    • Government causes major uproar with cultural budget.
    • Less money may go across the borders.
    • Poll of the week: a majority wants slower, but lawful and effective justice.

    Sándor Lezsák was one of the founders of the Hungarian party called MDF at the time of the country’s regime change from communism; it was in the yard of his house in Lakitelek where the meetings preparing the transition took place, where opposition politicians held discussions in the late 1980s.

    Lezsák later became a Fidesz politician and served as a MEP for the party until the 2026 election. His name also appeared in the state security documents published on Wednesday (4 November), which he immediately and vehemently protested against.

    “Everyone who spreads this vile lie will be held accountable for it in court,” he wrote.

    It soon emerged that his name indeed should not have appeared in the files.

    On Thursday morning the Historical Archives of the State Security Services announced that Lezsák’s name had appeared on the website due to an IT error. In reality he was not a network contact, but a person under surveillance.

    Fidesz politicians immediately seized on the case.

    “Tisza, in truly neo-communist fashion, is lumping perpetrators together with victims,” reacted parliamentary group leader János Bóka, demanding an apology from prime minister Péter Magyar and the resignation of cultural minister Zoltán Tarr.

    Magyar later publicly apologised to Lezsák.

    A belated step

    On 15 September the Hungarian parliament decided to make public, and searchable online, the list of people who cooperated with the communist secret services (the so‑called “network contacts”).

    In the first phase, part of the documents was made accessible on the site nyitottaktak.hu, while the recruitment dossiers – from which the stories of those recruited can be learned in more detail – will be published by 25 February 2027, the Memorial Day for the Victims of the Communist Dictatorship.

    Hungary is thus taking this step 37 years after the regime change, more than 20 years after the Czech Republic and Slovakia did so in 2004.

    Those we already knew about

    It was already known in the case of several well‑known public figures that they had cooperated with the secret services or had come into their sights.

    One such person was Nobel Prize‑winning biologist Katalin Karikó, developer of Pfizer’s vaccines, about whom it emerged in 2021 that state security had recruited her. At the time Karikó said she had been recruited under threat, but had not reported on anyone.

    It had also long been known that other politicians had been recruited: among them József Torgyán, former president of the Independent Smallholders’ Party, who in 1998 was Viktor Orbán’s coalition partner, and István Csurka, who led the far‑right party called MIÉP.

    The files also contain the name of György Nógrádi, one of Fidesz’s best‑known geopolitics experts, who often appears in Slovakia and was previously a guest at MKP (the party of the Hungarians living in Slovakia) campaign events. Nógrádi denies having been an agent.

    New names appear too

    On Wednesday (4 November) the whole of Hungary was feverishly browsing the site nyitottaktak.hu to see which familiar names might surface.

    There were indeed some surprises.

    By Thursday the lists had produced the names of several television personalities, singers, artists and other public figures. One of the best‑known is István Vágó, who for decades hosted popular quiz shows and was regarded as one of the most erudite figures on Hungarian television.

    The list also includes Tibor Dévényi, one of the first Hungarian DJs, who for decades hosted the popular children’s programme Three Wishes on public television. The Fidesz‑adjacent singer Róbert Szikora is likewise among the well‑known names; he has denied having ever reported on anyone.

    Among those on the list there is a sitting Constitutional Court judge (András Patyi), a former ambassador to Washington (András Simonyi), and even a former central bank governor (György Surányi).

    ]]>         Listen: The mental health toll of Europe’s migration policies https://euobserver.com/247374/listen-the-mental-health-toll-of-europes-migration-policies/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 10:38:01 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247374 Racism, violence, institutional abandonment and unbearable living conditions.  These are all factors that damage the mental health of migrants and exiled people. That’s exactly what migrants in Ceuta are experiencing since July.]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below: 

    Racism, violence, institutional abandonment and unbearable living conditions.  These are all factors that damage the mental health of migrants and exiled people. That’s exactly what migrants in Ceuta are experiencing since July. 

    Does the EU really care about migrants’ mental health? The conditions in which they often find themselves in Europe create stress, anxiety and a lack of hope. These have very concrete effects on their psychological state.

    Léa has been working in Ceuta since July as a volunteer for the non profit organisation No Name Kitchen, that supports migrants and refugees. In an interview with our partner inside the Sphera network, El Salto, she speaks about the migrants she has met so far. Her name has been changed:

    “In these months I have seen the change in the boys’ faces. As the weeks passed they transformed. It was them, but it wasn’t them anymore.”

    Read more

    Afghan pushback survivor fights ‘impossible’ evidence rules in European courts with new UN case against Greece

    When journalist Sarah Babiker from El Salto spoke to those who are closest to the migrants in Ceuta, she noticed that they all describe a climate of intense tension and speak about a mental health crisis.

    Léa is observing systematic violence on the city streets: “I didn’t find a single person who hadn’t had experiences of violence or racism with security forces or neighbors.” In this context, she says, more and more people are asking for care for mental health problems. Some do not request it explicitly, but would actually need it.

    Migrating is an obstacle course that takes a toll not only on bodies but also on mental health. Léa stresses that every phase of migration is traumatic: before crossing the border, during the crossing, and also on arrival. Migrants are experiencing wars, sometimes death and distress.

    As a result, they are more likely to develop post-traumatic stress, depression and anxiety. On top of this, there is the case of people who already had mental health problems beforehand and can no longer be followed up or treated correctly. 

    So how do authorities take that into account? Let’s be clear: access to psychosocial care is very limited in the support provided to migrants.

    Legislation varies from one EU member state to another, because there is no common European legislation on mental health care for new arrivals. 

    Read more

    Merz, Meloni and the EU: How political attacks on rescue charities are leaving migrants to drown

    What happens is that the measures in place often apply only to those with refugee status. There is often no care at all while people wait for a decision on their case. This takes months, if not years.

    What’s more, the language barrier and the fear of being deported often make it harder for people to speak openly and ask for help. In Ceuta, healthcare centres, or workers, are often difficult to access because of harassment from security forces, neighbours or, sometimes, the far-right. 

    For example, Léa recalls that one time when taking migrants to Médecins du Monde, they were forced to stop and get out of the car. The migrants believed for a few minutes that they were going to be deported. She describes how they were subjected to racist remarks, while the authorities refused to call Médecins du Monde to check that they were indeed heading there, preferring to arrest them.

    That’s why taking care of mental health cannot go without recognising the most basic human rights.

    Read more

    ‘Let me die’: tortured migrants and rescue ships face off against EU-sponsored Libyan forces

    The problem is that politics seems to go in the opposite direction: Several NGOs and mental health organizations have already pointed out that tighter border controls, temporary reception facilities and, more broadly, the hardening of migration policies risk worsening psychosocial distress. They also make it even harder to identify vulnerable people with mental health problems.

    So what do we do about it? In Sweden, Red Cross trauma centres treat refugees whatever their papers say, with interpreters in the room. In Ireland, a charity offers free counselling with no documents needed, and they insist that nothing is shared with immigration. In Germany, no less than fifty centres help survivors of torture, war and forced displacement.

    Those places care for everyone in their own language, without fear, factors that are essential to supporting migrants’ mental health.

    One last word to conclude: the struggle migrants face surely complicates their integration. But more importantly: this struggle doesn’t disappear when their status is cleared. 

    Even when allowed to stay legally on the territory, they face racism and discrimination, further poisoning their integration and thus feeding the far right discourse.

    ]]>         Trump’s mid-term election disaster is not good news for Nato or Ukraine https://euobserver.com/247149/trumps-mid-term-election-disaster-is-not-good-news-for-nato-or-ukraine/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 09:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247149 European governments may draw the wrong lesson. Americans voted on Tuesday about inflation, the Iran war and Trump himself, not about European security. Europe should not behave as if they had.]]> Donald Trump asked Americans to “pretend” he was on the ballot. They took him at his word. 

    Democrats won both chambers of Congress and flipped seven Republican Senate seats, some of them held by the party for decades. Trump had said in advance what he would do if this happened: he would veto everything.

    Europeans who were cheering for the Democrats can celebrate. For Europe, though, little is likely to shift, at least for now.

    Diplomats in Brussels expected little to change, and said so before the vote.

    Governments may still draw the wrong lesson. The Democrats have won the power to restrain Trump, but they cannot make American policy toward Europe predictable.

    Read more

    Lame duck or angry duck? Europe’s leadership largely silent on Trump’s election disaster, fearing backlash

    Congress can only slow Trump down

    A presidential veto override needs two-thirds of both chambers, and in the Senate most ordinary bills still need 60 votes to get past a filibuster. Democrats have neither. They will control spending bills and they can subpoena officials. 

    They can also block or delay nominees, which is enough to slow the administration down but not enough to run foreign policy from Capitol Hill.

    Congress already authorised $400m [€356m] a year for Ukraine security assistance in 2026 and 2027, in the defence law it passed last December.

    Democrats can push actual money through must-pass spending bills. A president cannot lawfully refuse to spend appropriated funds for policy reasons. 

    Presidential drawdowns from US stocks, delivery schedules and export licences remain largely in executive hands.

    Trump lost his emergency tariffs in the Supreme Court in February. He replaced them with a temporary global levy. When that expired on 24 July, new tariffs on imports from 60 economies took effect the same day, under a different law.

    Congress could rewrite the powers it delegated to the president, but that bill would meet a veto. Even Joe Biden, a president friendly to Europe, needed months to ease the steel tariffs after Trump’s first term, and he replaced them with quotas, not free trade.

    On Iran, war powers resolutions face the same veto, and attaching conditions to war money is politically hard while American troops are in the field. Before the war, the Strait of Hormuz carried oil and petroleum products equal to about a fifth of world consumption.

    Most of it went to Asia, but major disruptions still push up the prices Europeans pay.

    Nato withdrawal? Untested

    On Nato membership itself, the protection is stronger. A 2023 provision co-written by Marco Rubio, then a Republican senator from Florida and now Trump’s secretary of state, bars withdrawal from Nato without two-thirds of the Senate or an act of Congress.

    Whether it holds against a president who claims treaty withdrawal as his own power has never been tested in court.

    Congress went further a year ago. The December 2025 defence law limits what Pentagon money can be used for in Europe. It cannot pay for cutting US forces there below 76,000 for more than 45 days. Nor can it pay for removing major equipment, giving up bases, or handing the top Nato command to a non-American. 

    The Pentagon can still do any of this, but only after the secretary of defense and the US commander in Europe each certify the decision to Congress, submit the required assessments and then wait 60 days.

    The restriction applies to fiscal 2026 funds, and Congress is considering whether to extend it.

    Even if it survives, the law covers what is stationed in Europe. What Washington sends when a crisis comes, and whether aircraft based in Germany fly for European purposes or for operations somewhere else, is still decided in the White House and the Pentagon.

    Hegseth holds the cards

    The timing is bad too.

    The Pentagon’s review of US forces in Europe was to give secretary of defense Pete Hegseth at least four sets of options by 6 November, with the review finished in December.

    The new Congress only meets on 3 January, so Hegseth is scheduled to have the options weeks before any Democrat chairs a committee.

    Before the vote, there was a nagging fear in Europe that a Trump beaten at home would look for distraction abroad.

    Read more

    Trump likely to lash out in foreign policy if Democrats take Congress, warns ex-US ambassador to EU

    Josef Braml, the European director of the Trilateral Commission, warned on Wednesday (4 November) that the president may now push harder on tariffs, Nato and Ukraine.

    That may very well happen. But Europe’s own response is the more immediate concern.

    Europe now has rules that favour its own defence industry, in the European Defence Industry Programme (EDIP) and in the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) loans. The rules alone will not produce refuelling tankers or missile stocks. That takes money and years.

    A Congress more supportive of Nato and Ukraine could give governments an excuse to delay the expensive decisions that would make European defence less dependent on Washington.

    Trump’s term ends in January 2029, and the Democratic majority may last only two years. Europe cannot plan its defence around a two-year American election cycle.

    Americans voted on Tuesday about inflation, the Iran war and Trump himself, not about European security. Europe should not behave as if they had.

    ]]>         [Investigation] How the EU’s methane rules came undone, and ended up giving Trump exactly what he wanted https://euobserver.com/247183/investigation-how-the-eus-methane-rules-came-undone/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247183 The Trump administration wanted the EU’s methane rules gone. Internal documents show how the commission tried, and failed, to hold the line.]]> EU ambassadors will try for a third time on Friday (6 November) to agree whether to delay the EU’s methane rules for oil and gas imports by one year or three.

    Methane, a potent greenhouse gas, has become a major target of both climate regulation and industry lobbying. Capturing it is one of the “quickest and cheapest ways to curb global greenhouse gas emissions”, according to the International Energy Agency.

    For many months, the EU Commission vowed it would not reopen the rules. Yet in October, Europe’s methane rules, adopted in 2024 and due to start in two months, still ended up on the chopping block. Here’s the story of how we got here.

    Creole Spirit

    At a summit in Pittsburgh in late February, co-hosted by US gas lobby group LNG Allies, the EU’s top energy official, Ditte Juul Jørgensen, toasted a decade of transatlantic gas trade.

    In a keynote prepared by her team, she recalled how, ten years earlier, the first cargo of US liquefied natural gas (LNG) to Europe had crossed the Atlantic from Louisiana on a ship called the Creole Spirit.

    It was “a most fitting name” for a ship that “embodied both the energy heritage of Louisiana and the new spirit of transatlantic partnership”, reads her speech. Later that day, she sat on a panel on the EU methane rules with US gas lobbyists.

    LNG Allies later said she had “captured the spirit of the Transatlantic LNG Partnership perfectly”, calling her “a true friend of US LNG” who “graciously accepted nearly every speaking invitation we extended”.

    As the commission’s top energy official since 2019, she had steered the EU through the Russian gas crisis and a more than fivefold increase in US LNG imports, which perhaps explains her warm welcome in Pittsburgh.

    But to her also fell the task of defending the EU’s methane rules against a multipronged attack from the US oil and gas industry and an increasingly hostile Trump administration.

    Jørgensen’s speech is one of 55 documents released by the commission’s energy department under a freedom of information request by climate research group ARIA and shared with EUobserver.

    They include briefings, speeches and emails from the commission’s dealings with US officials and industry between March 2025 and May 2026. US dislike of the rules has been no secret. Trump officials and allied industry groups attacked them openly and regularly.

However, Czech national Aleš K. is still behind bars in China for allegedly breaching the country's security laws.]]> First published in Respekt.

    Yang Yiming, a suspected Chinese spy, has walked free after his arrest earlier this year in the Czech Republic.

    Prague Municipal Court judge Tome Frankič found that Yiming posed as a foreign correspondent for a Chinese media outlet while working for the country’s intelligence services. He accepted assignments to covertly pass on information he obtained about politicians and other public figures.

    And yet, the man was released this week on Monday (2 November). In the view of judge Frankič, the evidence against Yiming did not show he broke the law.

    Read more

    Czech businessman detained by Beijing faces espionage charges and could be part of swap with Chinese spy

    Suspected Chinese spy walks free

    In court, the prosecution failed to prove Yiming had “intentionally endangered or damaged the constitutional order, territorial integrity, defence or security of the Czech Republic, or undermined its sovereignty.”

    The trial of the Chinese man was the first of its kind in modern-day Czech Republic.

    Previously, espionage could be prosecuted only if police or intelligence services could prove that a person had obtained classified information such as government documents or intelligence-service materials.

    But the Czech security community argued for years that defining the offence of spying was defined too narrowly, and could not adequately tackle espionage.

    Indeed, collecting information on people’s private lives – whether it be their alcoholism or intimate relationships – could be enough to blackmail some to advance the interests of foreign powers.

    So the previous Czech government passed a new, broader criminal offence – unauthorised activity for a foreign power.

    Now, bringing someone before a Czech court requires proof of activities for a foreign power with intent to endanger the Czech Republic’s constitutional order, sovereignty, territorial integrity, defence or security.

    ]]>         Europe should beware of buying America’s increasingly unaccountable AI killing-machines https://euobserver.com/246875/europe-should-beware-of-buying-americas-increasingly-unaccountable-ai-killing-machines/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 10:13:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246875 As Washington hands its autonomous warfare roadmap to Musk and other defence-industry moguls, European leaders in Geneva must decide whether to copy a model that speeds up killing, while hollowing out accountability for civilian deaths.]]> Later this month in Geneva, states will gather for the Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons and decide whether to begin negotiating binding rules on autonomous weapons.

    More than 70 states have already indicated their readiness to do so. Meanwhile, Washington is moving in the opposite direction.

    The gap between Washington and its allies on autonomous weapons has direct implications for how responsibility is built into military technology. 

    On 30 September, the US department of war announced an Autonomous Warfare Command, meant to scale autonomous warfare across the US military by October 2027.

    The same speech launched Project Meridian, a 120-day study of the technologies the US military will need for future wars. The project will be led by tech oligarch Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey (CEO of defence firm Anduril), and US politician Newt Gingrich, with the group’s findings due in January. 

    Ethical and commercial issues abound. SpaceX is a backbone of US national security, and Anduril sells jammers, interceptors, and un-crewed combat aircraft to the US military.

    Critics have noted that Musk and Luckey would be identifying needs that their own companies already meet, and the announcement describes no recusal or disclosure mechanism.

    Others, such as professor Elke Schwarz from the Queen Mary University of London, have long shown how the commercial logic of technology firms shapes the ethics of violent technologies, treating moral and legal questions as engineering problems to be optimised away.

    Read more

    Russia’s faith in ‘error-free’ killer robots and global divisions expose the moral vacuum in AI warfare

    From a technical and legal perspective, this is neither possible nor desirable. Project Meridian promises that this logic will set the agenda. 

    What this agenda fails to cover is just as consequential. The US administration of president Donald Trump has dismantled the machinery that teaches militaries about civilian harm.

    The Pentagon’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence fell from 40 staff to nine in 2025, and the Pentagon’s own inspector general concluded the department no longer has the personnel and capabilities needed to meet its legal responsibilities.

    Organisations like Airwars, which document civilian harm from military operations, find themselves offering evidence to commands that have almost no one left to receive it, let alone learn lessons to improve practices over time. 

    Autonomy and AI-enabled targeting depend on high quality data and feedback. A system is only as good as what its operators learn from its errors.

    Research on the quantification logics of targeting, and on outdated intelligence feeding strike decisions, shows how easily speed and scale displace the judgment that precautions require.

    Accelerating autonomy while abandoning the ability to learn from past practices does not produce a more precise or legitimate military.

    It produces a faster one that repeats its mistakes, which will continue to exacerbate civilian harm in new theatres of war. 

    Read more

    First fully-autonomous drone kill Ukraine heralds ‘dystopian future of untethered weaponry’

    Washington exporting normalisation

    This issue is relevant to discussions in Geneva because technology that is built, bought and normalised in Washington is sold elsewhere.

    European militaries integrate, procure and operate alongside American systems.

    And the diplomatic track is losing ground on exactly this point: the Group of Governmental Experts’ final report softened what earlier drafts framed as obligations on responsibility and accountability into encouragement. 

    This moment also offers opportunities. Europe is in a position to answer with more than just words.

    Responsibility works best when it is designed into a system from the start.

    Read more

    Why Pope Leo is right to call on EU to regulate lethal AI weapons

    Precautions must be built in at the design stage, with deliberate friction where speed would erode judgment, meaningful human decision-making, and sustained engagement among developers, lawyers, and operators.

    States already have duties to review new weapons and to protect civilians. Applying these across the whole lifecycle of a system takes institutional will, and Europe is uniquely positioned to demonstrate this. 

    This will also strengthen European sovereignty. Relying on a handful of American vendors means importing their design assumptions along with their products.

    European standards for testing and assurance, limiting civilian harm written into procurement contracts, and legal review that begins at the design stage would give governments real choices about what they buy and on what terms.

    Any supplier, American or European, would have to meet them. 

    In Geneva, European governments should back the start of negotiations on a legal instrument, and they should write responsibility by design into their own procurement now, without waiting for a treaty.

    Europe should demand a different theory of responsibility from whoever supplies its autonomy.

      <title>US job growth exceeds expectations in October despite economic uncertainty</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/06/us-job-growth-october</link>
      <description><p>‘Low-hire, low-fire’ labor market shows sluggish growth but few layoffs, with an interest rate hike expected in December</p><p>The US added 165,000 jobs to the economy in October, a sign of resilience in the labor market amid ongoing war in the Middle East and inflation, according to new data released on Friday.</p><p>Economists had said the labor market has been stuck in a “low-hire, low-fire” state, in which job growth is sluggish but layoffs also remain low, but October’s data surpassed economist expectations. The <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/usemployment">unemployment rate</a> went down slightly to 4.1%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/06/us-job-growth-october">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>European and Asia-Pacific markets slide after Wall Street rout, while latest US jobs report beats forecasts</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/news/video/2026/nov/06/could-the-ai-bubble-burst-after-democrats-midterms-sweep-the-latest"><strong>Could the AI bubble burst after Democrats’ midterms sweep? - The Latest</strong></a></p></li></ul><p><strong>Despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year.</strong></p><p>The <strong>Nasdaq</strong> <strong>Composite</strong> index, for example, is still up 4.6% since the start of January – even though it’s more than 10% below its peak.</p><p>“The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe.</p><p>Big worries are colliding – the build-out of data centres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-tumble-ai-panic-markets-democrats-midterms-success-jobs-oil-dollar-latest-news-updates">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/05/former-trump-voters-economy</link>
      <description><p>Polling done for the Guardian shows plummeting support from a former key constituency of Donald Trump’s base</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/nov/05/what-happens-after-the-blue-wave-our-reporters-answer-your-midterm-election-results-questions">Q&amp;A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>Polling conducted by the Harris Poll for the Guardian before the election shows just how angry voters were and points to one key reason Republicans lost so badly: plummeting support from rural voters, once a key constituency of Donald Trump’s base.</p><p>Over the summer, 95% of Americans indicated they believed there was an <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/jul/07/cost-of-living-poll-groceries-gas">affordability crisis</a>, particularly because of steep gas and grocery prices.       <title>US stocks rise, dollar slides as investors digest Democrats’ midterm victories</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/04/us-dollar-slides-democrats-midterm-election-win-growth-fears</link>
      <description><p>Government bond yields fall while initial fears ease over impact of election results on world’s biggest economy</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/04/midterm-elections-results-senate-house-michigan-maine-mississippi-latest-updates">US midterm elections – live updates</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/explainer-midterms-trump-us-global-economy-markets">After US midterms, what will lame-duck Trump mean for global economy?</a></p></li></ul><p>US stocks have surged as investors digest the Democrats’ victories in the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a>, lifted by hopes that <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s turbulent policymaking would be restrained and shaking off initial fears about the impact on growth in the world’s largest economy.</p><p>The Dow Jones rose close to 3%, its best day in over a year, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the benchmark S&amp;P 500 gained about 1.5% each when markets closed on Wednesday afternoon, turning around overnight falls in US stock futures after the news that the Democratic party <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/03/midterm-election-results-live-updates">won control</a> of the Senate and the House of Representatives.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/04/us-dollar-slides-democrats-midterm-election-win-growth-fears">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>CVS Pharmacy will be separate from CVS Health, housing major insurer Aetna and benefits manager Caremark</p><p>CVS Health, the largest US healthcare conglomerate valued at $117bn, has announced its plans split off its pharmacy chain from its <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/money/healthinsurance">health insurance</a> and benefits businesses, ending an era in which healthcare companies grew into vast conglomerates.</p><p>In their announcement on Wednesday, CVS Health said they will split off its 9,000 pharmacies, in-store clinics and mail order prescription business into a business named CVS Pharmacy.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/cvs-health-pharmacy-insurance">Continue reading...</a></description>
