<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comFri, 06 Nov 2026 18:10:09 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Aer Lingus Pilot demoted in alleged ‘sham’ disciplinary process has lost out on €25,0000, WRC told]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/06/aer-lingus-pilot-demoted-in-alleged-sham-disciplinary-process-has-lost-out-on-250000-wrc-told/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/06/aer-lingus-pilot-demoted-in-alleged-sham-disciplinary-process-has-lost-out-on-250000-wrc-told/Fri, 06 Nov 2026 18:03:10 +0000Lawyers for an Aer Lingus pilot stripped of command duties three years ago say he has been deprived of over €250,000 in earnings by an allegedly “sham” disciplinary process pursued against him.

The airline has argued the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) should not make an order reinstating the pilot, Declan McCabe, as a captain, as final submissions were heard in a two-year legal battle on Friday.

An adjudication officer is now considering his decision on complaints of whistleblower penalisation by McCabe against Aer Lingus Ltd.

McCabe was demoted from captain to first officer for what the airline deemed breaches of his air safety reporting obligations while flying in command of an Airbus A321xlr which failed to link up with a radio navigation beacon coming into Dublin Airport before making a turn to re-establish contact.

The conclusion in a disciplinary investigation was that McCabe’s aircraft, with 156 passengers on crew aboard, was “flying in the wrong direction ... until air traffic control intervened” on the day, according to Captain Eamon Kierans, the manager who conducted the process.

McCabe said what happened was “a non-event from a flying point of view” and that relevant Aer Lingus manual left it up to his judgment to decide whether to report it. The company disagreed.

In a closing argument on Friday, McCabe’s barrister, David Byrnes, led by Setanta Solicitors, said Captain Colm Wynne and Aer Lingus’s ex-chief pilot Davina Pratt, “tried to take away the newly-minted captaincy my client had achieved ... for calling in fatigued” in 2011.

“This was because of the roster changes at the time, and there was tension between the union and the airline. Captain Wynne put the commercial interest of the company first, and set a deadly precedent,” he submitted.

“The message is clear: do not call into Aer Lingus fatigued,” counsel said.

It was “highly questionable” that Wynne had been involved from the start of the investigations into the events surrounding the 8th June, 2023 flight, despite later saying he had stepped away, Byrnes submitted

His client was supposed to be shielded by specific legal protections from disciplinary action for aircrew unless there was “firm, reliable evidence” their actions reached “the extremely high level of wilful culpability”.

Byrnes said the subsequent processes leading to his client’s demotion were a “sham disciplinary” and that it was “truly extraordinary” that Aer Lingus had asked adjudicator John Harraghy to “ignore the unfairness”.

Tom Mallon, appearing instructed by Arthur Cox LLP for the respondent, Mr Byrnes’s submissions on the standard of the investigation, disciplinary and appeal processes were not relevant to the case.

“The plane was in the wrong place [and] corrective action had to be taken, whatever was the cause of it,” he said.

“That can’t be glossed over, that disciplinary investigation. It was about conduct, not competence,” he added.

Byrnes said Aer Lingus “wants to get a million miles away from this with the jets turned up full blast [because] they know well that these processes are simply untenable”.

In submissions on redress, Byrnes said his client was entitled to a direction reinstating him to command with the rank of captain.

In all, he said, his client’s had been deprived of over a quarter of a million euro in pay since his demotion.

Byrnes said the jurisdiction went beyond financial loss and argued there was precedent for an award of “proportionate and dissuasive” compensation in the case – referencing the maximum jurisdiction of five years’ salary.

Mallon said the Supreme Court had made clear reinstatement was only to be awarded in “very rare” and “exceptional” circumstances.

Adjudicator John Harraghy closed the hearing said he would write to the parties with his decision next year.

]]>SAM BOAL<![CDATA[Aer Lingus profits slump by €28m as airline plans capacity and job cuts]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/06/aer-lingus-profits-slump-as-airline-plans-capacity-and-job-cuts/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/06/aer-lingus-profits-slump-as-airline-plans-capacity-and-job-cuts/Fri, 06 Nov 2026 07:51:12 +0000Aer Lingus has reported operating profit of €142 million for the third quarter of 2026, down €28 million year on year.

During the first nine months of the year, operating profits at the International Airlines Group-owned airline have fallen by 57 per cent, down from €250 million to €108 million.

Aer Lingus chief executive Lynne Embleton said increased competition, particularly in the North Atlantic region, “has fundamentally changed our operating environment”.

She said to address these challenges, the airline must focus on “reducing our costs and improving efficiency and productivity”.

The trading update from Aer Lingus said it has faced higher supplier and carbon costs and “significantly increased fuel costs” this year.

Aer Lingus said it expected to face these higher costs “through the airline’s upcoming seasonally weaker quarters and through 2027” .

To counter the impacts of the elevated costs, Aer Lingus plans to implement “network and organisation design changes” to reduce costs, which are expected to lead to an improvement in its operating margin.

Aer Lingus has plans to reduce flying capacity by 6 per cent, a removal of lower-margin flying and proposed reductions of 500 roles.

Embleton said in a call with media on Friday morning that department-by-department talks over reducing the headcount were ongoing and could be concluded this year.

“It’s a big restructuring [of the company’s head office]. We’re a long way down those conversations, which is at department-by-department level, and we’ve had expressions of interest for voluntary severance within that and we’re working through that process.

“I do hope that will be, if not done, largely done by the end of the year.”

Embleton said Aer Lingus had received “a lot of expressions of interest for voluntary redundancy” from cabin crew and “significant applications” from pilots since their own expression of interest procedure started a week ago.

She could not clarify how many expressions of interest the company has received in the redundancy programme.

The cost-cutting measures are aimed at delivering an operating margin of 12 per cent to 15 per cent at the airline, which Embleton said is required to secure investment and support future growth.

“We must adapt as a business to a competitive environment that is here to stay regardless of any future changes to fuel costs. Achieving this is critical to avoiding any further reduction in our flying capacity.”

She added management, unions and staff must “work together constructively” to put the airline in a position to manage the new competitive environment.

“This is essential in order to achieve an operating margin which will give us the investment needed to grow in the interest of all of our stakeholders.”

On Thursday, almost 30 flights across Europe were affected by “hoax” bomb threats, including an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome that was diverted to an airfield in northern France.

“It’s very difficult for our crew and our customers when an event like that happens,” Embleton said. “I think our crew behaved with impeccable professionalism. We are very proud of how they handled it.”

International Airlines Group chief executive Luis Gallego added the airline industry was “suffering” as a result of these incidents.

“The only thing we can do is to follow the protocols,” Gallego said. “We don’t have any other alternative than to follow the procedures. It’s easy to disrupt the operation with all these threats, but we don’t have a way to discriminate if something is true or is not true.”

Further details in the trading update said Aer Lingus passenger numbers rose by 1.8 per cent in the third quarter of 2026, compared with the same period last year.

It added competitive market conditions and a weaker yield environment had “limited the airline’s ability to offset higher fuel and other operating costs”.

During the third quarter, the airline announced some initiatives to raise further revenue, which included provision of Starlink wifi on its services. Starlink is now provided on almost all long-haul Aer Lingus flights and will at a later date be provided on short-haul services.

The airline also said next year it would begin to retrofit 10 Airbus A330 aircraft cabins and introduce a premium economy option for customers.

]]>Sam boal/Collins Photos<![CDATA[Ikea sales drop as group cuts prices to revive growth]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/06/ikea-sales-drop-as-group-cuts-prices-to-revive-growth/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/06/ikea-sales-drop-as-group-cuts-prices-to-revive-growth/Fri, 06 Nov 2026 13:34:51 +0000Ikea’s sales fell last year, with weak consumer confidence and geopolitical turmoil set to weigh on revenue and profits in 2027 even as the world’s largest furniture retailer cuts prices to try to resuscitate growth.

The group’s retail sales from its 519 global stores fell 2 per cent to €43.8 billion during the year to the end of August as weakness in China and the Middle East outweighed growth in Europe and Latin America, brand owner Inter Ikea said on Friday.

“It was a challenging year for us ... It is possible that this year will be challenging also. The market is not easy,” Jakub Jankowski, chief executive of Inter Ikea, said.

Ikea’s business has been volatile since the Covid-19 pandemic as challenges with supply chains and a weakening backdrop for consumer spending have hit its flat-pack furniture business.

The company responded in September by cutting prices on more than 1,000 products in a €1.2 billion investment designed to boost sales, the second time in the past four years that it has tried such a tactic.

After the pandemic increased shipping costs and pushed prices higher, Ikea cut its average selling price in 2023, a move that initially hurt revenue and halved its profitability.

Jankowski said on Friday that the price cuts of 15-25 per cent on popular products such as Billy bookshelves and Kallax storage units in more than 20 European countries would be part of a push on affordability by the Netherlands-based retailer that would take years.

“Being more affordable is not one year. It is a longer process for us, and then we need to work harder to get the wheels spinning,” he added.

Ikea is coming for your unwanted furniture – and your wallet

Ikea’s sprawling retail empire is controlled by two charitable foundations – based in the Netherlands and Liechtenstein – a structure that allows its managers to disregard short-term trends and some of the pressures a listed company would face and invest heavily if needed.

Ikea opened about 90 smaller stores in its last financial year and Jankowski said he hoped the figure for 2026-2027 would be 50 per cent higher as the retailer seeks to become more accessible to customers.

The chief executive of Inter Ikea, which owns the brand and concept of the retail empire, said more and more customers did not have a car or even a driving licence, making its traditional out-of-town warehouses unappealing. The company is instead opening smaller stores in city centres to gain access to more casual customers.

Jankowski said Ikea needed to improve the seasonality and relevance of its products, as some customers in these city-centre shops visited more frequently and wanted the offering to be refreshed.

The other leg of Ikea’s empire – Ingka, the group that generates 90 per cent of its retail sales – will report results this month. Inter Ikea said its own revenues fell 2 per cent to €25.9 billion while its net profit dropped 7 per cent to €1.4 billion last year. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[The man who lobbies for Ireland’s hotels: ‘A lounge boy today could be general manager in 20 years’ time on €250K’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/06/hotels-lobbying-chief-paul-gallagher-our-lobbying-was-behind-doors-not-on-radio/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/06/hotels-lobbying-chief-paul-gallagher-our-lobbying-was-behind-doors-not-on-radio/Fri, 06 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000“You could be the lounge boy today and be the general manager in 20 years time on a quarter of a million euros,” says Paul Gallagher, chief executive of the Irish Hotels Federation, of a career in hospitality.

Young people with aspirations of networking prominent politicians may be drawn to pursue a career in law, finance or property development. For nearly 50 years, Gallagher has been doing so in hospitality.

From humble beginnings working as a lounge boy in Madigan’s Pub in Donnybrook, Dublin 4 during the late 1970s to now serving as chief executive of the Irish Hotels Federation (IHF), Gallagher has experienced the length and breadth of the industry.

The bulk of his CV accounts for the 27 years he spent as general manager of Buswells Hotel. “A tremendous hotel, considered the third house of the Oireachtas ... years ago, the bell that used to call votes would ring in the hotel, somehow,” he says.

The hotel occupies four townhouses on Molesworth Street and stands at the corner of Kildare Street. Its bar is no more than a hop, skip and a stumble to the gates of Leinster House, where legislation affecting the entirety of the State is enacted.

“You end up becoming familiar with all the TDs,” Gallagher says, as well as their schemes: “a heave on a taoiseach, the formation of new governments”.

“For this job, clearly, if you know politicians – and I would know a lot of them – it’s quite helpful. If I have to advocate, and I do in my role, it is easier if I already know somebody at the other end of the phone.”

Those phone calls are often made from his office near Dartmouth Square in Ranelagh, Dublin 6. On a road that resembles an AI-generated image prompted by the term “quiet, leafy suburb”, the IHF’s headquarters is seamlessly aligned at the end of a row of redbrick townhouses.

In the first floor’s front room stands a long board table, with wooden plaques dispersed between the two sash windows and the names of former IHF presidents carved in gold plating across them. It looks like a small golf club’s diningroom, Gallagher jokes.

His office is in what would have been a secondary bedroom on the same floor, had the building continued to be used as a family home.

“I prepared for this role by meeting with some key individuals in the industry, some currently working in it and some who have retired from it, to get a perspective from them also as to what their sense is of where this business is going in the future and what they anticipate a new CEO doing to make sure that we get there,” Gallagher says.

He called into small hotels in rural areas around the country to speak with managers over coffee to get a sense of what they wanted for him, and met the major hotel chains (Dalata, Winward, Cliste) over lunch to gauge their requirements as well. “They have a different set of needs,” he says.

“The very smallest hotel needs the most support from me, and the larger ones don’t. The small hotels and guest houses would need assistance around legal matters, operational standards, safety authorities, environmental health officers and so on.

“Whilst the bigger guys would say things like the 9 per cent Vat rate on food – I mean, how important was that for them? And if we achieve that, what do we next look for? What are the next big things that make a difference?

“But there was a lot of commonality of what all the groups would say about the sector in general,” he adds.

One such shared struggle has been the price of food and, until July 1st this year, its heightened Vat rate. While last year’s budget dropped the tax from 13.5 per cent to 9 per cent, Gallagher says many hotels who were dependent on food sales were doing so “at a very, very marginal profit”.

“It was Peter Burke who championed that for us,” he continues, referring to the Fine Gael TD who was promoted to Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment just three weeks after Gallagher himself was appointed to his current role.

“A lot of our lobbying was behind doors – we weren’t really on the national radio. Our colleagues at the restaurant association probably were the most vocal, of course their sole business is food and drink while we have a more mixed portfolio of sales.

“I always felt that if we were to lobby one-on-one to try to influence government and ministers, that was probably the best place to do it. It wasn’t really for the radio, there wouldn’t have been a lot of sympathy out there for hotels,” Gallagher says.

“This was about viability, if they didn’t really get that support in the budget, we really felt that there was a real threat to a large sway of small hotels right around Ireland.”

Focused

Throughout the lobbying push, he says he was focused on “a rural, small town hotel” that serves as a “come-all hotel” for its local community in hosting weddings, funerals, communions and other life events. “More of their turnover would be from food and beverage rather than rooms – probably 70 per cent food and beverage and 30 per cent rooms,” Gallagher estimates.

“When I’m thinking about the 9 per cent, I have a hotel in my head. I understand it’s very labour intensive, it’s very hands-on, it’s probably also very exhausting for the owner because food inflation over the last four or five years has become extraordinary. It’s so difficult for them to be able to sit down and say ‘let me look and review my food costs’.”

Gallagher continues: “For us, it was a success in that we got the 9 per cent Vat rate. We had to wait six months after the budget to get it [the policy was announced on October 8th, 2025 but enacted on July 1st, 2026], but Peter Burke and the Government have committed that this will stay for the length of the term of this Government.”

Despite the policy change announced only eight months after taking up his current position, Gallagher makes no secret that the IHF will continue to push for reforms to facilitate the sector doing business.

“We recognise that this support of a 9 per cent Vat rate is enormously important – that doesn’t mean we won’t have asks in the future for other things we want,” he says.

Gallagher notes that the industry “used to enjoy a 9 per cent Vat rate on accommodation as well. We don’t any more, which is a bit of an annoyance.”

Founded in 1937, the IHF is the representative body for more than 900 hotels and guest houses employing some 75,000 workers around the State. It provides members with training programmes for operational upskilling and career development, as well as advice on legal and industrial relations matters.

Perhaps its most high-stakes practice, however, is its lobbying of Government ministers and State agencies to shape tourism policy in favour of the hotel business. But where to direct that advocacy has not always been clearcut.

Over the decades, successive governments have tossed and turned over where to place tourism in a ministerial portfolio. In the mid 1990s, it was lumped together with trade. Then, with sport and recreation. In 2002, the arts were added to the mix, but for one year was replaced with the broader term of culture.

From 2011 to 2020, transport, tourism and sport were somehow strung together as though they had anything to do with one another. Only transport survived the 2020 cabinet reshuffle in getting its own brief. For the next five years the department for tourism, culture, arts, gaeltacht, sport and media fell on Catherine Martin, then of the Green Party.

Last year, Burke took over as Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, with the tourism sector returned to a business department for the first time since the 1980s.

That is “the correct department”, Gallagher says. “We would have advocated that tourism belonged in an employment department. We were in the department of culture and sport and we never really felt that we were taken seriously. So, now we are in a serious department [and] we must make our case in a businesslike manner, and we do.”

Tying in with another subsection of its new department, he says hotels provide incredible employment opportunities, particularly for young people looking to get a foot on the career ladder.

“The sky is the limit, really, and because we do an awful lot of acquired learning, it means everybody has an equal chance to get that top job.

“Think about a resort hotel, it would have about 43 different careers. We employ graduates, we would have accountants, engineers, sustainability managers, spa therapists, chefs – they’re some of the qualified ones where they may have a degree, but everybody else won’t have a degree.

“Everybody else will probably join as a school leaver or in school during the summer holidays working in a bar. We have a great opportunity to bring young people into the business, some of them get the bug and think this is fantastic.”

Gallagher continues: “One in 10 jobs in the Irish economy is in hospitality and, in our business, we employ about 75,000 people in hotels. So we are a very large employer in the hospitality business and, while some people would come in and be on a lower wage, you could be the lounge boy today and be the general manager in 20 years time on a quarter of a million euros, or the head chef on €150,000.”

New hotels

One aspect of the industry that is, perhaps, less straightforward than climbing the company pay scale is constructing the hotel itself. “What we have in Ireland now is a distorted market for the development of new hotel accommodation. It’s all in cities.

“What you notice very quickly is that there is really no new hotel development outside of large urban areas in Ireland – and that isn’t good for tourism. If we are going to grow tourism in regions and in different seasons, we need more hotel stock right across the country.”

“They don’t have to be huge, but we have to have new inventory.”

This is where government can, and Gallagher says should, step in through various means. Accessing “low cost finance” through the Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF), a State agency directed by the National Treasury Management Agency ), is one option.

“I think a dedicated scheme just for hotels would be useful. That’s EU-guaranteed money that government would use through pillar banks to help bring about the creation of investment into new product and new register accommodation.

“There could be a local authority holiday on rates, perhaps for 10 years,” he adds. “Hotels are seen as the golden egg of a rate pair for most local authorities. We are substantial assets and we have a long life ahead of us. Typically a hotel would trade for 30 or 40 years and the local authority would get rates every year for 40 years.

“The cost of construction is a big problem and I’ve seen that right across the economy, not just in tourism but also residential apartments and offices.”

While certain restrictions imposed by the State’s intricate planning process prevent some hotels from refurbishing in the way they would prefer, Gallagher thinks “there have been some moves to address the planning problems, but obviously access or connections to utilities is going to be tricky”.

“That’s why I think hotels in the regions who have potential could put on more rooms, because they’re already on server sites – it’s a bit more difficult on greenfield sites. But there are possibilities of bringing other buildings into tourism that are already sitting there. Repurposing some buildings may be another option,” he says.

With options aplenty and enough ideas to fill the back bedroom of a Georgian townhouse, Gallagher is well placed to lead the industry into the future. The previous two CEOs of the IHF , Tim Fenn and John Power, led the organisation for 14 years each.

If Gallagher is to follow suit, that would bring him to the end of the 2030s. Where does he see the industry then?

“The emphasis for hotels will have to be on great design, great teams operating it, delivering exceptional customer service and giving people that lovely touch point for when they leave a hotel and they think ‘that was a superb experience, I feel refreshed, I feel revitalised’.

“And if they’re from overseas, they go home and become an advocate for Irish tourism – they tell their colleagues ‘God, if you want to go somewhere and just really feel in touch with yourself and with the world, be at ease and have a great experience, I think Ireland and Irish hospitality will deliver that absolutely, hand over fist.”

CV

Name: Paul Gallagher

Job: Chief executive of the Irish Hotels Federation

Age: 62

Lives: In Clonskeagh, Dublin 14

Family: Wife Mariea and two adult daughters (both accountants), Katie and Jessica.

Hobbies: “Rugby is a huge interest of mine, I’m an avid Leinster supporter.”

Something you might expect: “I’m passionate about strengthening our industry through training, developing people and building resilience. I’m pragmatic, frank and direct – sometimes too direct – but always fair, respectful and committed to making a difference.”

Something that might surprise: “I’m a keen competitive sea swimmer. This year, I placed seventh in the men’s Liffey Swim and was mentioned in this newspaper’s report on the race. Not bad for my 20th time competing.”

]]>Nick Bradshaw / The Irish Times<![CDATA[After the SuperValu cyberattack, your smart fridge might be the next target. Here’s what you need to know]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/04/after-the-supervalu-cyberattack-might-your-smart-fridge-be-the-next-target/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/04/after-the-supervalu-cyberattack-might-your-smart-fridge-be-the-next-target/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 12:41:50 +0000Do you feel differently about your smart fridge?

The high-tech home hub allows you to check what food you have in, suggest recipes, and manage the family calendar, should you be able to afford its not-insignificant price tag.

But this week’s cyberattack on Supervalu’s refrigeration systems might be forcing people to re-evaluate its position in their home.

Where could the next attack come from?

You might equally be eyeing your connected coffeemaker warily, worried about what it could be getting up to behind your back. You might consider unplugging the robot vacuum cleaner in case it goes rogue while you are out on the school run.

Jokes aside, the recent spate of attacks on seemingly harmless systems should give us pause for thought. The problem with many of these connected devices is that as soon as you hook anything up to the internet, it opens up a chink in your armour , no matter how hard we try to lock it down.

It is a trade-off that we might not be aware we are making at the time – but it is a common thread in the modern world. For the sake of convenience, we give up a little security. Even with the most diligent company in charge of maintaining the security of the appliances, there is always a risk that something will go wrong. And with the growth in artificial intelligence (AI), the chance of a previously undetected vulnerability rearing its head has suddenly been magnified.

You might wonder why hackers would want to attack a smart home device in the suburbs of Dublin. While we may not have thousands of euro of stock to destroy, or disposable income to pay out ransoms, we do have something that is valuable: our data. And that, as we know, is worth a lot of money in the right – or wrong – hands.

There is also the chance that our smart home devices, unpatched and open to exploitation, may be used as part of an attack on a high-value target.

Stop the bots: Six key steps to securing your smart home

In recent days, a joint operation between public and private partners in the tech industry took down a global botnet that had been hidden in set-top boxes across 200 countries. The botnet, which was placed on the devices before they were sold, surreptitiously used the set-top boxes and internet connections of those unlucky enough to have installed them in their homes.

This is not a new threat. Botnets have been carrying out large-scale attacks for years. One example: in 2016, the Mirai botnet took over up to 560,000 unsecured or weak cameras, printers, and DVR players and knocked out Twitter, Reddit, and Netflix, among others.

So what can we do to protect ourselves? Besides cutting off the connection, that is, although you could argue there is no compelling need to have an oven or coffee maker with an internet connection.

There is some help on the way from the bureaucrats, with various rules regarding security being implemented at an EU level, forcing manufacturers to adopt a secure-by-design approach. But we can’t rely on them to fully shield us from all the risks.

There are ways to protect ourselves: keeping up to date with software releases to patch up any security holes is a given;buying reputable brands rather than settling for cheap, unbranded technology from online marketplaces is another. Changing the default passwords on devices is another tip from security experts.

But we need to be aware of what could be coming down the line.

Then came the ransom demand]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/06/i-could-see-all-my-files-on-my-computer-going-one-by-one-so-i-tried-to-shut-everything-down-but-it-was-too-late/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/06/i-could-see-all-my-files-on-my-computer-going-one-by-one-so-i-tried-to-shut-everything-down-but-it-was-too-late/Fri, 06 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000When small business owner Sarah* returned from a lunch break, everything seemed normal. “Everything happened so fast. I looked for a file, but it was blank. There was nothing behind it,” she says. “I could see all my files on my computer going one by one, so I tried to shut everything down but it was too late.”

Data published by insurance broker Gallagher and the Centre for Economics and Business Research in July found as many as two-thirds of Irish businesses have been hit by at least one cyberattack in the past year. Over a third suffered more than three attacks in the 12-month period.

The costs varied. Thirty per cent said they had incurred legal costs; a similar percentage found their revenue was impacted. More than 20 per cent were fined by the regulator, and almost a third were unable to serve customers in the downtime following the incident.

Cost

So where do businesses turn for help? Ireland has a cluster of big-name cybersecurity companies with their European bases here, such as Trend Micro, Fortinet, Malwarebytes and SolarWinds. But there is also an expanding home-grown sector, providing a launch pad for new enterprises, with companies such as Tines, Siren, UrbanFox and Cytidel going global from Ireland. According to Enterprise Ireland, there are 140 “pure play” cybersecurity companies located here, both Irish and foreign-owned.

In 2024, there were more than 8,100 cybersecurity professionals employed in Ireland. It is an area that seems destined to grow, even as AI takes over some of the load.

AI is also playing an outsized role in stoking fears. When the PHP vulnerability was discovered recently, it was down to AI. The flaw in the scripting language, which is used by a significant number of websites on the internet, had been present for a decade, escaping detection by human reviewers. But AI unearthed it, prompting immediate action from website owners who had to patch systems urgently.

AI-fuelled wave

There are fears of an AI-fuelled wave of sophisticated attacks, and it is colouring views of the technology as a whole. Organisations have a narrow window to defend themselves, the letter warned.

“Organisations increasingly recognise that they cannot prevent every incident. So their attention is shifting toward detection, containing and business continuity,” PwC’s O’Keefe says. “It isn’t a matter of preventing every attack. It is how well you operate through and recover from one.”

European Central Bank (ECB) officials are increasingly using euro zone growth figures that exclude Ireland.

It’s not only the inherent volatility of Irish GDP but the fact that it encompasses business activity carried out in other parts of the world, otherwise known as “contract manufacturing”.

The latter occurs when a third party (typically in a lower-cost jurisdiction) manufactures products on behalf of the domestic company. Because national accounting rules track when goods change ownership rather than when they cross borders, this activity is recorded in our export data.

According to one estimate, contract manufacturing accounts for about a third of Irish GDP. Apple getting third-party operators in China to produce iPhones accounts for a big component.

Hence the bulge in Irish GDP is a total distortion for both Ireland and Europe.

The term leprechaun economics was first coined by US economist Paul Krugman when he applied it to a surge in GDP here in 2015. That year Irish GDP jumped by 26 per cent in one quarter, a rise that was later revised upwards to more than 30 per cent.

The relocation of intellectual property assets to Ireland by big multinationals – including Apple – was the main reason. The knock-on impact of this relocation has been a surge in corporate tax receipts.

In 2014, the State’s corporate tax haul was €4.6 billion. Last year it was just under €35 billion. The Department of Finance predicts it will climb to nearly €45 billion by the end of the decade.

For the past 15 years, Ireland has been smeared as a tax haven, accused of facilitating wholesale corporate tax avoidance. The GDP distortions and turbocharged tax receipts only reinforce the smear.

In reality, it is the new era of monopoly capitalism and the porous US tax system that has landed Ireland in this position.

Apple records higher annual revenue than the GDP of developed nations such as New Zealand, Finland and Portugal, meaning the country that houses its non-US headquarters (Ireland) will inevitably encounter data distortions.

A question remains as to whether the iPhone maker’s tax strategies – and those of its tech peers – were done with the tacit approval of US authorities, which may have been happy to see its brightest corporate stars prosper.

Europe’s headline growth numbers are being parsed by analysts to see the impact of inflation; to see if Germany is finally emerging from a three-year slump; to see if France can grow its way through the current turmoil; but there’s a smudge in the viewfinder, a smudge called Ireland.

]]>Alain Jocard<![CDATA[Europe is again eyeing Ireland’s corporate tax revenue]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/05/europe-is-again-eyeing-irelands-corporate-tax-revenue/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/05/europe-is-again-eyeing-irelands-corporate-tax-revenue/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 10:39:36 +0000The EU is struggling to put together a budget package for the next seven years. This has left European Council president António Costa casting around for new sources of funds that can shore up the budget sums by increasing the bag of tax resources over which the EU has direct control.

The risk for Ireland is that corporate taxes are again in the frame. And as the biggest EU recipient of multinational corporate taxes, the Government could befacing another diplomatic battle to protect Irish revenues.

Costa has been looking at options that would funnel some tax revenues away from countries where multinationals now pay their tax – including Ireland – into the central EU pot.

In focus, in particular, are the payments resulting from the recent OECD corporate tax reform plan, which has provided yet another boost to Irish coffers. It is part of an old story of Europe eyeing Irish corporate tax receipts, but the recent growth in revenues has left Ireland particularly exposed.

The picture is still a little muddy as Costa, who is charged with seeking a compromise on the budget, tries to put together a plan to satisfy demands from the “frugal” northern countries – led by Germany – who are seeking lower national contributions and a cut to the proposed size of the budget – and eastern and southern states fighting to protect the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and cohesion funding.

But the issue may be raised at next week’s informal summit of EU leaders in Dublin, in advance of what is meant to be a crunch summit in Brussels at the end of the month.

The backdrop – Costa’s coffers

EU member states are trying to agree a budget – or so-called multiannual financial framework – to cover the years from 2028 to 2034.

Ireland, as EU president, had put forward a proposal for an 8 per cent cut in the original €1.76 trillion proposal (in 2025 prices) by the European Commission. But this was criticised by all sides, leading Taoiseach Micheál Martin to observe it was an exercise in trying to “reconcile the irreconcilable”.

Ireland’s EU presidency proposes budget cut of €141bn for the bloc

The job of seeking compromise now passes to Costa, who has to try to bang heads together among EU leaders.

As part of this, he is looking for new sources of what are called “own resources”, which is funding that goes directly to Brussels rather than forming part of annual contributions from member states.

The proposal – target companies

To try to bridge the gap between the desire of the “frugal” countries to contribute less and the need for a bigger EU centralised budget, there has been a range of proposals to raise additional taxes that would go directly to Brussels, or divert existing taxes in their direction.

The European Parliament, for example, has proposed a range of measures, including a new gambling levy and a special tax on cryptocurrency.

And the idea of a levy on the revenues of companies with sales of more than €100 million has been circulating in the discussions, though it is strongly opposed by Germany.

To try to break the deadlock, there has been a series of reports – including in Politico and a number of special online tax services – that Costa’s team are looking at diverting some of the additional funding resulting from the OECD tax deal to the central EU budget.

Sources in Dublin confirm this has been floated, but say a firm proposal has not yet been made. But, with strong French support, it looks likely to emerge in discussions in the next few weeks on the new budget.

The exposure – Ireland’s extra revenue

Ireland has done remarkably well over the past decade as a result of two OECD corporate tax deals.

The initial 2015 agreement led companies to change their tax planning in a way where more funds fell to be taxed in Ireland. (This happened largely because many relocated intellectual property assets from offshore havens to Ireland).

The latest OECD deal – agreed in 2021 – had been expected to be a mixed bag for Ireland.

The State stood to lose from a part of the deal that would have moved some of the taxing rights on corporate profits away from countries such as Ireland – where they have corporate headquarters – to bigger European countries where digital multinationals did much of their business.

In the end,this part of the OECD deal has fallen through.

The second part of the OECD deal set a minimum rate of 15 per cent for tax on profits of big multinationals. Although this has only been partially implemented – the US has important exemptions – the 15 per cent rate was mandated as a minimum in the EU.

Ireland thus has a basic 12.5 per cent corporate profits tax and an additional 2.5 per cent charge on the biggest companies. It is this additional money that Costa appears most likely to have his eye on.

The mechanics – as yet uncertain

Various sources say Costa is testing the waters at EU capitals and so the shape of what he may propose is unclear.

However, he has clear French support for a move on corporate tax, and this will put Ireland firmly in the frame. The amount Ireland will collect as a result of the 2.5 per cent charge is significant – the Fiscal Council has said it could amount to some €5 billion, or about 13 per cent of total expected corporate tax revenues this year.

Former OECD tax head Pascal Saint-Amans told Politico the sense of the new plan was that multinational activity in Ireland was about managing their business in EU markets.

And so it could make sense to redistribute tax in this way – in effect, it would have a similar impact to the part of the 2021 OECD plan that has never gone ahead to redistribute some taxing rights away from countries such as Ireland.

The odds – still unclear

Ireland, along with other EU member states, has fought off several previous proposals to effectively pool elements of corporate tax revenues into a central EU budget.

Those with greyer hairs may recall the alphabet soup that was the proposal for the common corporate tax base (CCTB), which later evolved into the common consolidated corporate tax base (CCCTB). These circulated for more than a decade before being formally withdrawn in 2023.

Tax has primarily been a national competence in the EU – countries decide what to tax and by how much. And, ultimately, countries have a veto on tax issues, and the EU budget plan must be agreed by all 27 member states.

But a new focus on corporate tax would be uncomfortable for Ireland, forcing the Government to use up political capital resisting any plan and again underlining the extraordinary bounty flowing into the Irish exchequer.

Other EU countries argue that some of this is at their expense.

Donald Trump has argued likewise. And a newly energised US Congress may again start probing where and how big American companies pay their taxes.

Changes in the fortunes or plans of the big multinationals who pay tax here remain a big risk in the years ahead. But so do politics in the US and around Europe.

Ireland’s revenues are now so enormous that they are attracting way more international attention than the Government would like.

]]><![CDATA[Hybrid working isn’t the problem, it is how to manage it]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/05/the-pitfalls-of-hybrid-working-when-managers-are-left-on-their-own-to-deal-with-staff/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/05/the-pitfalls-of-hybrid-working-when-managers-are-left-on-their-own-to-deal-with-staff/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 05:49:00 +0000

Break-up songs like Prince’s Nothing Compares 2 U (a smash for Sinéad O’Connor), Dolly Parton’s I Will Always Love You (ditto Whitney Houston) and Miley Cyrus’s Flowers have long been popular culture staples. But who knew that breaking up with full-time office work would be so agonising for business culture – and especially for the line managers left to negotiate the wreckage?

Workplace tension continues between leaders who demand a return to the office and workers who want flexibility to help defray the cost of living, and to better cope with commuting times and care commitments.

The whole debate about whether or not hybrid, or remote, is actually workable, is the wrong question to ask, says Tatiana Andreeva, professor in organisational behaviour at Trinity Business School, who studies hybrid work and collaboration.

Instead, how can employers embrace hybrid in a way that creates sustainable value for the business, employees and society?

More than a third of the labour force now works either a hybrid arrangement or a fully remote one – accounting for an estimated 530,000 people – according to a forthcoming report from the National Economic and Social Council.

In 2026, about 35 per cent of the labour force worked from home either usually or sometimes, whereas before the Covid-19 pandemic, only about 14 per cent of employees worked from home to some extent.

Even though this is a relatively new way of working, those managing these arrangements may be largely left on their own – without training, support or even simple tips for communicating with hybrid workers.

New report on impact of hybrid working in Ireland to deliver its findings

The problem isn’t with remote work itself, but in how it’s managed, says Andreeva. “We can make it work if the people who are actually managing it on a daily basis – line managers – are better prepared. If we fix this group, the spillover effects for the organisation will be amazing.”

The resources already exist to make this possible too, she says. Grow Remote, for example, is a government-supported social enterprise that helps employers, managers and remote workers thrive through online training, resources and community connections.

New ways of working

In the past decade, line managers have taken on more HR responsibilities (onboarding, interviews, appraisals), but the power to manage hybrid work policies and team-oriented ways of working has been taken from them. Andreeva, Dr Jordi Trullen (ESADE Business School) and Jim Copeland (Maynooth University) interviewed 36 line managers across 32 organisations to understand their shifting responsibilities, their reaction to hybrid work policies and the obstacles they face.

Most of these qualitative in-depth interviews were with line managers working in US multinationals in Ireland. The study found that hybrid policies were mostly set centrally without consulting line managers, who then had to adapt them informally with little training or information on how to manage hybrid teams.

The interviews revealed some worrying trends. Line managers reported that their organisations gave them no say on remote policies, no insights into remote workers’ schedules, and no training or support on how to manage them. They’re flying blind while being expected to deliver the same or better levels of productivity.

Although line managers are expected to support or reinforce compliance, they were typically not given access to live or recent individual-level attendance data or monitoring tools. This limited their ability to intervene effectively or anticipate issues within the team.

Many managers also expressed concerns over the official reasons provided for returning to the office, as these were often not convincing. This, and getting little or no notice on policy-change announcements, limited managers’ ability to persuade their subordinates to follow the policy.

Managers identified persistent challenges with hybrid work co-ordination. Yet few received any structured training or support on how to manage these dynamics.

“The line managers feel that there’s an assumption in the organisation that if you were a manager during Covid that you know how to do it, and that is why training doesn’t come up,” says Andreeva.

Hybrid teams require complex co-ordination due to staggered schedules and individual exceptions. But, instead of reporting these difficulties to leadership, line managers operated from a place of fear, and often withheld details of these operational challenges to prevent a full return to working from the office for everyone.

Managing hybrid

Andreeva has been working on a book chapter with Prof N Sharon Hill of George Washington University School of Business to help address the information deficit in understanding hybrid work dynamics and best practices. Hill developed the CAARE framework (configuration, autonomy-alignment, relationships, equity) in 2023 and her work was published in MIT Sloan Management Review.

‘One of the managers in our study added 15 minutes with no work-related agenda to daily team meetups to allow the team to connect casually, compensating for lost in-person informal lunchtime chats’

Tatiana Andreeva, Trinity Business School

The CAARE framework helps organisations and managers think through and implement remote and hybrid ways of working with their team.

Configuration

Remote and hybrid teams have a different shape and rhythm compared to teams that work entirely from the office. Configuration is a strategic way to establish agreements on how members will work together.

What’s the real reason your boss wants you back in the office?

“Team agreements may, for example, specify core hours of availability, expected response times for communications, and procedures for providing updates on work status,” says Hill.

Atlassian and Dropbox designed tool kits for managers to help them co-develop these charters with their teams. Managers are encouraged to review these charters regularly with teams as employee preferences and situations may change.

Autonomy and alignment

To be effective, there needs to be a balance between individual autonomy and team alignment. Grow Remote found that some companies do this in a quick and clever way that works best for their team.

NearForm trained their managers to introduce asynchronous daily stand-ups. Each morning, team members answer four questions in Slack (How are you feeling? What have you done? What will you do today? Do you need help?). The manager scans responses for blockers instead of holding a daily call. The regularity of these check-ins ensures alignment, while also giving employees autonomy in where and when they work.

Relationships

“One of the managers in our study added 15 minutes with no work-related agenda to daily team meetups to allow the team to connect casually, compensating for lost in-person informal lunchtime chats; another added a five-minute fun fact slot in weekly meetings, inviting one of the team members to share something that you wouldn’t know about them,” Andreeva says.

In both cases, the manager’s aim was to provide space for informal connection and relationship-building.

Spotify developed “Talk it Through” training for their managers, as a part of their “Heart & Soul” mental health strategy. This training coached managers to include wellbeing check-ins in every one-to-one meeting with employees, to identify signs that colleagues might be struggling, and signpost appropriate support.

Equity

Managers can use several strategies to ensure they’re not unduly rewarding those they see in person more regularly, or proximity bias.

Redesigning work and decision-making processes are key. “For example, a transparent, clear system to monitor and evaluate performance that focuses on results-based metrics, discussed in relation to the autonomy-alignment component, helps mitigate bias in performance appraisal and rewards.”

The trust-building strategies discussed for the relationship component and team communication charters can also help to mitigate the perception that employees who are out of sight are not working as hard as those on-site.

To help managers make fair decisions, Spotify compares promotion rates and pay increases between employees each compensation cycle, and flags outliers, if any.

Margaret E Ward is chief executive of Clear Eye, a leadership consultancy. margaret@cleareye.ie

Sales of existing homes, which represent most of the market, were, however, down by 2.2 per cent.

But overall revenues at the division, which includes Paddy Power, Betfair and Sky Bet, increased 4 per cent to $889 million, boosted by strong growth in online casino games.

Last month Flutter confirmed it would cut 240 jobs at its Dublin head office from a total of 1,400 across the Irish and UK business to counter increased British betting tax.

Globally, Flutter will pause a share buyback programme to ​prioritise investment, cutting debt and cost savings, its new chief executive, Dan Taylor, said on Wednesday, after the company reduced its profit forecast for a fifth successive quarter.

Flutter, the world’s largest online gaming company, has been forced to lower its profit expectations ​as higher regulatory costs, increased competition and strategy missteps slowed previously booming US growth.

Taylor, who took charge in October, ⁠said his four immediate priorities would be to build on the company’s US leadership position, capture ‌opportunities ‌in ​the nascent prediction market sector, increase value from its non-US portfolio and simplify the company’s operating model.

Flutter shares were 1.9 per cent lower in premarket ⁠trading in New York.

“Delivering against those priorities ​will require faster execution, tough decisions and disciplined ​investment,” Taylor said in a statement.

He told Reuters he was confident of deleveraging ‌the company’s balance sheet over the next ​12 to 18 months towards its target leverage range of two to 2.5 times earnings.

The ⁠company’s leverage ratio has risen to ⁠4.6 times earnings from ​2.2 18 months ago, before acquisitions in the US, Italy and Brazil.

Flutter, whose business includes US sports betting market leader FanDuel, also has a plan announced in August to save $500 million (€439.45 million) by 2029.

Just over two years ago, when Flutter promised up to $5 billion to shareholders, it had expected the US betting boom to more than double its core profit to $5 billion by 2027.

By the end of June, the buyback had returned $1.37 ‌billion to shareholders.

Flutter is now ⁠forecasting a 7 per cent fall in full-year core profit to $2.5 billion from the $2.66 billion flagged in August and $2.59 billion expected by analysts. The latest cut was due to ‌adverse sports results and a sports betting ban in Brazil.

Taylor said, however, that the underlying performance in the US was ahead of expectations. – Additional reporting: Reuters

]]>Spencer Platt

A collection of artefacts associated with the Vandals and dating back almost 2,000 years has been handed anonymously to a museum in eastern Poland.

The collection includes a sword, spear and javelin heads, shield components and spurs. Museum staff do not know who originally discovered the burial or exactly where it was located, leaving the circumstances of the find largely a mystery.

The Father Stanisław Staszic Museum in Hrubieszów announced in a Facebook post that the objects had been passed to them anonymously through an intermediary.

The items are in poor condition and will undergo urgent conservation, with the iron components of the weapons particularly vulnerable after centuries in the ground.

They were also exposed to high temperatures during a burial practice in which the deceased was burned along with their personal belongings. The museum says that the nature of the objects indicates that their owner held a high social position.

The most notable object is a sword preserved in three pieces, reflecting the Vandal practice of deliberately breaking or bending weapons and other grave artefacts as part of funeral rituals. The collection also contains two spearheads, both broken.

Other items include a shield boss with a spike, a shield grip, a fragment of a knife, a belt buckle and two spurs. Fragments of a bone comb and a bronze fibula, used to fasten a cloak, were also recovered.

 

The circumstances surrounding the discovery and recovery of the objects remain unknown, but the museum says that, according to the information it has received, the burial site was discovered in an agricultural field several years ago in the municipality of Werbkowice.

“We intend to verify the exact location through archaeological excavations, most likely next summer,” they added. “Based on the information we have gathered, there are strong indications that there may be more similar burials in the area that have been disturbed by agricultural work.”

The opportunity to recover the objects and transfer them to an appropriate institution arose only recently. The museum said that a local metal detectorist played a key role in arranging the transfer, acting as an intermediary in securing the artefacts.

The recovery of the artefacts follows another recent archaeological discovery in the same region. In August, the museum announced that a metal boss from a warrior’s shield dating to the second century was found at a scrap metal yard near Hrubieszów.

The Vandals were an ancient Germanic people believed to have reached the territories of present-day Poland around the 3rd or 2nd century BC.

They lived in the region for several centuries and are generally associated by researchers with the Przeworsk culture, which flourished across parts of present-day Poland during the Iron Age and Roman period.

Around the turn of the 4th and 5th centuries AD, amid the expansion of the Huns, they left Central Europe and moved westwards into the declining Roman Empire. As the Vandals left Central Europe, the Slavic population gradually moved into the region over the following centuries.

]]> Polish deputy PM proposes “constitutional reset” to resolve crisis around top court https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/06/polish-deputy-pm-proposes-constitutional-reset-to-resolve-crisis-around-top-court/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 08:29:30 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106439

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

The leader of one of the parties in Poland’s ruling coalition has put forward plans for a “constitutional reset” that he hopes can resolve the crisis around the country’s top court.

The proposal, presented on Thursday by deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, head of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), would remove all current judges on the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) and allow new judges to be chosen only with the approval of 60% of members of parliament and the president.

To take effect, the measure would require amending Poland’s constitution, something that has happened only twice since the document was adopted in 1997 and which also requires a three-fifths majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament.

Deeskalacja sytuacji wokół Trybunału Konstytucyjnego jest konieczna aby przywrócić obywatelom niezależny sąd konstytucyjny. Apelują o to przedstawiciele organizacji społecznych, Rada Przedsiębiorców, Naczelna Rada Adwokacka, Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka i Episkopat Polski.… pic.twitter.com/3RCsKRlSiM

— Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) November 5, 2026

Kosiniak-Kamysz’s announcement comes amid the fallout from events last Friday, when eight new judges elected to the TK this year by the government’s majority in parliament seized control of the court.

They announced that its chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, had been suspended for failing to fulfil his duties, including by refusing to allow most of those judges to take up their seats on the court.

Święczkowski denounced the takeover as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the tribunal’s remaining six judges, who, like him, were appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, which brought the TK under its political influence when it ruled from 2015 to 2023.

 

As well as pitting judges aligned with the national-conservative PiS, which is now the main opposition party, and the current more liberal government against one another, the dispute also centres around the legitimacy of certain judges.

The government points to the fact that PiS unlawfully appointed three judges to the TK in 2015. As a result, both Polish and European courts have found the tribunal in its current form to be illegitimate.

Meanwhile, Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of the eight judges appointed by the government’s parliamentary majority this year, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications.

The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”

But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026

The standoff has led some NGOs and experts to call for a “constitutional reset”, whereby the TK would be reformed to make the process of selecting judges more consensual and less politicised.

Indeed, the current government even proposed legislation in 2024 that would have required new TK judges to be approved by a three-fifths parliamentary majority. The plans would also have removed unlawfully appointed judges from the PiS era and annulled rulings they were involved in.

That prompted the president at the time, Andrzej Duda, who was also aligned with PiS, to send the bills to the TK, which was still packed with PiS-era judges, for assessment. The tribunal rejected them as unconstitutional the following year.

Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025

Now, Kosiniak-Kamysz has proposed new legislation intended to resolve the issue. His solution would create a mechanism under which parliament, at the request of the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS), could declare the TK “permanently incapable of performing its duties”.

Such a status could only be declared with the support of a three-fifths majority of both houses of parliament – the Sejm and the Senate – combined. It would have to come at the request of the KRS because, says Kosiniak-Kamysz, the terms of judges cannot be shortened without the participation of other judges.

The process of appointing new TK judges would involve the speaker of the Sejm proposing candidates after obtaining the opinions of the heads of the Supreme Court and the Supreme Administrative Court – which are separate from the TK – as well as professional bodies representing legal professions.

The candidates proposed by the speaker would also have to receive the prior consent of the president. For a new TK judge to be approved, they would have to receive the support of three fifths of members of the Sejm and Senate combined.

💬 336 głosów posłów i senatorów. To wykracza poza większość jakąkolwiek koalicyjną dzisiaj sformułowaną – @KosiniakKamysz w Warszawie pic.twitter.com/iLUuM5TSxQ

— 🍀 PSL (@nowePSL) November 5, 2026

Whereas TK judges currently all serve nine-year terms, under Kosiniak-Kamysz’s proposal, five of the judges would serve three-year terms, five of them six-year terms, and the final five would serve for nine years.

Unlike now, the new judges would not have to swear their oath before the president, but before parliament.

Kosiniak-Kamysz emphasised, however, that the measure was intended as a “one-time” emergency tool. “Later, we will return to the method of selecting judges described today in the constitution, or a better one, if there is a majority for it.”

The current method of choosing new TK judges requires only the support of a majority in the Sejm. However, judges must then swear an oath “before the president”, an issue that has become a bone of contention this year.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

Kosiniak-Kamysz’s plans would require changes to Poland’s constitution, which specifies the manner in which TK judges are chosen. A constitutional amendment requires the support of a three-fifths majority in the Sejm and a simple majority in the Senate. It does not need presidential approval.

PSL itself has only 28 members of the 460-seat Sejm and four senators. Kosiniak-Kamysz acknowledged that “it won’t be an easy road” to win the necessary support for his idea.

He appealed not only to his fellow ruling parties, but also to opposition groups that have expressed their backing for a constitutional reset, such as the centre-right Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) and far-right Confederation (Konfederacja).

On Thursday evening, one of Confederation’s leaders, Sławomir Mentzen, shared a photo of himself meeting Kosiniak-Kamysz, with the caption: “It’s going in the right direction”.

Idzie ku dobremu. pic.twitter.com/zk6lZpi3DL

— Sławomir Mentzen (@SlawomirMentzen) November 5, 2026

However, some voices within the ruling coalition expressed scepticism towards the idea. Borys Budka, a former leader of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) – which is the largest governing party – said it was “hard to imagine changing the constitution alongside someone like PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński”.

Tomasz Trela of The Left (Lewica) likewise said that, “if anyone thinks The Left will change the constitution arm in arm with PiS, they’re mistaken”, reports Polsat News.

]]> Chinese fashion platform Shein to invest €500 million in Polish logistics hub https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/05/chinese-fashion-platform-shein-to-invest-e500-million-in-polish-logistics-hub/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 13:10:48 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106412

Chinese fast fashion platform Shein has announced a €500 million (2.2 billion zloty) investment to expand its logistics centre in Poland, a move it says will create around 2,000 new jobs by the end of this year.

The announcement comes amid growing controversy over the impact of Chinese e-commerce platforms on European businesses and follows a recent decision by the European Union to introduce a special fee on low-value parcels sent from outside the EU and European Free Trade Area.

SHEIN investește 500 mil. euro în Polonia. Extinde hub-ul logistic europeanhttps://t.co/WNbib4dFta pic.twitter.com/KiI1AB4wFM

— Cristi Dorombach (@piticu21) November 4, 2026

The investment will expand Shein’s existing logistics facility in Magnice, near the city of Wrocław in southwestern Poland, which has been operating since 2022.

The expansion will bring total employment at the site to around 10,000 by creating 2,000 jobs in logistics, supply chain management, technology and warehouse operations, according to local news service Wroclaw.pl. The facility will also host 6,500 autonomous robots for sorting items.

Shein says that the move will help it cut delivery times in Europe, allowing some orders to arrive within 48 hours.

“This investment in Poland clearly demonstrates our commitment and belief in the potential of the European market,” said Leonard Lin, the firm’s global head of public affairs.

“Poland has become one of the pillars of our operations in Europe,” he added. “This latest investment is a testament to our confidence in the country’s potential, the competencies of its workforce, and its business environment.”

 

The expansion comes as Shein faces a tougher trading environment in Europe. Its sales in the region fell by 13.9% year-on-year to $3.77 billion in the second quarter, while net profit dropped by 67%.

The decline comes as the EU steps up efforts to curb the influx of low-cost imports from Chinese platforms such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress, which European retailers say pose unfair competition.

In July, the bloc introduced a €3 fee on parcels worth less than €150. From 1 November, a further €2 handling fee was added to all imported parcels, regardless of their value, to cover customs processing costs.

China overtook Germany to become Poland’s biggest source of imports for the first time in July, ending a period of around 35 years in which Germany had consistently held top spot https://t.co/U6rQwfEJ7I

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 16, 2026

Shein has also faced accusations of labour-law violations at its facilities in China, including concerns that it may use cotton produced through forced labour.

The company disputes many of the allegations, saying that it prohibits forced and child labour and regularly inspects working conditions at its suppliers.

China is an increasingly important trading partner in Poland. In July, it overtook Germany to become Poland’s largest source of imports for the first time, driven by rising purchases of cars, computer hardware and consumer goods.

]]> Six detained in Poland on suspicion of exporting military components to Russia https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/05/six-detained-in-poland-on-suspicion-of-exporting-military-components-to-russia/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 11:36:51 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106418

Poland has detained and charged six people – five Poles and one Russian – suspected of running an operation to illegally supply Russia with military components. Investigators say that over 2 million zloty (€450,000) worth of equipment was smuggled into the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.

The arrests, which took place on 21 October and 2 November, were announced on Thursday morning by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) and National Prosecutor’s Office.

🚨 ROSYJSKI WYWIAD. PRZEMYT CZĘŚCI DO PRODUKCJI UZBROJENIA. 6 ZATRZYMANYCH.@ABW_GOV_PL rozbiła grupę podejrzaną o działalność na rzecz rosyjskich służb specjalnych.

🔴6⃣ osób zatrzymanych,
🔴2⃣1⃣przeszukanych lokalizacji,
🔴 4⃣osoby z zarzutami szpiegostwa – wszystkie trafiły… pic.twitter.com/L90n3rf5rY

— ABW (@ABW_GOV_PL) November 5, 2026

Prosecutors report that all six suspects have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group that sought to export weapon components from Poland to Russia in violation of a ban on such trade.

Four of the suspects have also been charged under Poland’s espionage law, accused of acting on behalf of Russian intelligence in return for financial benefits. Those four individuals have been placed in pretrial detention. The other two were released with preventative measures put in place.

The ABW says that the criminal group “illegally supplied Russia with significant quantities of military components, including those used in the production of ammunition and weapons systems”.

“This type of activity may lead to the strengthening of the Russian arms industry and the military capabilities of the Russian Federation, and thus pose a serious threat to Poland’s security and interests,” wrote the agency.

 

Prosecutors say that the group operated at least between June 2023 and December 2025 in Poland, Lithuania and Russia. Members were responsible for procuring goods and transporting them to Kaliningrad, which borders Poland and Lithuania.

“Vehicles equipped with hidden compartments were used to transport the goods,” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The suspects repeatedly crossed the Polish-Russian border, and some of the transports were intercepted by Polish border guards.”

Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, revealed that the six suspects include five Polish citizens, aged 25 to 52, and one Russian woman, aged 37.

Onet, a leading news website, reports, based on unnamed sources, that the Russian citizen acted as a liaison between the group and the foreign intelligence agency behind the operation.

Funkcjonariusze @ABW_GOV_PL zatrzymali 6 osób podejrzanych o udział w zorganizowanej grupie przestępczej działającej przeciwko Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej. Wśród zatrzymanych jest pięciu Polaków w wieku od 25 do 52 lat i 37-letnia Rosjanka.
🛑 Sąd – pod zarzutem szpiegostwa -…

— Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 5, 2026

Poland has seen a huge rise in espionage cases in recent years. The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined.

Last month, a Polish man was jailed for five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of an airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland.

In July, a Russian married couple with refugee status in Poland were convicted of working as spies on behalf of Moscow. In October, a member of Poland’s military reserve, who holds both Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, was detained on suspicion of espionage.

]]> Polish far-right leader Braun to face second trial https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/05/polish-far-right-leader-braun-to-face-second-trial/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 09:45:21 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106399

Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun will again stand trial, after prosecutors filed an indictment against him for a series of anti-Ukrainian, anti-Jewish, anti-LGBT and anti-EU acts committed during his presidential election campaign last year.

Braun is already separately on trial for a number of other alleged crimes, including an attack on a Jewish religious ceremony in parliament. He is also facing further charges for a range of other alleged offences.

Grzegorz Braun stanie przed sądem. Prokuratura Okręgowa w Warszawie skierowała dziś akt oskarżenia za zuchwałą kradzież flag Ukrainy w Białej Podlaskiej i Unii Europejskiej w Katowicach, zniszczenie wystawy LGBT w Sejmie oraz zniesławienie organizatorów akcji Żonkile i Muzeum…

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 4, 2026

On Wednesday, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw announced that it had indicted Braun for four alleged crimes. It was able to do so after the European Parliament, where Braun sits as an MEP, stripped him of immunity earlier this year.

One of the charges, for criminal defamation, stems from Braun’s claim, during a televised presidential debate in April last year, that the yellow paper daffodils distributed each year in Warsaw to mark the anniversary of the 1943 Jewish Ghetto Uprising against German Nazi rule are “symbols of shame”.

Prosecutors say that Braun’s words were “extremely xenophobic, manipulative and aggressive”, and that they defamed the organisers of the daffodil campaign, in particular the POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews in Warsaw.

During the same debate, Braun also warned about the “Judaisation” of Poland, saying that “Jews have far too much say in Polish affairs”. That prompted protests by some of his opponents, one of whom filed a notification to prosecutors.

Poland had the second-highest household electricity prices in the European Union in the first half of 2026 after adjusting for differences in the cost of living, new Eurostat data show. Prices in Poland were also among the fastest-rising in the bloc.

Poland’s relatively high electricity costs reflect the country’s continued reliance on coal, which results in EU charges for carbon emissions, and its taxes and levies, which make up the largest share of household electricity bills anywhere in the EU.

In nominal terms, Polish households paid €29.99 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh) for electricity in the first half of 2026. This was the seventh-highest price among the EU’s 27 member states and above the bloc-wide average of €28.32.

Ireland (€38.71 per 100 kWh) had the highest prices, followed by Germany (€36.18) and Belgium (€35.75). The lowest costs were recorded in Hungary (€11.39), Malta (€12.68) and Bulgaria (€13.41).

However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in the cost of living, Poland ranked second in the EU, at 41.12 PPS per 100 kWh.

Only Romania had higher prices, at 46.89 PPS. The lowest prices when measured in PPS were recorded in Malta (13.75), Hungary (14.7) and Luxembourg (15.47).

Poland’s electricity prices, in PPS terms, rose by 10.7% compared with the second half of 2025, which was the second-biggest increase in the EU after Finland. They were also up 17.6% compared to the first half of 2025, the fourth-largest rise in the bloc.

 

One reason why electricity prices in Poland remain high is the country’s continued reliance on coal, which last year generated just over half of power, by far the highest proportion in the EU.

Almost all coal used in Polish power plants is mined domestically and is among the most expensive in the world to extract. Additionally, burning it also produces high carbon emissions, which power generators must pay for under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS).

These costs contribute to the high taxes and levies included in household electricity bills, which accounted for 39% of the final price in Poland in the first half of 2026. This was the highest share in the EU, ahead of Germany (23.6%) and well above the bloc-wide average of 18.6%.

“In Poland, only one-third of our electricity generation is carbon-free. We have to pay for the rest – often dearly,” noted Polish energy journalist Jakub Wiech, commenting on the data.

Without taxes and levies, the nominal price of electricity in Poland would have been just under €16 per 100 kWh, below the EU average of €20.27.

However, Bartłomiej Orzeł of the Project Tempo think tank notes that electricity prices in Poland would, in fact, be even higher were it not for the huge state subsidies paid to support the unprofitable coal mining sector, which amount to billions of zloty a year but also shield end consumers from the full cost of extracting coal.

He told news website Interia that mines actually sell coal to power stations at a price below the cost of extraction.

Warzecha, who is primarily associated with right-wing weekly Do Rzeczy, says he was told that the decision had been made for “security reasons”.

The head of the Mieroszewski Centre, Łukasz Adamski, revealed that the list of journalists attending the tour had been agreed between the two organisers and forwarded to the relevant Ukrainian state authorities, who previously raised no objection.

However, on Monday afternoon, Warzecha announced on social media that he had been held at the Ukrainian border and told to wait in a room. The journalist remained there for over seven hours before being informed that he was banned from entering Ukraine for three years.

Adamski commented that, while he “recognises Ukraine’s sovereign right to decide whom to grant entry…restricting journalists’ work on state security grounds…creates fertile ground for unfriendly commentary”.

At the time of writing, there had been no comment from the SBU regarding its decision to issue an entry ban against Warzecha.

 

In his journalistic work, Warzecha has at times been critical of Ukraine, for example over its honouring of historical nationalist figures, and has called for a reduction in social benefits given to Ukrainian refugees in Poland. However, those views are within the Polish mainstream.

Warzecha has also voiced support for Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. In February 2023, on the first anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion, he expressed satisfaction that Ukraine defended itself so effectively.

However, Do Rzeczy, with which Warzecha has been associated for around a decade, has taken a tougher position on Ukraine. In 2024, its front cover warned of the “Ukrainisation of Poland”, a phrase often used by the far right to warn against the growing presence and influence of Ukrainians.

Adamski said that the visit to Ukraine had been arranged specifically with the aim of “representing diverse editorial perspectives”. The Mieroszewski Centre last month arranged a similar visit for Ukrainian journalists to Poland.
