Poland’s ambassador to the United Nations, Krzysztof Szczerski, has resigned, becoming the third Polish ambassador to do so since a government-backed move by a group of judges to take control of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw.

All three of the departing ambassadors were previously aides or advisers to former President Andrzej Duda, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. They have criticised the attempt to oust the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed to the court under PiS.

Following the resignations of Poland’s Ambassadors to China and Romania, Prof. Krzysztof Szczerski, Poland’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, has also submitted his resignation.

All three are senior state officials and experienced diplomats who have served at the…

— Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) November 2, 2026

On Monday afternoon, foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór announced that Szczerski had “submitted a request to shorten his diplomatic mission at the UN”, where he has served as ambassador since 2021.

Szczerski’s resignation followed those of Jakub Kumoch, Poland’s ambassador to China, and Paweł Soloch, the Polish envoy to Romania, who quit their posts on Friday and Saturday, respectively.

While Szczerski has not yet commented on the reasons for his departure, Kumoch and Soloch made clear that their decisions were motivated by Friday’s move to suspend Święczkowski from the TK.

Soloch wrote that the “attempt to unlawfully take over the Constitutional Tribunal” left him with “no possibility of continuing to serve as ambassador”. Kumoch said his decision was a “matter of conscience”, as “there are certain things I cannot explain abroad without losing face, and I have no intention of speaking ill of Poland”.

There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice.

Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026

Szczerski previously served as a member of the European Parliament for PIS. In 2015, he joined the chancellery of PiS-aligned President Duda, later becoming the head of his cabinet and then head of his International Policy Bureau.

Kumoch was a member of Duda’s National Development Council, an advisory body to the president, before serving as ambassador to Switzerland, Turkey, and then China. Soloch was the head of Duda’s National Security Bureau from 2015 to 2022.

On Monday, after Szczerski’s resignation, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski suggested that the three ambassadors had quit at the urging of the current president, Karol Nawrocki, who is also aligned with PiS.

Sikorski sardonically suggested that, in contrast to Polish ambassadors who quit in 1981 over the imposition of martial law despite “risking vengeance from the communist regime”, the newly resigned trio “will surely be handsomely rewarded for their heroic deeds”.

 

The developments are part of a much broader fallout from the crisis around the TK, which began on Friday evening when large numbers of riot police appeared outside the court.

It soon transpired that a group of eight judges appointed by parliament to the TK this year – but five of whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in – had entered the court and declared that Święczkowski had been suspended from his position for failing to fulfil his duties.

Święczkowski, who before becoming a TK judge previously served as a member of the former PiS government, declared their actions unlawful and an attempted “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the six other justices appointed when PiS was in government.

Święczkowski has also been supported by Nawrocki, who dramatically entered the court in the early hours of Saturday morning, clashing physically and verbally with the self-proclaimed acting head of the court, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court.

The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG

The developments have created an unprecedented situation at the TK. However, the court has been in crisis since 2015, when Duda and the then-PiS government – which came to power that year – unlawfully rejected three judges appointed by the former parliament and replaced them with three of their own.

The current government, a broad coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, does not recognise the TK due to those illegitimate judges and has ignored its rulings since replacing PiS in power in December 2023.

This year, Tusk’s coalition began appointing judges to fill vacancies on the court. It has condemned Nawrocki and Święczkowski for refusing to accept those judges, saying that their actions are unlawful.

Given those circumstances, Tusk and his government have argued that tough action is necessary to restore the legitimacy of the TK. On Saturday evening, Tusk gave an address to the nation declaring that there can be “no compromise” over the rule of law.

"On some issues, there can be no compromise," declared Prime Minister @donaldtusk in an address to the nation on the crisis around the constitutional court.

However, a number of legal experts – including many who were highly critical of PiS’s policies towards the TK and other courts – have expressed doubts over the manner in which Korwin-Piotrowska and her colleagues have sought to take control of the tribunal.

Further developments are expected on Tuesday, when Korwin-Piotrowska has called a general assembly of the tribunal. However, it is uncertain that she will obtain the necessary quorum of 10 judges normally required for the assembly to be valid.

While the eight judges appointed by the ruling coalition this year are all expected to attend, those appointed under the PiS government appear likely not to.

Polish police have launched a special operation to secure the area along the border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad after receiving information that acts of sabotage may take place there in the coming days.

The operation – which has involved sending additional officers, including counter-terrorism forces, to the northeastern Podlasie and Warmia-Masuria provinces – was first reported by broadcaster RMF and confirmed by the national police chief, Marek Boroń.

“Police are putting security measures in place around the Kaliningrad region in anticipation of possible incidents that could lead to acts of sabotage,” he told RMF. “This is based on information we also have from external security services.”

“We are responsible for ensuring the safety of the citizens living there, as well as for facilities and any situations that may pose a threat to society,” he added, noting that the police were coordinating their operation with the army, border guard and security services.

RMF reports, based on unnamed sources, that Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW) and agencies from unnamed allied countries last week issued a warning that sabotage activities could take place on the Polish-Russian border, potentially including border violations by armed groups.

 

In a separate statement, the national police headquarters told RMF that the ongoing operation is “directly related to the situation taking place in our country today, that is, acts of sabotage…and the actions of eastern services”.

That was a reference to the activities of Russia and its ally Belarus, which have in recent years carried out a series of acts of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” against Poland and other countries in the region.

A spokeswoman for the police headquarters, Katarzyna Nowak, told broadcaster TVN that they were unable to provide any further information on the nature of the operation as the details are confidential.

— Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) November 2, 2026

On Thursday last week, the deputy police commander, Tomasz Michułka, issued an order for officers to be on “full readiness” between 2 and 8 November due to the “operational situation across the country”.

Some had interpreted that order as related to the situation around the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw, where riot police were called in on Friday to secure the court amid protests against an attempt by a group of government-backed judges to take control of the TK.

However, on Friday night, the police issued a statement “emphatically denying” that the order had anything to do with the situation at the TK. They said that it was, in fact, “related to the current threats regarding acts of sabotage and subversion”.

The following day, Boroń himself wrote to police officers confirming that Thursday’s order had been issued in response to “attempts to destabilise our country by foreign intelligence services from the east”.

List Komendanta Głównego Policji do funkcjonariuszy pic.twitter.com/3jTMdme1bz

— Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) November 1, 2026

Earlier this year, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism identified Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe. Those operations have included an arson attack that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and an attempt to derail a train.

In September this year, a Russian military helicopter crossed the border from Kaliningrad and remained in Polish airspace for around 42 seconds before returning.

In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload entered Polish airspace from Ukraine before landing in a field in eastern Poland.

The Polish government has regularly warned in recent months that Moscow is planning further provocations against eastern NATO member states, including potential border violations.

Ambitious Wrexham AFC have named former EFL boss Shaun Harvey the club’s acting CEO following the shock departure of Michael Williamson.

American Williamson has been a key figure in their meteoric rise to the Championship since joining the club – owned by Hollywood duo Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac – in 2024 but has left abruptly. 

“We thank Michael Williamson for his two years at Wrexham and for his work taking the club from League 1 to the Championship,” said Reynolds and Mac.

“Since our takeover five years ago, Wrexham have had historic success on the pitch and won hearts all over the globe. We remain focused on our most important task: to make the Wrexham community proud.

“Shaun Harvey has been an integral part of this journey from the beginning, and we know Shaun will give every support to Phil Parkinson and the lads on the pitch while keeping the broader Wrexham community roaring us on.”

Williamson held senior roles at Inter Milan and in Major League Soccer before joining Wrexham in the summer of 2024 and was named Football Industry Leader of the Year in 2025.

He did not always prove a popular figure with Wrexham fans, however, with news of his sudden exit being welcomed by some on social media. 

How Wrexham’s rise has stalled

No-nonsense Harvey, 56, has worked with Reynolds and Mac since their takeover of then-non-league Wrexham in 2021, first as an advisor and then joining as a director in 2023. 

An experienced football administrator, he was chief executive of the English Football League for six years until 2019, following spells at Leeds United and Bradford City. 

The club’s dizzying ascent, chronicled in the docuseries Welcome To Wrexham, has stalled after three successive promotions carried them from the fifth tier to the second in 2025.

They narrowly missed out on the play-offs last season but have made a mixed start to the new campaign and currently sit 16th in the Championship.

]]> 2475270Frank Dalleres Frank Dalleres UK’s wealthiest financier Michael Platt sues own lawyer for professional negligence https://www.cityam.com/uks-wealthiest-financier-michael-platt-sues-own-lawyer-for-professional-negligence/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 15:15:59 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2475121

The UK’s wealthiest financier, Michael Platt, and his hedge fund are suing their former lawyer for alleged professional negligence and preparing for a trial. The claim was filed in September last year against Malcolm Gammie KC, a barrister at One Essex Court, following the billionaire and his firm being in a long-running dispute with HMRC [...]]]>

The UK’s wealthiest financier, Michael Platt, and his hedge fund are suing their former lawyer for alleged professional negligence and preparing for a trial.

The claim was filed in September last year against Malcolm Gammie KC, a barrister at One Essex Court, following the billionaire and his firm being in a long-running dispute with HMRC over the tax treatment of earnings on senior traders and partners at Bluecrest under a so-called partner incentivisation plan (PIP).

Gammie, a senior tax barrister, represented Bluecrest, Platt, and Bluecrest’s former chief financial officer and partner, Andrew Dodd, in the First Tier Tribunal in 2017 and then in 2021 at the Upper Tribunal.

When the case reached the Court of Appeal in 2023, the judges ruled that senior traders and partners at the firm must pay income tax on the incentive plan rather than a lower corporation tax rate, which Bluecrest had been paying.

In the judgment, the judge had criticised Gammie’s legal approach, pointing to an analogy which Gammie drew between the PIP incentive plan and a partner who withdraws capital from the partnership and describing it as “not exact” and “apt to mislead.”

In a case management conference on Friday ahead of a trial, the Commercial Court heard issues concerning tax treatment in relation to the incentive plan after Platt’s decision to move the hedge fund’s operational headquarters from London to Geneva in 2010 for tax purposes.

The court also heard issues concerning whether Platt and Dodd’s bank and credit card statements dating back 17 years should be used as evidence in the trial, which Bluecrest’s barrister said would be “both time consuming and could turn into an expensive wild goose chase.”

The trial is expected to assess whether Gammie acted negligently by not advising Platt and Dodd to use Swiss tax residency arguments during the legal dispute with HMRC, and whether this led to “a lost opportunity” to pursue different arguments, Bluecrest’s barrister said.

He added that if the documents “can be found, perhaps there will be thousands of pages, which might mean the defendant could make intrusive inquiries” about other things.

Judge Mr Justice Stanley told the court the documents “should be included” but said “it will require careful thought to be given on how the bank statements are disclosed and how they are deployed if they are to be deployed in a public trial”.

Members of an LLP, a structure Bluecrest uses, are treated as self-employed partners, meaning they don’t pay the 15 per cent employer’s national insurance contributions on their pay.

HMRC taking ‘aggressive’ stance on LLPs

This comes after a separate landmark ruling in July in which the UK’s Supreme Court ruled against the hedge fund run by Platt, finding that partners in a Limited Liability Partnership (LLPs) must be taxed as employees rather than as self-employed profit-sharers. Bluecrest now faces a near £200m tax bill as a result of the ruling.

The judge unanimously rejected BlueCrest’s argument that its partners were technically self-employed and therefore not subject to the same income tax and national insurance as normal employees.

The ruling sent shock-waves through the professional services sector, whom the vast majority use the LLP structure, raising concern over whether it would leave them liable to pay hefty tax bills to HMRC.

City AM has since revealed the UK tax authority is actively writing to limited liability partnerships (LLPs) as firms race to reassess their members’ tax status after the landmark legal ruling, even as both sides “hold their cards close to their chests.”

Gammie and HMRC declined to comment. BlueCrest was contacted for comment.

The trial date is yet to be decided.

It’s that time of year again: when Wales try and win a game of rugby while thousands of fans boycott matches at their Principality Stadium.

There are thousands and thousands of tickets still available for Wales’ three autumn fixtures in the inaugural Nations Championship finals month.

They take on Japan this weekend before matches against southern hemisphere giants New Zealand and Australia. It could spell millions in lost revenue for the Wales Rugby Union. But can you blame the fans?

It looked as if the side were on the up, defeating Italy and Fiji as well as the Barbarians between March and July. A rout in AI and tech stocks has wiped trillions off global markets. For City AM’s Midday Markets newsletter, Ali Lyon chews over what it all means.

It’s been one of those mornings when analysts have woken up and reached for their morbid bon mots of choice. “Bloodbath” has proven popular. So too, “capitulation-level event” or “sea of red”. And others have simply opted for an unadorned: “extraordinary.”

Whatever one’s preferred descriptor, there is only one markets story on town this Friday: the historic, tech-driven sell-off afoot in global markets, and whether the AI revolution has gone from boom, to bubble, to crash.

Before we get into why this is happening, and what it might all mean, it’s worth reflecting on the events that led us here. It all started, really, when traders began to digest the consequences of this week’s US midterms.

As well as the cost of living – not to mention voters’ enormous misgivings at the Trump administration’s unapologetic cronyism – data centers were firmly on the ballot this Tuesday. And as the ‘blue-nami’ swept through the world’s largest economy, it was clear the scale of the Democrats’ win would presage a slowdown in America’s AI infrastructure rollout.

At US market open on Thursday, the Nasdaq and New York’s S&P 500 fell four per cent and three per cent respectively.

And since then, contagion has well and truly set in, with tech-heavy Asian stock markets all notching up serious falls. The Nikkei – Japan’s blue-chip index – dropped over six per cent while we were all asleep. As did Korea’s Kospi, which has become a bellwether for AI sentiment and was forced to halt trading amid liquidity concerns.

In all, trillions have been wiped off global stock markets, in a rout that has led some investors openly to speculate whether the artificial intelligence boom that has defined the past few years in markets is now firmly in reverse.

What does the AI sell-off mean?

There are, in my mind, three big things worth noting in and among all this. First is that, while today’s rout is striking in its severity, it by no means represents a sudden or drastic change.

Tech stocks – particularly those most exposed to the furthest excesses of AI exuberance – have been on a downward trend for much of the past couple of months.

Companies like Sandisk – which makes memory chips for data centers – may have fallen by 22 per cent yesterday, but that fall was itself off the back of a 45 per cent drop in the preceding month-and-a-bit. And most of the the so-called hyperscalers – Nvidia, Meta, Alphabet and Tesla – are all trading considerably down on the start of the year.

Second, even if this is the start of a period of protracted share price falls, it would by no means herald the end of the AI boom at large. Firms and individuals are still adopting the technology at a rate of knots – and the productivity boom derived from it is by no means jeopardised by today’s shift in market sentiment.

Think back to the dotcom bubble of the early noughties. Investors got well ahead of their skis then, too. Pets.com – the poster child of worldwide web enthusiasm – reached peak valuation of $400m despite only ever generating $5m in revenue and losing over $60m a year. But its overdue crash did not stop the internet becoming the defining innovation of its time, nor slow folks’ adoption of it.

One thing that is certainly worth keeping an eye on though – the final element of the three – is what it may mean for the US and global economies. There is an understandable view in some quarters that the fate of the stock market is dislocated from that of the real economy: that Wall Street and Main Street don’t interact as much as one might think. But – and this is especially true in the US – the ‘wealth effect’ as it is known is a powerful thing.

If people look at their pension pot or stocks and shares Isa over here – or their individual retirement account the US – and they see it looking healthy, they’re more likely to buy that car for which they have been pining, or go our for that indulgent dinner. But when it looks less rosy, as will be the case today, then the opposite is true. Demand consequently slows, and economies grind to a halt.

All of which, is a very long-winded way of saying, there’s a lot going on in AI and markets at the moment. And no-one, least of all me, can say for certain where we’ll find ourselves next.

The Bank of England’s unanimous decision to raise interest rates to four per cent reflects serious concerns over persistent inflation, not just external shocks. The government most now address root cost issues rather than blaming external factors like the war in Iran, says Emmanuel Igwe

The war in Iran has been central to the Bank of England’s considerations around interest rates for the most of this year. In September, only three of the nine members of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted to raise rates. But this changed this week as, for the first time since August 2023, all nine members voted to increase the Bank Rate. Although eight members supported the rise from 3.75 to four per cent, Catherine Mann wanted the Rate increased to 4.25 percent. The Bank settled on an increase to four percent.

This decision does not come as much of a surprise to the markets, though the unanimity was unexpected. Economists had expected a seven-two split, with those not voting for an increase assumed to support a hold. A unanimous vote reveals something important: the Bank does not consider energy shocks to be a temporary blip. During the press conference, the Bank admitted that, although the shock has not yet passed through to wider wages and prices, it did not want to sit idle and wait until it does.

Central bankers typically overlook temporary supply shocks such as increases in oil prices as they only lead to a one-time increase in the price level, not persistent inflationary pressures. More concerning are second-round effects, such as businesses raising prices to protect profit margins and workers asking for increased wages to keep up with the rising cost of living. 

Running hot

CPI inflation was up from 3.1 in August to 3.5 percent in September, driven mostly by rising fuel prices. 68 per cent of businesses in the Bank’s October Decision Maker Panel said that energy shocks are behind their intentions to raise prices. The OBR expects inflation to peak at 3.75 percent early next year. The forecast from the Bank, released today, shows a gloomier prospect: a rise in inflation of up to five per cent by mid-2027.

In addition to this, the economy is running hot. It is welcome news that Britain was the fastest growing economy in the G7 in the first half of this year. But this is a low bar, and even our modest growth has been met with knock-on price effects from global energy trade. This creates an environment in which businesses pass rising costs to shoppers through raising prices. The Bank says this affected its decision to increase interest rates.

Impact on households will vary. For those with tracker mortgages, payments will go up immediately, while lenders will pass on interest rate increase to those with variable rates within a month. Those with a fixed mortgage rate will be initially insulated from the rate increase but will face a sharp payment increase when their current deal ends and they must remortgage. In a rare bit of good news, those with cash savings, such as prospective first-time buyers, would finally earn a bit of interest after a long while.

Businesses will perhaps suffer more. Firms already shouldering inflated energy bills due to the Iran war now have to contend with higher borrowing costs. Small businesses heavily reliant on variable-rate credit lines and overdrafts will feel it first. This will cast a shadow on the business investment that was the catalyst for Britain’s economic growth this year. Markets are pricing in the prospect for up to four more quarter-rate rises by the end of 2027. If this persists, businesses will see their profits squeezed well into next year. 

To the Treasury, the Bank’s decision was a verdict on the Chancellor’s first Budget. With a fiscal headroom of £15bn – down from £23.6bn recorded in March – the OBR estimated that higher than expected inflation would add £14bn a year to government borrowing costs this parliament. If markets expect a long run of rate rises, debt interest will eat into whatever buffer the Treasury has left.

Critics such as the New Economics Foundation call today’s decision “an act of economic self-harm”. But to hesitate at this moment would be fatal. When a central bank hesitates to act when businesses are signalling to raise prices, it risks losing a grip on market expectations. By raising rates today, it limits the intensity of rate hikes later. Higher interest rates may cool domestic demand, but they cannot lower energy prices or open the Strait of Hormuz. 

Things may change.Energy prices fell after the US midterms this week in an expectation of de-escalation in Iran. Governor Andrew Bailey was careful not to promise more rises. For those in the committee who were doveish such as Alan Taylor and Swati Dhingra, today’s decision was more of an insurance than a firm belief that we are stuck here.

The job now falls to the government to tame supply-driven inflation. Yet the current Treasury strategy features a £4bn sticking plaster that consists partly of a £100 energy rebate that does nothing to alter the trajectory of CPI – shaving only a negligible 0.1 percentage point. The Chancellor must confront the root problems: inflated energy costs, much of which has nothing to do with Iran. He could begin by removing green and social levies from household bills. According to Prosperity Institute research, green initiatives are already set to increase bills by the equivalent of £1,400 per household by 2031. An EU summit looms on 20th November, where Andy Burnham’s proposed UK-EU alignment on carbon costs could just make matters worse. The public might accept pinning the blame on Iran this time round, but neither the Bank nor the government can get away with it indefinitely.

Emmanuel Igwe is an economist at the Prosperity Institute

Similarly, budget carrier Ryanair has hedged about 80 per cent of its fuel needs in the current year at €67 per barrel but this protection is set to slip to only 25 per cent hedged at about €95 per barrel from next year.

    HMRC’s upcoming new powers, which allow it to recover tax debts directly from bank accounts, raises questions about how the taxman calculates debt.

    The new powers, unveiled by Chancellor John Healey in the Budget, effective from July 2029, will allow HMRC to automatically deduct debts from holders who fail to engage with the taxman despite being able to pay.

    The powers extend to tax debts up to £5,000 for current and savings accounts, and up to £10,000 for companies. Under the current direct recovery of debts rules, HMRC can take money directly from accounts only if the debt is over £1,000, provided at least £5,000 remains in the accounts.

    This is Labour’s latest move to close Britain’s tax gap. The difference between tax owed and collected stands at £59.2bn in the 2024/25 tax year. The government estimated that the new powers will help raise £50m within the first year, £255m in 2030/31 and £320m in 2031/32.

    James Kipping, head of private client at MHA, said that despite HMRC proposing protections for vulnerable taxpayers, there should be “genuine concern” over how it concludes the debt amount is correct and final, and how it may “distinguish refusal to engage from inability to engage” from taxpayers.

    Kipping also highlighted concerns about what data HMRC uses to determine income and affordability, and how quickly a taxpayer can halt the process and get the money back if HMRC gets it wrong.

    “The significant development is the proposed creation of something approaching an HMRC-imposed payment plan, with the department determining affordability and then causing recurring payments to be extracted from the taxpayer’s account,” Kipping added.

    California has rejected wealth taxes in referendum in a referendum where the ‘no’ campaign was largely funded by self-interested billionaires. It’s the right result for the wrong reason, says Kristian Niemietz

    The final results are not in yet, but unless the remaining uncounted votes are wildly out of the tune with the counted ones, California’s wealth tax proposal has been defeated at the ballot box. 

    ‘Proposition 40’ would have meant a one-off tax of five per cent on net wealth above a threshold of $1bn, payable by people who were residents of California in the beginning of 2026, meaning that leaving the state in order to avoid the tax would not be an option. 

    For those of us who are critical of the current wealth tax fad, though, this referendum victory could be a poisoned chalice, emboldening supporters rather than discouraging them. The opposition may win the referendum, but lose the political narrative. 

    California is home to about 260 billionaires, and the No side in the referendum relied heavily on donations from them, or more precisely, a prominent subset of them. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone contributed over $100m to the campaign. Additional donations from reasonably well-known super-rich people brought the total campaign budget up to about $300m, which enabled them to easily out-spend the pro side by a ratio of almost ten to one. 

    In one sense, the reliance on billionaire support is wholly unsurprising. Suppose you think wealth taxes are a bad idea, and you want to run a campaign against them. Who do you ask for financial support? Of course that’s going to be the people who have both the money to support your campaign, and an obvious interest in doing so. The average Joe is not going to spend money on preventing the introduction of a tax that they will never pay. Sure, opponents will argue that the economic cost of a wealth tax will ultimately fall on the average Joe, not just – or even primarily – on the billionaires who make the transfer to the tax office. But that argument will not be remotely obvious to most people: it takes a lot of explaining, and in order to explain it, you need to be able to finance a campaign first. You are not running a year-long education campaign about tax incidence, second-order effects and unintended consequences. 

    However, while convenient in the short term, opposing wealth taxes in this way comes at a long-term cost. By relying so heavily on the support of people who have an obvious financial self-interest in opposing wealth taxes, you contribute to the impression that financial self-interest is the only reason why someone could possibly oppose wealth taxes. In that way, you play into the hands of their most populist proponents. 

    Slopulism

    I have debated wealth taxes multiple times over the past 18 months or so, on TV, on the radio, at university debating societies. I have found that different people support wealth taxes for very different reasons, and in different ways. The more fair-minded supporters will accept that there are serious, legitimate economic arguments against them. It is just that they – and this is where we differ – do not see this as a reason for abandoning the idea altogether. For them, it is just a reason to be ultra-careful in the design of a wealth tax, and to get the details right. 

    Polanski-style slopulists, on the other hand, refuse to debate in such terms. They will tell a story in which modern politics is a battle between The People, who are good and pure, and The Billionaires, who are rapacious, extractive and divisive. The Billionaires impoverish The People, and then they engage in a divide-and-rule strategy, using their obscene wealth to distort public debate, and foment Hate And Division among The People. In that version of events, economic arguments are just disguised class interests. If you oppose wealth taxes, you must be either a plutocrat defending your ill-gotten gains, or you must be a mercenary in their pay. 

    If I tried to peddle a story along those lines, I would treat the California referendum as a godsend. Had Proposition 40 won, its supporters would now have to deal with the practicalities of a wealth tax, and in due course, with a backlash from disappointed campaigners. Now, the Polanskiites will interpret the result as just another example of billionaires subverting democracy. They will interpret the very defeat of the wealth tax as an illustration of why a wealth tax is necessary in the first place. 

    That’s why, as a critic of wealth taxes, I have to admit that I almost wish the other side had won. 

    Dr Kristian Niemietz is the outgoing editorial director of the Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA). He is the author of the report ‘Fool’s Gold: The case against the wealth tax, and suggestions for alternatives’.

    Chery’s new electric SUV is comfortable, roomy and loaded with kit, and it’s a close relative of the Jaecoo 7 that topped Britain’s sales chart in September. I drove a pre-production car in China, and if you want an EV with a name people will ask about in the company car park, it deserves a look, though the price will decide whether it deserves your money.

    Lepas L6 EV price and UK launch date

    The Lepas L6 EV is a comfortable, roomy electric family SUV with a long kit list and an official range of up to 279 miles, and on my drive it earned a place on any electric SUV shortlist. The steering is its weak spot, and the value case can’t be judged until Lepas names a price.

    That price hasn’t been announced yet, but order books are due to open in the final quarter of this year, and dealers are already taking registrations of interest. The brand is on sale here already with the L8, a bigger plug-in hybrid SUV that costs £34,900 in Essence trim and £37,900 as an Elevate, which shows where Lepas is pitching itself. Motorpoint expects the L6 to start at around £30,000 to £32,000.

    I drove a pre-production L6 EV over several days between Shanghai and Chery’s headquarters in Wuhu. It impressed me with its comfort and straightforward performance, although the steering felt artificial.

    The L6 shares its technology with the Jaecoo 7, Chery’s plug-in hybrid SUV that was the UK’s best-selling car in September, and it joins Chery, Omoda, Jaecoo and the L8 in the company’s push into Britain. Its electric rivals include the Skoda Elroq, Kia EV3 and Volkswagen ID.4.

    Who makes Lepas, and why does it exist?

    Lepas is Chery’s newest brand, launched in April 2025. At the 2026 Chery International User Summit in Wuhu, which was the other reason I was in China, I asked Zhong Wei, Lepas’s deputy chief executive, why the world needed it.

    For Mr Zhong, the brand reflects a shift in what buyers want. As people become more discerning, he says, they look for a car that expresses their personality and taste as well as getting them from A to B. Chery’s existing brands can’t satisfy every customer in the same way, he explained, so the company created a marque with its own identity, built around what he calls an elegant lifestyle of new-energy vehicles, intelligent technology and a more considered ownership experience.

    That’s a big ask in Britain, where plenty of company-car drivers and private buyers have stuck with European badges for years. They’ll want to know what a Lepas is worth after three years, and because the brand is so new here, there’s no track record to tell them.

    What is the Lepas L6 EV like to drive?

    I drove the L6 EV on multi-lane expressways, across the flat roads of the Yangtze River Delta and along more scenic mountain routes.

    It felt comfortable throughout, and acceleration was strong enough to make overtaking straightforward without the abrupt surge some electric cars produce. It also stayed composed on faster roads, in rain or shine (the part of China we were in seemed to deliver four seasons in one day). The cabin had enough room for four of us and our luggage, so it made a relaxed family car.

    The L6’s main weakness is its steering, which lacks the feedback you get from some European brands. If all you want is a comfortable, easy SUV, you’ll barely notice, but if you enjoy a more connected drive, it’s the part of the L6 most likely to disappoint.

    These impressions are based on a pre-production car, so the finished UK version may have different suspension and steering settings.

    Lepas L6 EV range and charging

    The L6 pairs a 65kWh battery with an electric motor producing 217PS and 275Nm of torque. Lepas quotes a 0 to 62mph time of 7.9 seconds and an official WLTP range of up to 279 miles.

    Driving in China isn’t always easy, especially in downpours (it’s almost as tricky as London), so I kept my eyes on the road rather than the instruments for much of the trip. We covered 360km (223 miles) in a day on fairly fast expressways, in humid weather with the air-con running the whole time, and the range never became a worry.

    Efficiency on that route hovered around 3.5 miles per kWh. That works out at roughly 225 miles from a full battery, about 50 miles short of the official figure, which is a fair result for fast driving in the heat with the air-con on, and it should cover most commutes for several days between charges.

    Maximum DC charging power is 120kW, and Lepas says a 30 to 80 per cent top-up takes about 22 minutes. How the L6 copes with a British winter and UK chargers is something I’ll find out on the UK-spec drive.

    Lepas L6 EV interior, boot space and technology

    The dashboard has a 13.2-inch touchscreen and an 8.88-inch digital driver’s display, and the system is quick and easy to use. There’s also a Hello Lepas voice assistant, which I didn’t try because I don’t speak Chinese. The cameras are crystal clear, making parking a doddle even when you’re jetlagged in the middle of a Chinese service station, and I think they’d earn their keep in tight city streets and underground car parks, especially in London.

    There are only two trims, Essence and Elevate. Both get 19-inch alloy wheels, a panoramic sunroof, a heated steering wheel and windscreen, 50W wireless phone charging, a 540-degree camera system, 22 driver-assistance functions and a 3.3kW vehicle-to-load socket. The Elevate adds heated and ventilated, electrically adjustable front seats, leather-effect upholstery, a power tailgate, an eight-speaker Sony stereo and parking assistance that includes remote parking. My pre-production car seemed to mix equipment from both, with fabric seats in place of the Elevate’s leather-effect finish.

    We drove four-up for most of the trip, and there’s room for three across the back seat. All our luggage went into the 410-litre boot, which grows to 1,334 litres with the rear seats folded (we didn’t need to try that), and a 99-litre compartment under the floor is handy for charging cables or a work laptop you’d rather keep out of sight.

    Lepas L6 EV company car tax and running costs

    For company-car drivers, the L6 sits on the same 4 per cent benefit-in-kind rate as any electric car in the 2026/27 tax year, rising to 5 per cent from April 2027. If it were priced at £35,000, in line with the L8, that would be roughly £560 a year in tax for a 40 per cent taxpayer and £280 for a basic-rate one.

    Private buyers will want to see the price before judging value, but the warranty is reassuring, with seven years or 100,000 miles on the car and eight years or 100,000 miles on the battery. RAC roadside cover comes free for the first year and can be renewed for up to seven years if you service the car at a Lepas dealer.

    Is the Lepas L6 EV worth buying?

    The L6 EV has the makings of a credible electric family SUV, with useful performance, a practical cabin and a long list of standard kit. The big unanswered question is value.

    What we like

    • A claimed range of up to 279 miles, and about 225 miles in hot, fast real-world driving.
    • Comfortable cruising and plenty of room for a family and its luggage.
    • A long list of standard technology, including a 540-degree camera system that makes parking easy.

    What worries us

    • Steering that felt artificial.
    • No confirmed UK price.
    • Unknown resale values for a brand that’s new to Britain.

    Whoever bought a BMW i7 new three years ago has watched well over half its price disappear, which is rotten luck for them and a gift for anyone shopping second-hand. Better still, a luxury EV registered before April 2025 escapes a tax that a new one pays for five years.

    If you’ve ever fancied a BMW i7, the used market has made it a lot more realistic. Three-year-old cars are listed at dealers from about £45,000, according to AutoUncle listings we checked on 5 November, while the cheapest new i7 costs £104,230. Figures Auto Express published on 29 October show it’s part of a pattern, because the i7, Porsche Taycan, BMW i5, Audi e-tron GT and Mercedes EQS and EQE are all expected to be worth less than a third of their price new after three years and 36,000 miles.

    Those Auto Express numbers are forecasts of what a car bought new today will fetch in part-exchange, set against its average list price, or the price of one version where it names one. Dealers ask more than part-exchange value, and plenty of these cars were sold with hefty discounts, so not every first owner has lost quite this much, but the size of the drop shows you where the bargains are.

    Which luxury EVs lose the most value

    1. Porsche Taycan

    Average price new £162,255, expected value after three years about £50,475, so it’s expected to lose about £111,780.

    No electric car in Auto Express’s figures loses more cash, though the average is dragged up by Turbo S and Turbo GT versions costing well over £150,000, and 2023 cars are listed from about £51,000. A 2023 car is the version before the 2024 update, which Porsche says brought up to 35% more range, so look up the official range for the exact car you’re looking at rather than going by a new one’s brochure.

    2. BMW i7

    Average price new £143,530, expected value after three years about £46,050, so it’s expected to lose about £97,480.

    AutoUncle showed 21 three-year-old i7s for sale on 5 November, from £43,998, with most between about £47,000 and £63,000. Auto Express reckons the i7 is the wiser used buy of the two big electric limousines, ahead of the Mercedes EQS. Our motoring reporter Tim Barnes-Clay reviewed the facelifted 2026 i7, and two of the changes he found matter if you’re buying an older one. The update lifted BMW’s range figure to as much as 452 miles from 388, so a 2023 car won’t go as far on a charge, but it also took away the iDrive rotary controller, which Tim missed and which a 2023 car still has.

    3. BMW i5

    Average price new £110,045, expected value after three years about £34,650, so it’s expected to lose about £75,395.

    The i5 is the electric 5 Series, long the default choice in the executive car park. Auto Express’s average is higher than the list price of even the top i5 M60 Touring (£98,425), so treat the cash figure as rough, but keeping about 31% of its value is the number that matters. It only went on sale in late 2023, so used ones are mostly 2024 cars or newer, and that’s fine for tax, because what counts is the date the car was first registered.

    4. Audi e-tron GT

    Price new £107,875 for the S e-tron GT, expected value after three years about £33,150, so it’s expected to lose about £74,725.

    The e-tron GT shares its underpinnings with the Taycan, so it’s the closest thing to a Porsche with four rings on the bonnet. Auto Express’s figures are for today’s S e-tron GT, while 2023 cars are the earlier e-tron GT quattro, and used ones are thinner on the ground. One we found, a December 2023 car with about 13,700 miles, was up for £46,850, which AutoUncle reckons is about £5,000 more than it’s worth.

    5. Mercedes EQS

    Price new £104,540 for the EQS 450+ Premium, expected value after three years about £32,375, so it’s expected to lose about £72,165.

    The EQS gives you S-Class space and quiet without an engine, and 2023 EQS 450+ saloons were listed from about £41,500 on 5 November. Auto Express isn’t a fan, though, and says rivals including the i7 are simply better all-round packages.

    6. Mercedes EQE

    Price new £86,615 for the EQE 350+ AMG Line Night Edition, expected value after three years about £26,850, so it’s expected to lose about £59,765.

    The EQE is the smaller EQS, roughly an electric E-Class, and it’s the cheapest way into this club. AutoUncle had 29 three-year-old EQE 300s for sale on 5 November, between about £29,000 and £37,000, which is about what a new Volkswagen Golf costs. Cheaper electric cars lose even more in percentage terms, led by the Lexus UX 300e, and we’ve rounded those up separately.

    Why a used luxury EV is cheaper to tax

    What matters is the date on the log book. GOV.UK’s vehicle tax rate tables say any electric car first registered before 1 April 2025 never pays the £440 Expensive Car Supplement, however much it cost new, so it pays the £200 standard rate. Electric cars registered since then pay £10 in their first year, then £640 a year for the next five if their list price was over £50,000, which covers every car on this list.

    That’s £2,200 over five years that a car registered before April 2025 never pays. October’s Budget raises the standard rate to £210 from April 2027, but the gap stays, and our guide to this year’s car tax changes covers the rest of the rates. Check the first registration date on the V5C before you buy, because an i5 registered in March 2025 and one registered in April look the same on the forecourt but don’t cost the same to tax.

    In London, any electric car is ULEZ-free, and the Congestion Charge is £13.50 a day rather than £18 as long as the car is registered for Auto Pay, while plug-in hybrids pay the full £18. That matters if you want a 7 Series, because in 2023 BMW UK sold it only as the electric i7 or as a plug-in hybrid such as the 750e. Drive a 2023 750e into the zone on about 230 working days a year and the charge comes to £4,140, against £3,105 in an i7, so the i7 saves £1,035. Add the £440 supplement the 750e pays until its sixth year on the road and the i7 comes out almost £1,500 a year ahead. From April 2028, though, electric cars will also pay 3p a mile on top of road tax, which is about £270 a year if you cover 9,000 miles, and Regit has worked out what pay-per-mile tax will cost you at other mileages.

    What to check before you buy

    A 2023 car will only just have had its first MOT, so the service history tells you more than the MOT record. Ask for a battery health report, which shows how much of the original capacity is left, and check how long the battery warranty has to run. Make sure both charging cables come with the car, look at the tyres (heavy EVs get through them quickly) and get an insurance quote before you fall for one, because a car that’s cheap to buy is still expensive to insure.

    When you’ve found the one, put its number plate into Regit’s free car valuation and you’ll know whether the dealer’s price for that i7 or EQS is fair before you start haggling.

    Our verdict

    Let someone else pay for the first three years. A 2023 BMW i7 from about £45,000 is our pick, because it has a back seat built for being driven around in, keeps the rotary controller the new one has lost and costs £200 a year to tax. If you’d rather drive than be driven, the Taycan from about £51,000 is the more exciting car, and the EQE from £29,000 is the cheapest way in, but whichever you choose, get the battery checked and the insurance quoted before you sign.

    Mortgage holders are bracing for a “painful rise” in payments after the Bank of England tightened monetary policy for the first time since mid-2023.

    The Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee raised interest rates to four per cent in a bid to stop inflation spiralling out of control amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. 

    But the decision will cause a further squeeze on home owners, who are already struggling against rising bills, as higher borrowing drives up mortgage costs.

    Around 2.3m households are due to come off fixed rate deals by the end of 2027, and could face higher bills when it comes to remortgaging. 

    The majority of borrowers secured deals during periods of low rates, meaning they could see monthly repayments rise by hundreds of pounds.

    Polling from City AM/ Freshwater Strategy, found 29 per cent of people believed they would be unable to afford the rise in bills off the back of the rise in mortgage bills.

    According to Moneyfacts, the average two-year fixed mortgage rate stood at 5.87 per cent at the beginning of November. The average five-year fix was at six per cent.

    Fixed mortgage rates are largely influenced by financial markets’ expectations of future interest rates and don’t reflect immediate shifts in the base rate. But the hawkish split of Monetary Policy Committee members, who all voted for a hike, may push fixed rates up as lenders price in the prospect of a higher rate regime.

    “For mortgage holders, today’s decision will add to the pressure on household finances, particularly…those approaching the end of a fixed rate deal,” said Alexandra Loydon, group advice director at St James’s Place.

    “With household budgets already stretched, even a small increase in monthly repayments could add to financial pressures.”

    Tracker mortgage woes

    The small number of households that are on tracker mortgages can expect a near-immediate rise in repayments. The products follow the fluctuation of the Bank’s central rate.

    Tracker mortgage holders can expect a £30.72 monthly increase to their mortgage repayments, according to UK Finance.

    Financial advisers said that while the sharp rise can be painful in the short term, those willing to hold on until rates come down again could secure a better deal in the long run.

    Samuel Mather Holgate, managing director of advice firm Mather & Murray Financial, said: “For borrowers who can tolerate some uncertainty, a tracker mortgage could prove considerably better value, particularly if inflation pressures ease.”

    But, David Hollingworth, associate director of L&C Mortgages, said there is “no guarantee that rates don’t keep on climbing”, warning people to only take on a tracker mortgage if they can handle the financial uncertainty.

    Variable deals

    Meanwhile, those on a standard variable rate (SVR), where the rate is set at the discretion of the lender, could also face higher repayments.

    John Fraser-Tucker, head of mortgages at Mojo Mortgages, warned that letting your mortgage roll onto a SVR could “easily be the most expensive mistake a borrower could make right now”.

    Roughly, 470,000 deals are on SVR, and if a lender decides to pass on the 0.25 percentage point increase in full, the average homeowner will see their monthly repayments increase by £14.28.

    “The rate rise is likely to mean people with variable rate mortgages see another painful rise in their outgoings, so will need to find savings elsewhere,” said Sarah Coles, head of personal finance at AJ Bell.

    “This is easier said than done, because prices have already been climbing, particularly at the pumps, and life is set to get harder in January, when a horrible hike in energy prices turns the screw on people’s budgets.”

I checked into Canggu’s oldest and newest luxury hotels to find out https://www.cityam.com/is-bali-dead-i-checked-into-canggus-oldest-and-newest-luxury-hotels-to-find-out/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 14:42:22 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474935

    Is Bali dead? Anna Moloney checks into Canggu's first hotel, Hotel Tugu, and the new five-star Regent resort to explore how the digital nomad capital is changing.]]>

    Home to matcha bars, padel courts and beach clubs, Canggu is the poster child for Bali’s digital nomad transformation, but overtourism has seen some ward visitors away from the area. Anna Moloney checked into Hotel Tugu, the first hotel opened in Canggu, and The Regent, the coastline’s new, five-star luxury resort, to see how the area is still changing

    In Robert Frost’s well known poem The Road Not Taken, it is “the path less traveled” that is upheld as the superior choice for its speaker. “Two roads diverged in a wood, and I—I took the one less traveled by, And that has made all the difference.”

    I can only imagine, then, the contempt with which Mr Frost would regard my decision  to holiday in Bali – the road very much well travelled by, especially by well-to-do westerners just like myself.

    Indeed, the island is now so popular (the annual number of international visitors has climbed 173 per cent in the last decade, clocking in at just under 7m in 2025) that its previous evangelists (who visited on gap yahs 10 years ago and told us all how fabulous it was) are quickly distancing themselves, shrieking things like “Bali is dead!” as they hurry off to Borneo.

    Within Bali itself though, we can narrow the road most travelled even further, with that most trampled path of all leading straight from Denpasar airport to Canggu. 

    Located on the southwestern coast, Canggu, a once sleepy fisherman’s village, has become the island’s digital nomad HQ, overflowing with matcha bars, luxury villas and beach clubs. You may recognise it from Instagram, where ‘Bali reality versus expectations’ videos frequently showcase ‘nightmare scenes’ of thousands of tourists packed cheek to cheek at popular sunset spots. Alongside the wellness scene, and similarly to the Thai islands, some clubs are open eye-wateringly late, attracting young, twenty-something crowds intent on ‘finding themselves’ amid seas of neon body paint. And while it may only be 12 miles from the airport, but journey times can stretch anywhere between 45 minutes to over two hours due to the region’s infamous traffic, with the village’s small roads often left in gridlock.

    Indeed, the consensus of almost all good online advice on how to “do Bali well” in 2026 is to avoid Canggu, so that’s where I went first. Alas, popularity has never been something to put me off a holiday (I hold the inane belief that popular things are popular because they are nice), and if you want to understand how dramatically the island has changed just in the last couple of decades, there is no better place to start. 

    Tugu: The first hotel in Canggu

    The development of Canggu has been swift, and unanticipated. 

    The first ever hotel in the area, the now five-star Hotel Tugu Bali, where I checked in, was opened in 1997 by Anhar Setjadibrata, a former Indonesian medical student who was taken by the beauty of Canggu, then just rice paddies, temples and the white sand beach. Today it’s managed by his daughter, Lucienne Anhar, who told me they could never have expected Canggu to become what it is today.

    “Almost overnight, it switched,” she told me, pinpointing the moment to somewhere around 2015. The people who have come have also changed, shifting from honeymooners and hippy surfers to those interested in what Lucienne calls the ‘new Canggu’ – great restaurants, cafes, padel and gyms: “I think there are more restaurants and cafes per m2 in Canggu than even NYC.”

    Tugu though is decisively of the old Canggu, steeped in history not only as the area’s original guesthouse but in a literal sense too, as a self-defined ‘museum hotel’. Duly, around the hotel you’ll find genuine Indonesian artefacts collected by Lucienne’s father, who opened Tugu partially as a way of storing and exhibiting his pieces, from rare portraits of Indonesian royals to Ming vases rescued from historical shipwrecks. Even the main lobby, a massive wooden pagoda supported by at least a dozen pillars surrounding a towering statue of the Hindu god Garuda, is a 150-year-old sacred ceremonial hall transported from a village in central Bali, which makes for a striking hangout spot amongst the rows of new built, laptop-friendly cafes. The guest lodgings themselves take the form of wooden villas built in a traditional Javanese style, strung together by planked footpaths hung over lotus ponds. 

    The hospitality is traditional too, by which I mean very, very good. When I checked in and realised I had booked my room for the wrong date (completely my fault), they changed my reservation fuss-free on the spot, and promptly moved on to press rice grains onto my forehead by way of a welcome blessing. They also offer a unique service in that you can have breakfast wherever you want on the property, with the Tugu staff happy to set up a table in your room, the main lobby, or along one of the garden pathways.

    Just steps from the beach, Tugu also represents prime real estate, and Lucienne confirmed that many have tried to buy it to put “another high rise building there”. ‘High-rise’ in this case admittedly means only a few storeys though, with Canggu still strictly regulated by the island’s 50-year-old ‘coconut tree’ rule, which prohibits buildings from exceeding 15 metres in height.

    The Regent Bali: The new rich kid on the block

    Notably, while I was visiting, Tugu had recently acquired one such ‘high rise’ (four-storey) neighbour in the form of Regent Bali Canggu, a new mega luxury, five-star resort which is now the biggest hotel in Canggu. With room rates over double that of Tugu, it’s a unique arrival for the area both in scale and price point, signalling a departure from the affordable luxury (cheap massages, acai bowls) that has traditionally drawn tourists to the area. Lucienne said she welcomed the arrival, which she hopes will “elevate” Canggu’s image to something more “upscale”, a new, new Canggu perhaps moving on from its digi nomad residents, who some locals told me are already mass migrating to Lombok and Uluwatu.

    Indeed, staying at the Regent next, I could almost feel my nose starting to tip upwards as I was immediately swept up in golf carts and warm towels.

    It’s a resort that’s been a long time in the making, with planning starting around 2010, potentially crucial to its financial viability: according to Asia-based hospitality consultant Matt Gebbie who has led research into the Bali tourism boom, in Canggu “if you haven’t owned the land for a generation, you are too late”, with rates finally catching up to more accurately reflect the high quality product on offer. “Luxury offerings in Bali are now earning the rates they deserve.”

    Duly, the Regent is plush and beautiful. It’s been thoughtfully designed in a kind of stacked formation that progresses downhill to the beach. If you stand at the top and look down your eyes will follow a beautiful symmetry of layered pools, lined with palm trees, that culminate in the sea crashing at the bottom. The sea in Canggu is not particularly suitable for swimming, so this prime pool real estate is a particular luxury of the resort.

    So too is the spa. You can’t go to Bali without getting a massage but my one at the Regent was among the most memorable, taking place on a warm sand bed that tipped forward and back as you lay on it – slightly unsettling but you soon learn to trust the grip of the sand. The spa complex itself is thoughtfully designed to incorporate outside hanging wicker meditation pods. For me, the addition of Dyson hairdryers with diffusers (a rarity any fellow curly-haired travellers will know the gift of) particularly impressed.

    Cure is the resort’s fine dining option, and you can watch the sunset over the beach as you enjoy the delicious nectar of chef Andrew Walsh, whose original Cure restaurant in Singapore was awarded a Michelin star. The food is inspired by Asian and European flavours, not least from Walsh’s Irish heritage, and I particularly enjoyed the absurdity of chomping down on Irish potato bread (brown-sugar crushed and dipped in a bacon and spring onion emulsion) while watching the Indonesian sun set. 

    A new, new Canggu

    Is Canggu done? Hardly. Yes the traffic and crowds and constant construction noise are real problems – especially for locals – but to write off the entire area as a fad that has been done is as reductive as the original mania that crowned it an undiscovered paradise in the first place. Yes the traffic is bad, but that’s because lots of people want to go there (because it’s fun!) and it’s especially worth a couple nights if the majority of your trip is going to be in Bali’s more spiritual pockets. Instead, Canggu is evolving once again, and the arrival of the Regent marks an interesting addition of resort-scale luxury. 

    Personally, as I waved goodbye to the Regent on departure, sipping on the iced coffee packed for me by the staff on checkout, I thought back to the Robert Frost poem: if this is the path well travelled, god don’t take me off it. 

    Rooms at Hotel Tugu Bali start from around £153 per night.

    Rooms at Regent Bali Canggu start from £369 per night.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004.
