Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Where the tiredness comes from

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.

]]> In a series of staged online sales, people selling a used gadget with a known flaw often owned up to it more than buyers predicted — the sellers reported caring more about honesty and fairness, and less about the price, than the buyers assumed https://siliconcanals.com/s-in-a-series-of-staged-online-sales-people-selling-a-used-gadget-with-a-known-flaw-often-owned-up-to-it-more-than-buyers-predicted-the-sellers-reported-caring-more-about-honesty-and-fairness-and/ Fri, 18 Sep 2026 02:00:00 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109366

Across five studies of secondhand-market haggling, sellers were often more candid than buyers expected. Three minutes of small talk before the haggling narrowed the gap, and so did asking buyers to think about the seller's conscience first.]]>

A pair of speakers, two years old, is up for sale online. When no music is playing, they give off an annoying static noise, and the listing does not say so.

A buyer’s message ends with a pointed question: “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” In one of the experiments built around that exact question, 85 percent of sellers mentioned the noise, and fewer buyers than that expected their seller to mention a problem.

Shira Garber and three colleagues staged a string of these secondhand sales online across five main studies and a pilot, added a second pilot that surveyed people about what drives negotiators, and reported the results in an open-access paper in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin this July. Buyers, they found, often underestimated how honest sellers would be. Sellers also reported more concern with being honest, fair and kind, and less concern with the money, than buyers credited them with.

How often did sellers come clean?

In each of the five main studies, some participants played sellers of a secondhand device with a defect they had been told about: an iPod whose battery drained fast, an electric scooter with a faulty battery, the speakers with the static. The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

The way the question is asked

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

A few minutes of small talk

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

Across the study, buyers rated their seller’s likely honesty at 6.56 on a ten-point scale, while coders scored the sellers’ actual replies at 7.51. Among pairs who chatted first, that difference was no longer statistically significant. Sellers’ scores did not differ significantly between the two conditions. The chat raised buyers’ expectations of honesty instead.

Study 4 tried a different nudge on 358 participants. Some buyers were asked about the seller’s moral concerns before predicting, others afterward. Thinking about the seller’s conscience first raised buyers’ expectations, and the gap was nearly halved.

It did not close. The authors suggest one reason: 85 percent of sellers in that study disclosed, a rate higher than in the matching condition of Study 3 for reasons they say are not readily apparent.

Where the suspicion comes from

Study 2 measured three motives, adding the pull of money to the two that Study 1 had tracked. The 214 management undergraduates who took part rated, on a seven-point scale, how much the seller had been weighing being decent, feeling guilty, and getting the best price. Sellers put their concern with being a decent person at 4.99, and buyers guessed 3.78. Buyers put the seller’s interest in money at 6.03; sellers reported 5.06.

The sellers still cared about the money. They cared about it less, and about their own decency more, than the buyers pictured.

The paper’s explanation leans on moral typecasting, the idea that people tend to see others as either doers or feelers, rarely both. A seller holds the object and the information, so, the authors argue, a buyer casts them as a doer, and the competitive setting makes that doer look like someone chasing an advantage rather than guarding a clean conscience. In the abstract’s words: “While sellers tended to be honest because of moral identity concerns, buyers expected them to be driven primarily by self-interest.”

Two duller explanations get a hearing too, and the authors say their own mechanism is not the only one. Poor forecasting in general, they point out, gives no reason to expect guesses to run low rather than high. Plain caution, a buyer bracing for the worst to avoid a loss, gets mixed treatment: the Study 4 discussion offers it as a possible added force, while the general discussion says it cannot explain the results, because in the first pilot observers with nothing at stake still underestimated the sellers.

Their mediation analyses deserve a lighter touch than the abstract’s sentence suggests. Buyers and sellers answered parallel versions of the motive questions rather than the same ones, and the authors say the results should be “cautiously interpreted” for that reason. Sellers rated their motives after choosing whether to disclose, which leaves room for a flattering story told afterward, though the authors argue buyers’ parallel ratings may reduce that concern. And in Study 1, the measure of anticipated guilt and related feelings showed no significant difference between buyers and sellers.

Small stakes, narrow scope

The stakes stayed small. Most bonuses were paid by lottery, and a seller in Study 1 had a five percent chance of earning at most $7. The authors grant that low stakes may keep self-interest from fully switching on, while citing earlier work that finds self-interest at work even when stakes are small.

The honesty studied was one kind: telling a buyer about a defect the seller knew. Misrepresenting a bottom price or inventing urgency, both named by the authors, were outside the design. They describe the findings as “based primarily on Western participant samples,” and the sales were one-off exchanges between strangers, chosen to keep reputation largely out of play. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

Suspicion is sometimes the sensible response, and the paper says so. A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. The paper does not argue for trusting everyone. It asks for work on when doubting a counterpart’s honesty hurts a negotiator and when it protects one.

Every finding in this piece comes from the published text and tables of one paper, read by an editorial desk that reports on research and does not train negotiators; the supplementary files the paper points to could not be opened. The studies compared predictions with replies across hundreds of people, which says something about buyers and sellers like the ones studied, taken as groups, and cannot tell anyone whether the particular seller in their inbox is being straight with them. For a purchase that matters, sensible safeguards include an independent inspection, a written description of the item’s condition, and the buyer protection some platforms offer.

This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Examining what the honesty gap does to the outcomes of negotiations is what they call an important next step; they also call for testing the idea where far more money is at stake.

]]> Quote of the day: “Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself” https://siliconcanals.com/d-quote-of-the-day-sometimes-you-find-yourself-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-and-sometimes-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-you-find-yourself/ Thu, 17 Sep 2026 10:45:39 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109380

What happens when your plans collapse, your phone dies, and you're stranded at a gas station thousands of miles from home—and it's the best thing that could've happened.]]>

The last time I was properly lost, I was standing at a petrol station somewhere north of Chiang Rai with a dead phone, a warm bottle of water and a dog who clearly ran the place. My bus had left without me. I had four hours to wait, nothing to do and no way to tell anyone about it.

It was the calmest I had been in about eighteen months.

Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself.

Yes, it is the sort of line that ends up engraved on a bracelet and screwed to somebody’s kitchen wall. Both of which have happened, it turns out. I went looking for whoever wrote it and found nothing, only evidence that it has been circulating since at least 2014 with no author attached. Anonymous, then. It holds up better than most things sold at a craft market.

Nowhere is mostly an absence of audience

Here is what I think the line is really about. Nowhere has very little to do with distance. It is any situation where nobody knows your job title.

In a city you are surrounded by people who already have a version of you loaded. The neighbour who thinks you are the loud one. The old colleague who still introduces you by the thing you did in 2019. You end up performing that version without noticing, because it is easier than correcting everybody.

Take the audience away and something odd happens. For a day or two you feel faintly useless, because nobody needs anything from you. Then the noise drops. You start hearing your own opinions, which are less impressive and a good deal more honest than the ones you say out loud.

That is the whole mechanism. No mysticism required.

The year my diary went blank

I lost my business, restaurants, during the pandemic. The deal was agreed over a phone call while I sat on a plastic chair in a dining room with the lights off, and it was the least bad option available to me at the time.

For years my day had been decided for me by suppliers, staff rotas and the seven o’clock rush. Then it was not. I woke up on a Tuesday with an empty calendar and genuinely no idea what a Tuesday was for.

I would love to tell you this was peaceful. I reorganised the same cupboard twice. I developed strong opinions about a neighbour’s parking. I rang people I had not spoken to in five years and could hear them wondering what I wanted.

The useful part arrived about three months in, once I had run out of things to tidy. With no restaurant to point at, I had to work out what I would actually do with a day if nobody was paying me for it. The answer was writing, which was inconvenient, as it pays considerably worse than a burger.

You can get lost for the price of a bus ticket

You do not need to sell a business or fly to Patagonia. Nowhere comes in small doses and most of them are free.

Pick a district of your own city you have no reason to visit and spend three hours there on foot. Not a famous one. A dull one, with hardware shops and a wet market and nothing on sale to anyone carrying a suitcase. I do this in Bangkok about once a month and I have never regretted it, though I have frequently regretted the shoes.

Go somewhere your phone cannot help you. Not switched off, just outgunned: the lanes are not on the map and the only language on offer is one you do not speak.

Be a beginner at something in public. Take a class where you are visibly the worst person in the room. It is physically uncomfortable for about twenty minutes. After that it stops mattering, and what is left is quite close to fun.

And if you do travel, leave one day entirely unplanned. No booking, no list, no reservation you have to walk fast to reach. Most people schedule a trip so tightly that they never get further than a warmer version of their normal week.

What actually turns up

Let me manage expectations. You do not come back from a petrol station with a revelation.

What you come back with is a shorter list. Two or three things you thought you cared about turn out to belong to somebody else. One or two things you have never mentioned to anyone are suddenly all you think about when there is nothing else to think about. That is it. It looks like very little on paper. It does not feel that way at thirty-eight, when you are still doing a job you picked at twenty-two to impress someone who stopped watching years ago.

There is a trap in this, though. Some people use the middle of nowhere as somewhere to hide, and the giveaway is that they keep having to go back. If every trip is an escape from the same unaddressed thing at home, the scenery is doing the work of a conversation you have been avoiding. Distance is excellent for seeing a problem clearly. It has never once solved one for me.

The dog at the petrol station, for the record, took no interest in any of this. He sat under the ice cabinet, moved twice in four hours, and had evidently worked something out about Wednesdays that I am still catching up on.

They’re often people whose sense of dignity was undermined so regularly that protecting it became something close to a full-time occupation https://siliconcanals.com/d-psychology-suggests-people-who-appear-offended-by-everything-arent-usually-seeking-drama-theyre-often-people-whose-sense-of-dignity-was-undermined-so-regularly-that-protecting-it-became-something-c/ Thu, 17 Sep 2026 10:45:02 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109377

Chronic offense-taking isn't performative outrage—it's a trauma response masquerading as oversensitivity.]]>

I used to think of a certain kind of person as a weather system. You know the type. You ask how the traffic was and somehow you have insulted their driving, their neighbourhood and their late mother. Everything lands as a slight. Everything requires a correction.

For years my take on this was simple and a bit smug. Attention seekers. People who enjoy the theatre of being wronged.

Then I started reading the actual psychology, and it turns out I had the story backwards. The people who seem offended by everything are rarely shopping for a fight. Most of them are running a security detail, and they have been running it since they were small.

When insults were the weather, everything looks like an insult

Here is the mechanism. If you grow up somewhere that regularly treats you as a target, your brain gets very good at spotting incoming fire. That is not a flaw. In the original environment it was survival. The problem is that the skill does not switch off when you move somewhere safer.

Psychologists call this hostile attribution bias, and it shows up early. Researchers followed around 1,300 children across nine countries and gave them scenarios where someone’s behaviour could be read as an accident or as deliberate. A shove in a corridor. A joke that could go either way. The children who consistently read hostile intent went on to show higher rates of persistent aggressive behaviour, even after accounting for how aggressive they had already been.

Two children see the same shove. One files it under accident, one files it under attack. Twenty years later, one of them is the adult who somehow takes offence at the weather report.

Being told you are too much is its own training

The other route in is quieter and I suspect more common.

Some people are not knocked around. They are simply corrected, constantly, about their own inner life. You are not upset. You are not tired. That did not hurt. Stop being dramatic. Clinicians call this an invalidating environment, a setting that consistently dismisses or punishes someone for expressing what they feel or need.

The theory behind that term was built to explain a specific clinical picture, so I would not go throwing it at your touchy colleague as a diagnosis. But the underlying logic travels. If your read on your own experience gets overruled a thousand times, you learn something ugly. You learn that your sense of things will not be taken seriously unless you make it loud.

And making it loud is exactly what the rest of us punish. We call it oversensitivity. We are reading the receipt and ignoring the purchase.

The tax the sensitive person pays

None of this is a free pass, and here is where it stops being sympathetic.

Researchers describe a disposition they call rejection sensitivity, meaning a tendency to anxiously expect rejection, spot it readily, and react hard when you think you have found it. People high in it tend to be less satisfied in their close relationships, and their partners report the same.

The trap is that the vigilance manufactures the thing it fears. You brace for the cold shoulder, so you go cold first. Your partner feels the chill and pulls back. Now you have evidence. Now the system that was built to protect your dignity has quietly started demolishing it.

I have watched this happen up close, over what I promise you was a genuinely neutral text message. There was no villain in that story. There was a very old alarm and a very ordinary Tuesday.

What actually helps when you are on the receiving end

Arguing about whether the offence was reasonable is a losing game. The alarm is not calibrated to this conversation. It was calibrated years ago, by somebody else.

Try naming the feeling without conceding the facts. Something like: I can see that landed badly, and I did not mean it that way. That costs you nothing on the question of intent, and it grants them something rare, which is agreement that their reaction was real. It does more work than an hour of you proving your innocence.

Be boringly consistent. Vigilance responds to evidence, not reassurance, and that takes months. You cannot talk someone out of a threat detector. You can only give it a long run of days where nothing bad happens.

And hold your line anyway. Understanding why someone snaps is not the same as accepting being snapped at. You can say plainly that you will not be shouted at and still mean everything above.

And if the thin skin is yours

Then start somewhere other than whether you were right. You often are. Slights are real, and some of the people telling you to calm down are exactly the ones worth watching.

The more useful question is what the alertness is costing you. Running security is expensive. It eats your Sundays. It makes you rehearse conversations that never happen and re-read messages for tone that was never there. My grandmother had a version of this. It made her formidable company. I think it also made her lonely.

So build a delay. When something lands wrong, wait a day before you respond. Graciousness has nothing to do with it. You are checking whether the feeling survives a night’s sleep. Usually it does not. The ones that do are worth taking seriously, and now you can take them seriously without the static.

The Robot Report https://www.therobotreport.com/ Robotics news, research and analysis Thu, 05 Nov 2026 22:48:14 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 https://www.therobotreport.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/cropped-robot-report-site-32x32.png The Robot Report https://www.therobotreport.com/ 32 32 How did Agility Robotics perform on its first day on the stock market? https://www.therobotreport.com/how-did-agility-robotics-perform-on-its-first-day-on-the-stock-market/ https://www.therobotreport.com/how-did-agility-robotics-perform-on-its-first-day-on-the-stock-market/#respond Thu, 05 Nov 2026 22:48:14 +0000 https://www.therobotreport.com/?p=590137 Humanoid developer Agility Robotics ended its first day of trading on the Nasdaq just 2% above where it started, at $11.49.

The post How did Agility Robotics perform on its first day on the stock market? appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

Agility says its Digit 5 humanoids can lift up to 50 lb. | Source: Agility Robotics

Earlier today, Agility Robotics began trading on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker “AGLT.” The company claimed that it is “the first pure-play legged humanoid company to go public.”

Agility started the day trading at $11.26 per share, above the initial $10 per share price used in the SPAC deal. It was a day of ups and downs, as it was for many tech stocks. It hit its lowest price at $8.40, and its highest at $12.15.

The company ended up closing the day trading slightly above (2%) where it had started, at $11.49. Other pure-play robotics providers did not fare so well.

Serve Robotics, another publicly traded robotics company that offers sidewalk delivery robots, ended down 12.45%. Surgical robotics leader Intuitive Surgical ended down 2.82%. Symbotic, which provides end-to-end warehouse automation, ended down 2.47%. In addition, PROCEPT BioRobotics Corp., which provides robotic aquablation therapy, ended down 6.42%.

While Unitree, another humanoid robotics provider, doesn’t trade on the Nasdaq, it is public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange’s STR Market. It’s one of the only other publicly traded humanoid robot providers.

Unitree first debuted on the market at 150.80 yuan ($22.55 U.S.), and saw some quick success, hitting a high of 1,100 yuan ($164.46) that day. Just a few weeks after debuting on the market, it was down almost 53% from its first-day high. The company is still working to climb back up to those numbers.

In addition, China has reportedly tightened its own requirements for initial public offerings for humanoid robot startups.

Technology and AI-related stocks struggle across markets

Note that the entire Nasdaq is down 5.52% today, which means Agility was beating this overall trend. Much of these losses were concentrated in AI-related stocks.

NVIDIA ended the day down 9.26% from its opening price. AMD ended down 17.26%, while Qualcomm dropped 9.49%. Microsoft was down 3.58%. Rockwell Automation was down 14.15%.

In hospitals, hygiene is critical. But the cleaning process, which is time-intensive and difficult to scale, remains manual work. This often means the process is also inconsistent. Healthcare facilities are under pressure to care for more patients with fewer resources. These challenges are why the Silicon & Embedded division at GlobalLogic helped Haystack Robotics engineer a mobile robot to handle disinfection.

The project started during the COVID-19 pandemic, when disinfection became a critical use case for robots.

“Obviously, this was a big use case at that point of time, in terms of being able to sanitize hospitals and care facilities,” Kunaal Mahanti, physical AI lead at GlobalLogic, told The Robot Report. “So [Haystack] came up with this concept of being able to do disinfection better.”

“While there were disinfections which are happening manually, it wasn’t really good coverage,” he added. “We were really the engineering and collaboration partner there to see how we can take this concept and make it.”

The result is an autonomous mobile robot (AMR) that combines real-time perception, edge-based intelligence, and navigation to deliver hospital-grade UV disinfection with minimal human intervention. The Santa Clara, Calif.-based company said it can operate safety alongside people, interpret its surroundings, and adapt to changes in its environment.

GlobalLogic aims to create a scalable platform

When designing its robot, Mahanti said GlobalLogic didn’t want to just quickly design a system for one use case or environment.

“We wanted to make it an expandable platform,” he explained. “The idea was that you can look at, for example, the track part of it, which is the thing that is carrying the robot, independent of what it is carrying, which is the UV. Architecturally, you keep them separated so that we can mount other things at a later date.”

“It went from a concept to what would be an architectural foundation, so that it’s not just that one product,” said Mahanti. “It actually becomes a class of solutions that we can build for the same industry segment.”

While GlobalLogic hasn’t done many other deployments in hospitals, Mahanti did say the company used some of the base components of the UV robot for other projects.

“When you look at the platform that moves, there are things that have come out from there in terms of the control of the motors,” he said. “Then we use ROS to do the programming and the sensor fusion part, that is reusable, and we’ve used that. So, if not necessarily the same device, but that architecture broadly.”

Navigating the challenges that come with hospitals

Healthcare facilities are crowded, chaotic, and involve many closed-off spaces, making them difficult for robots to work in.

“The known part was that, obviously, you have to interact with humans. The unknown part is that there are doors, there are things that need to be opened, and you can’t always just barge in,” Mahanti said.

This is different from more common use cases for mobile robots in warehousing or manufacturing, which typically involve open-spaces that are easy to navigate

“There are two modes that we ended up building for [the robots],” noted Mahanti. “Essentially, one was this autonomous mode, where it would navigate and find the right room. The other was a ‘follow me’ mode, in which case it would follow a caregiver or a nurse.”

This means the caregiver can open doors and ensure spaces are ready for the robot to enter. It also means a patient wouldn’t be blindsided by a robot entering their room, for example.

However, designing an AMR that can work in these complex spaces has created benefits in other parts of GlobalLogic’s business. With a much higher bar for safety, the company could apply the platform to other industries.

“The other learning is just being able to be in an environment where you cannot be loud, for example, when we are designing the motors or looking at what we need to put in [the robot],” said Mahanti. “Those things are specific to this industry, but then dealing with that has helped us build machines with higher fidelity elsewhere, where it is not necessarily a given, but it’s a good thing to have. Why wouldn’t you want to have a nice quiet thing that doesn’t interfere with the rest of the environment?”

What’s holding back robotic adoption in hospitals?

While more robots are making their way into hospitals, most people cannot yet walk into their local hospitals and find robots roaming the halls. This is still an emerging area for robotics, so what challenges still exist? Mahanti said three things come to mind.

The first is cost. “There needs to be an ROI,” he replied. “For example, if you look at this use case during COVID, at that point of time, you needed less people in the hospitals. You needed to be safe. It was a big issue. So that ROI was justifiable.”

Second is compliance with medical standards, which becomes much trickier when deploying robots that will interact with the public and patients.

Third is the perception of robots. Mahanti acknowledged that hospital staffers don’t want a big, bulky robot taking up space in busy corridors and elevators.

Prem Balasubramanian, chief technology officer of GlobalLogic, said that safely integrating into hospital workflows is also challenging.

“There are clearly safety concerns, from multiple angles. Navigating in a very human-crowded situation is not easy,” he said. “For a disinfectant use case, if a robot waits for people to keep moving and then slowly moves, you’re okay. But if you’re using it for anything else, like if a doctor calls and you have to get something fast to help a patient or bring some stuff, a robot could get stuck because it sees people moving and it can’t move.”

The hospital is difficult on its own, and it’s made even more difficult when you consider how made-for-humans they are, said Balasubramanian. For example, a robot might be able to navigate an emergency room in a perfect condition with no obstacles, but the addition of patients who constantly moving or being moved and staffers running around to solve critical issues make navigation much more challenging.

“The entire workflow within a hospital is built for humans. You can’t just fit a robot in thinking it’s a human. So, there is work to be done in converting some of the workflow, the spaces, everything,” Balasubramanian said.

Liber-0 achieves 36.0% overall success in a zero-shot evaluation of 60 tasks proposed by GPT-6.

LiberAI has introduced Liber-0, a world action model (WAM) pretrained on more than 2.2 million hours of human experience. The Beijing-based startup said the model combines human video with glove-recorded motion and embodiment-conditioned learning to transfer human manipulation experience to robots.

A central test of Liber-0’s generalization is whether it can perform target tasks without robot demonstrations collected specifically for them. LiberAI evaluated the model on a separate suite of 60 GPT-6-proposed tasks, distinct from its internal scaling benchmarks: 20 pick-and-place (PnP) tasks, 20 non-PnP manipulation tasks, and 20 challenging non-PnP and long-horizon tasks.

Examples from the suite include placing a pen in a pencil case, pushing a drawer closed, and a longer sequence in which a pen is placed in a pouch and the pouch is stored in a drawer.

LiberAI reported task success rates of 63.5% on pick-and-place tasks, 34.0% on non-pick-and-place manipulation tasks and 10.5% on challenging non-pick-and-place and long-horizon tasks, with an overall success rate of 36.0% across 600 trials.

Here, zero-shot means the evaluated checkpoint was not trained on robot demonstrations collected specifically for these target tasks; pretraining still included robot data.

Why learn from people?

Robot manipulation has traditionally relied heavily on demonstrations recorded on a specific robot for a specific task, usually by a human operator teleoperating the machine. That data closely matches deployment, but collecting it can be slow and expensive, particularly when new tasks or robot platforms require additional demonstrations. Human activity is far more abundant, and much of it is already on video.

The obstacle, according to LiberAI, is that human video does not translate directly into robot commands. Cameras sit in different places, hand poses estimated from video are noisy, and human bodies move differently from robots.

Liber-0 connects human experience with robot action in three ways. First, LiberSense Glove, LiberAI’s data-collection system, directly records hand movements, helping link human video to the motions behind it. Second, LiberAI’s robot platform uses camera views and hand, wrist and waist movements that more closely match those of humans, making skills easier to transfer. Third, a Unified Embodiment Representation gives the model information about body shape and joint movement, so it can adapt actions to the body performing them.

Liber-0 jointly predicts future video frames and actions. This lets it learn from ordinary videos without action labels alongside glove and robot recordings that include measured motion.

Human-to-robot transfer. Conceptual illustration of how action-grounded human recordings and visual and kinematic alignment support transfer to LEO.

Learning actions that robot data lacked

Glove data can also introduce behaviors missing from a policy’s robot data. LiberAI trained policies whose robot demonstrations covered only pick-and-place, while glove demonstrations included actions such as folding, pressing and opening. Performance was measured as a progress score, a 0 to 100 measure that credits partial completion, across four pick-and-place and six non-PnP tasks. With robot data alone, the non-PnP progress score was 2.2. Adding glove recordings of those actions raised it to 47.5, and to 54.6 when the glove set also included pick-and-place, close to the 56.3 scored by a policy trained on robot demonstrations of every action. This controlled experiment is separate from the 60-task suite: the actions appeared in the glove demonstrations but not in the policies’ robot demonstrations.

A separate experiment examines whether glove recordings can reduce the need for robot demonstrations. In an eight-task evaluation on LiberAI’s robot platform, where the full robot and glove pools contained equal numbers of demonstrations, a policy trained on 25% of the robot pool plus 100% of the glove pool reached a progress score of 75.6. A policy trained on 100% of the robot pool scored 72.8.

In that setting, glove recordings delivered comparable performance with 75% fewer robot demonstrations. The saving applies to robot demonstrations specifically, as the mixed policy still drew on the full glove pool. Because glove collection does not require a robot at each site, LiberAI says experience can be gathered from more people, in more places, and potentially at lower cost.

Robot post-training added 2.2 and 1.5 points, to 83.6 and 73.8. LiberAI said the small gain indicates the pretrained model already captures much of the capability needed for the evaluated tasks.

As robot fleets scale, charging becomes an operational challenge. Understanding how to optimize charging for fleets of mobile robots is key to getting the best performance from the fleet throughout the day.

Ben Waters, CEO of WiBotic

With growing deployments, charging is becoming more than a question of how long a battery lasts or how quickly it can recharge. Charging strategy can affect fleet uptime, facility infrastructure, maintenance requirements, and even the size of the batteries that robot manufacturers need to carry.

Ben Waters, CEO of WiBotic, recently joined The Robot Report Podcast to discuss how those considerations are changing as robot fleets scale.

He also discussed opportunity charging, the tradeoffs around fast charging, WiBotic’s move toward higher-power systems, and how charging data could help operators identify power problems.

WiBotic expands beyond its traditional robotics markets

What has changed recently at WiBotic, and how is the market maturing?

Waters: Overall, WiBotic has diversified into a few different markets, but all the while, robotics has really been growing, as we all know, over the last last one to two years for sure.

That was a big motivator for us to pursue getting into some adjacent markets. Take, for example, floor care, medical carts, space, and defense applications, all of which are markets that really use the same product as our longstanding robotics customers from a wireless charging, autonomous charging perspective.

Flash-forward a year of focusing on that and putting all the internal operational, sales, and engineering teams in place to support different markets. Here we are a year and a half later, and robotics is booming everywhere you look, right? I mean, all of our legacy customers in robotics have had significant volume growth this year.

We are seeing huge growth in automotive AMR adoption. We are seeing growth in outdoor robotic inspection for energy substations, and a lot of outdoor applications are growing. And then there’s the wild card of humanoids.

Wireless charging is a really interesting dynamic in humanoids as far as what it can enable and how it can improve uptime and eliminate some of these Achilles’ heels issues that humanoids have around downtime.

Opportunity charging changes the equation for large robot fleets

As fleets of mobile robots grow, where does charging start creating operational friction?

Waters: The big trend as charging relates to operational impact is what we’ve probably talked about before with Gene [Demaitre]. WiBotic has always looked at as a great opportunity for wireless charging. But, you know, it takes a while for fleets to get big enough for it to truly make sense. And I think we’re finally at that place. And what I’m referring to is opportunity charging.

So it’s the concept of “Don’t just put the chargers on the sides of the factories.” And then when the battery on the robot gets to 20%, that robot might be on the far side of the factory. Now it’s got to drive 10 minutes while watching out for everything else and while being ignored by the fleet management for doing a task, even though it’s in an area where a task needs to get done, right? Because it has to go charge.

That strategy, which is arguably easier to implement at a small scale, because you can truly just say, “If any one of these robots’ batteries hits 20%, stop and go drive to the charging station.” That’s fairly easy to implement. That gets really complicated, and that leads to a lot of unwanted downtime when the fleets start to get bigger. Even like fleets of 20 to 40, this becomes a bottleneck.

We need to implement opportunity charging. And it doesn’t make sense to do opportunity charging with anything but wireless. Because if you did it with contacts, your robots would be hitting the contacts so many more times. And even if you had the world’s most strongest contact, it still would require maintenance at some point, times all of the chargers in your fleet.

If the robot does a task and it’s got 10 seconds to sit there, well, a charging station should be positioned right where that robot naturally is going to sit.

You could look at that as well. It’s only charging for 10 seconds, but if you do that often enough, it’s adding substantial energy back into the batteries across the fleet and allowing these things to run 24/7.

You can completely eliminate that. Just allow the robots to stay in the loops where they’re operating when you employ opportunity charging. So that’s really the trend that we’ve been seeing and the demand we’ve been getting, and the main reason why companies are looking for wireless power.

How should companies think about charging during system design instead of treating it as an accessory at the end?

Waters: If I boil it down to three things, I think companies should be thinking about power infrastructure. I’ll come back to a few details on these. Where are your electrical outlets, and how many of them do you have, and are they rated for enough power to handle all the chargers you want to deploy? So think about that up front. That bites people. We’ve seen a lot when you think about that too late.

I think people are really questioning. How big of a battery do I need? Do I need a battery that supports an eight-hour runtime? Do I need a battery that supports super fast charging? In the world of batteries, most of these types of things trade off with each other.

They might be overdesigning it. They might be adding way too much battery cost for what they really need, especially if they’re thinking about charging strategies.

We still hear a lot of customers be like, “We need to charge these things as fast as humanly possible.” And we’re going to listen, and we’re going to assume the customers made the right choices for the right reasons.

Have you seen a data sheet from the battery manufacturer that says what that’s gonna do to lifetime? Is that worth it?”

And then the third thing for sure is maintenance. If you wait till you’ve already finished your design, and you’re starting to deploy and haven’t thought about those things, then almost surely, you will get bit by every one of those things within at least a couple of months, if not sooner.

As fleets of mobile robots grow, the need for interoperability among systems increases. The Association for Advancing Automation, or A3, yesterday published ISO 21423:2026, a new international standard for communications among industrial mobile robots, or IMRs, regardless of vendor or model.

“Companies want to choose the robots that fit their applications and have those robots work together on the same floor,” stated Carole Franklin, director of standards development for robotics at A3. “Many leading industrial users of mobile robots have asked for an interoperability standard for years.”

“Now, ISO 21423 gives manufacturers and users a common basis for communication across fleets, no matter where in the world their facility is located,” she added. “This standard can help companies expand automation with equipment from different vendors and make better use of the robots they already have.”

ISO 21423 addresses IMR interoperability

Developed by ISO Technical Committee 299, ISO 21423 Robotics – Industrial mobile robots – Communications and interoperability provides a common set of requirements for automated guided vehicles (AGVs), autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), and similar systems from different suppliers operating in the same facility.

The new standard specifies how IMRs, fleet managers, and other equipment exchange information and request actions. Robots can share their location, speed, direction, condition, tasking and availability with one another, A3 explained.

For end users, this means fewer cases of robots interfering with each other’s paths or path planning, which improves robot availability and system efficiency, asserted A3. A common protocol could increase competition in the market and support innovation, it said. One benefit of an ISO standard on this topic is that it can be adopted in countries all around the world.

ISO 21423 also covers communication with machines tended by robots; enterprise resource planning (ERP) tools; and industrial building systems such as lifts, automated doors, and alarms. “ISO 21423 represents the first non-safety robot standard that A3 has helped produce, and highlights A3’s continued leadership in robotics standardization efforts,” said the Ann Arbor, Mich.-based organization. The standard is available at the A3 online store for $373. A3 members can purchase the document for $320.

ThermAffyx both securely positions and warms patients during robot-assisted surgeries. Source: Gentherm

Many healthcare advances come from within that industry, but innovations from other industries can also find a role. Gentherm Medical has designed its ThermAffyx Patient Safety System based on thermal management experience from the automotive industry.

The system both securely positions a patient and provides patient warming for robot-assisted surgery. Gentherm Inc. said ThermAffyx does both while minimizing the amount of space required and without the need for forced-air equipment.

The Novi, Mich.-based company launched the system at the Association of periOperative Registered Nurses (AORN) Global Surgical Conference this year. Gentherm noted that numerous medical professionals told it that “almost all of their robotics patients are hypothermic.”

Adam Hauke, global director for product strategy and innovation at Gentherm, replied to the following questions from The Robot Report.

Gentherm addresses Trendelenburg challenge

What is the challenge that ThermAffyx addresses, and how are patient positioning and hypothermia handled conventionally?

Hauke: The ThermAffyx Patient Safety System combines active patient warming and secure positioning into a single solution, helping address two critical perioperative challenges: maintaining normothermia and reducing patient movement during surgery.

The current standard of care consists of forced-air warming solutions and a securement pad. Historically, warming and positioning have been addressed independently because, in many surgical procedures, they do not significantly interfere with one another. However, that’s not the case in most robotic-assisted surgeries.

These procedures frequently require patients to remain in Trendelenburg positioning, where the body is tilted head-down to provide surgical access to the pelvis and lower abdomen. Patients may remain in these positions for extended periods while robotic systems are docked and utilized.

This positioning introduces several challenges, including increased pressure and shear forces that can contribute to pressure injuries, the potential for nerve-related complications if positioning is not optimized, and the risk of patient movement or shifting during lengthy procedures. Underbody securement pads are designed to address these positioning challenges.

At the same time, maintaining normothermia becomes more challenging because robotic equipment occupies the physical space that traditional over-body warming solutions must be deployed in. In these situations, clinicians often rely on under-body warming approaches, but they are difficult or impossible to use in robotics because they would interfere with the underbody securement pads used for safely positioning the patient.

Suddenly, warming and positioning are no longer separate considerations. They are competing for the same real estate.

How much do patients move around during surgical procedures?

Hauke: In the routine course of things in the operating room, “patient movement” is not tracked. “Patient movement,” if it is recorded it is done so as “light anesthesia.” It is usually referring to if the patient’s anesthetic wears off prematurely and they move a hand or leg type thing.

No one is measuring anything on the OR table related to patient movement, as everything is under the sterile drape at that point. The only way the surgical team knows if a patient moves, is if there is tension on the robotic instruments typically.

Any unintended patient movement during robot-assisted surgeries can vary greatly based on a number of factors. There are multiple contributing individual factors such as patient weight, height, and body proportions, as well as procedure-based factors such as the patient position, the steepness the OR table is tilted to and whether or not other positioning solutions are used such as stirrups.

If there is a shift related to Trendelenburg, it’s usually noticed by anesthesia as difficult respirations or a drop in capnography. An actual measurable shift in a patient on the OR table doesn’t occur very often and is not currently a recorded stat.

Submit your innovation now!

Is there a weight or size range for the system?

Hauke: The ThermAffyx System is intended for adult patients and has been tested on individuals up to 297 lb. [134.7 kg]. The Pad is designed so that a patient can be positioned anywhere within the heating zone to receive active warming.

The Pad’s safety sensors do not require direct patient contact to function. As always, clinicians should follow their facility’s protocols and guidelines for safe patient positioning.

Does Gentherm’s system require more power than existing setups?

Hauke: No, ThermAffyx runs on standard hospital electrical outlets.

Is there any danger of thermal or electromagnetic interference with certain surgical instruments?

Hauke: We have mitigated the risks of compatibility with other devices as far as possible. The system has been designed and verified to comply with all applicable industry standards and FDA guidance — including compatibility with electrocautery, diathermy, defibrillation equipment, RFID devices, wireless power transfer devices, and 5G cellular networks. Therefore, the risk of thermal or EM interference is low.

However, there is always residual risk of issues occurring. We do not control the design and use of external devices that may be used in combination with ThermAffyx, and thus cannot guarantee other devices have been designed to meet the same standards or that devices are being used per the manufacturer’s labeling.

ThermAffyx moves toward the market

How is the system progressing toward commercialization?

Hauke: Commercialization is well under way. Our teams are in active trials across the country with strong adoption in both new accounts and our legacy Gentherm accounts.

How difficult was it to get U.S. Food and Drug Administration clearance?

Hauke: Although Gentherm is an expert in patient warming devices, gaining FDA clearance for ThermAffyx took careful development planning and execution. This is the first and only all-in-one product to have Class II indications for use for maintaining normothermia and securement.

To ensure the proper steps were being taken, we started the process with a Q-Sub to the FDA to receive their feedback on our claims and validation plan. We then implemented the appropriate design and testing per the FDA feedback to validate our claims.

An additional requirement with the FDA is to prove the usability of your device. The operation of the device must fit flawlessly into clinicians’ regular workflows to ensure the system can be used safely without introducing complexity. Nurses and anesthesiologists provided critical inputs to the design through focus groups, then validated the design in extensive hands-on usability studies.

Does this add to the cost of OR equipment or surgical procedures?

Hauke: While ThermAffyx does add incremental cost for the technology — lower than most capital budget thresholds — the more important consideration is its potential impact on reducing costly downstream complications.

By helping to reduce the risk of unintended perioperative hypothermia, patient movement or pressure related injuries, the system may help avoid adverse events that can increase length of stay, require additional treatment, and drive higher overall costs of care.

In robotic surgery, these procedures are already supported by established reimbursement structures and procedure codes, making this technology a natural fit within the existing surgical workflow.

Will you be selling it directly or through third parties?

Hauke: ThermAffyx is available for purchase through Gentherm’s U.S. contract sales team.

Are there other potential use cases for ThermAffyx and its component technologies?

Hauke: ThermAffyx was specifically designed to address the challenge of maintaining normothermia in patients undergoing minimally invasive and robotic-assisted procedures, particularly in gynecological, urological, or general surgery cases that require patient positioning in tilt.

However, its innovative 3-in-1 design offers benefits that extend well beyond these initial applications.

By integrating warming technology into a pressure redistributing underbody foam pad, ThermAffyx can help support patient temperature management in a wide range of surgical settings where maintaining normothermia can be difficult including orthopedics, cardiovascular, colorectal, and plastics cases.

The post 28 Zero-Day Findings in Less Than Two Days: What AI-Speed Discovery Means for Robotics appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

What AI changes about vulnerability discovery

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

  • Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot
    A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly.
  • Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence
    Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence.
  • Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control
    An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working.

A published patch still needs to be proven safe

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

Three questions can help teams respond:

  • Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots.
  • What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior.
  • How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

From discovery to safer deployment

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, watch for VicOne’s upcoming white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

]]> The European Commission has adopted the 2027 European Innovation Council (EIC) Work Programme, allocating €1.8 billion to support DeepTech startups, scale-ups and researchers across Europe.

The funding package aims to help promising technologies move from early-stage research to commercialisation, while improving access to investment for women-led and DefenceTech companies.

Ekaterina Zaharieva, Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation, says: “This is how it puts our Startup and Scaleup Strategy into action: mobilising more capital, stimulating customer deals, cutting complexity, and making bold investments on the technologies that will shape our future. And, as we shape the next EU research and innovation programme, our task is to turn Europe’s scientific excellence, talent and industrial strength into new companies and lasting competitiveness.”

The programme marks the final EIC funding package under Horizon Europe 2021–2027, the EU’s research and innovation framework.

A significant part of the programme focuses on expanding access to growth capital. This includes completing the €1 billion commitment to the Scaleup Europe Fund, launched in 2026 and managed by investment firm EQT. The fund aims to attract at least €4 billion from other investors and support European technology companies through investments averaging more than €100 million.

Alongside this initiative, the EIC will continue supporting startups through its STEP Scale Up scheme, targeting companies developing strategic technologies. The 2027 programme also completes funding allocations of €200 million for defence investments and €25 million for the Advanced Innovation Challenges pilot, both introduced in 2026.

These measures form part of the EU Startup and Scaleup Strategy and the Competitiveness Compass, two initiatives intended to strengthen Europe’s innovation ecosystem and address obstacles faced by technology companies seeking to grow.

Established under Horizon Europe in 2021, the EIC has a budget exceeding €10 billion for the 2021–2027 period. Since its launch, it has supported more than 800 companies and nearly 700 research projects, providing financial assistance at different stages of technological development.

Its investment arm, the EIC Fund, has already invested close to €2 billion in more than 375 deep tech startups, attracting approximately 3.5 times that amount in co-investment.

The programme also expands support for women-led startups through a redesigned Women TechEU initiative, doubling individual grants to €150k. A new European Prize for Women Innovators in Quantum will also be introduced, complementing the existing European Prize for Women Innovators and recognising female entrepreneurs working in quantum technologies.

Another priority is helping EIC-backed startups secure their first customers. New measures will connect companies with public and private procurers, allowing them to test emerging technologies and explore potential commercial applications.

Support for dual-use and defence technologies will remain part of the EIC’s activities, reflecting the EU’s interest in strengthening its technological capabilities across strategic sectors.

At the same time, the Commission intends to reduce administrative complexity and make funding more accessible to innovators at different stages of development.

]]> Munich-based aviation startup VÆRIDION has raised €30 million in a Series A2 funding round and selected for a €94.5 million grant from the European Commission’s Innovation Fund, bringing the combined value to €124.5 million.

The investment round was co-led by Dutch investors SHIFT Invest and Invest-NL, with participation from existing backers World Fund, Project A and Vsquared Ventures. PAYBACK founder and DeepTech investor Alexander Rittweger also joined the round. VÆRIDION has raised approximately €60 million to date, excluding the newly announced EU grant.

Ivor van Dartel, founder and CEO of VÆRIDION, says: “Over the past year, we have turned the Microliner from a validated design into hardware, with exceptional capital efficiency. Our propulsion and battery technology is now being tested at our own facility in Oberpfaffenhofen. This equity round enables us to build our first conforming aircraft. The Commission’s selection of CAROLUS supports the next step: establishing the industrial capability for Microliner production.

“Building out of Europe, our mission is to make regional flying commercially viable and accessible again, in Europe and for operators worldwide.”

VÆRIDION’s announcement comes amid other European funding rounds for next-generation aircraft and aerospace technologies in 2026.

In France, AURA AERO announced a €50 million Series B to advance its electric and hybrid-electric aircraft programmes, while HyLight raised €13 million for hydrogen-powered autonomous airships. In the UK, Greenjets secured €35 million for aerospace propulsion technology and Skyfly raised €8.91 million for electric aircraft development.

Elsewhere, Denmark’s Acodyne secured €2.5 million for unmanned cargo aircraft, while Germany’s SPREAD AI raised €25 million for industrial engineering software serving sectors including aerospace.

Together with VÆRIDION’s €30 million equity round, these selected announcements represent approximately €164.4 million in financing, excluding VÆRIDION’s separately selected EU grant.

EU-Startups previously covered VÆRIDION’s €14 million Series A in December 2024, led by returning investor World Fund.

Daria Saharova, Managing Partner at World Fund, adds: “For the past half century, Airbus has shown that Europe can build aircraft the world buys. VÆRIDION is writing the next chapter with a fully electric aircraft, built in Bavaria, with a clear path to certification. Investing in the future of aviation is Europe’s power play, and I am proud to back Ivor and the team.”

Founded in 2021 by former Airbus manager Ivor van Dartel and headquartered in Munich, VÆRIDION is developing fully electric aircraft designed to make short-distance regional aviation more economically viable.

Its flagship aircraft, the Microliner, aims to carry nine passengers over distances of approximately 400 kilometres, connecting regional destinations that have become increasingly difficult to serve profitably using conventional aircraft.

The €30 million investment will finance the development of VÆRIDION’s first certification-conforming aircraft and further propulsion testing. Meanwhile, the €94.5 million Innovation Fund grant is intended to support the CAROLUS project, which will establish and scale up a final assembly facility at Oberpfaffenhofen Airport, near Munich.

The project was selected from 358 applications as one of 12 large-scale projects, making VÆRIDION the only German company and the only aviation project selected in this category. The grant remains subject to the completion of an agreement expected in 2027.

The Microliner combines a glider-inspired wing with patented modular battery technology and a multi-engine propulsion system driving a single propeller. It is being developed in passenger and cargo configurations, with a targeted range of 400 kilometres carrying nine passengers under Instrument Flight Rules, or up to 550 kilometres carrying four passengers under Visual Flight Rules.

The company is targeting operating costs below €0.40 per seat-kilometre, which it believes could allow operators to offer tickets at prices comparable to first-class journeys on Germany’s ICE high-speed trains. Its broader ambition is to restore regional connections, including services linking smaller German cities and airfields that are no longer served by commercial airlines.

Thijs Gitmans, General Partner at SHIFT Invest, adds: “Regional aviation is one of the clearest cases where electrification makes both environmental and commercial sense. VÆRIDION has chosen a certification pathway regulators already understand and has delivered real hardware on a disciplined budget. We are proud to lead this round and to back a European champion in electric flight with European funding.”

The company reports customer commitments for more than 130 aircraft, representing a potential value exceeding €730 million. Its launch customer is Belgium-based ASL Group, with the first Microliner delivery targeted for 2030.

In March 2026, VÆRIDION opened its production and testing facility at Oberpfaffenhofen Airport, where it has since powered on its electric engine for the first time. The facility was acquired following the insolvency of German electric aviation startup Lilium.

The startup is now preparing to integrate its battery packs and propulsion system into a ground-testing platform known as a copper bird. Alongside wind-tunnel testing, this work will support the development of its first certification-conforming prototype, currently targeted for late 2027 or early 2028.

With engineering activities in Munich and Delft, and production planned in Bavaria, VÆRIDION intends to expand its European team as it progresses towards flight testing, certification and industrial production.

]]> Green Voltis, a Stockholm-based route-to-market (RTM) optimiser that uses AI to operate and trade battery storage across European power markets, has raised €13.5 million in a Series A round, with Lochpine Capital as the sole investor.

The company optimises standalone battery storage and co-located renewable-plus-storage projects, with more than 1.2 GWh under contract and in operation.

Martin Kievit, CEO and co-founder of Green Voltis, said, “Every new gigawatt of renewables makes Europe’s grid harder to balance, and flexibility now sets the pace of the energy transition. We built Aether and Chronos to turn storage and renewable plants into assets the grid can rely on and investors can bank on. The next wave of demand comes from AI. Data centres need power faster than grids can deliver it, and the intelligence that operates a battery can also manage a data centre’s energy. Green Voltis will provide the AI energy infrastructure layer between the grid and compute. With Lochpine Capital as a long-term partner, we are ready to build it.”

Founded in 2024 by Kievit, Ali Shi, and Gino Zhang, Green Voltis is an AI-native platform that trades, protects, and optimises renewable energy assets across markets and years. It claims to replace manual energy trading and fragmented EMS tools with a fully autonomous AI optimisation system.

According to the company, as Europe builds battery storage faster than ever, grid connections are slowing and becoming more complex, and new grid-forming requirements have added another hurdle that many control systems weren’t built for. This has led to prices across day-ahead, intraday, and balancing markets now moving every 15 minutes, making revenues hard to predict and projects harder to finance.

Green Voltis claims to cover the full path from grid connection to trading. Its engineering team handles hot commissioning and ancillary-services prequalification, so projects start earning sooner. 

Its energy management system, designed in Sweden and called Chrono, controls the site, is certified against grid codes and supports grid-forming operation. Aether AI, its trading agent built on time-series foundation models, forecasts prices and stacks revenue and capacity across several markets at the same time, rather than committing a battery to one market at a time. 

Additionally, the Swedish startup offers bankable commercial structures, including revenue sharing, tolling and revenue floors, that help owners secure project finance.

Green Voltis reported that its managed assets have consistently outperformed the Clean Horizon index, an independent benchmark for battery storage revenues. The company has market access in place or underway in 10 European countries.

The company is now applying the same capabilities to AI infrastructure. In Europe’s main data centre hubs, grid connections can take seven to ten years, and regulators from Ireland to Finland are starting to require new data centres to provide grid flexibility. 

Through its Power-to-Compute business, Green Voltis aims to connect the grid on one side and compute on the other, running data centre sites as grid-friendly flexible assets so that compute can get power sooner. It has a pipeline of around 120 MW of powered land in the Nordics and will partner with compute operators to develop it.

Blake Niu, Partner and Head of Private Equity at Lochpine Capital, said, “As renewables take a larger share of the energy mix, grid connection and power trading are becoming key to the value of energy assets, and they are among the scarcest capabilities in Europe’s energy transition. 

“We followed this field for a long time before choosing Green Voltis. The team combines AI-native technology with a global industrial perspective, and its operating results, which have consistently beaten the industry benchmark, show what it can do. We believe Green Voltis can become a leading operator of flexible energy assets in Europe and create greater value where AI and energy meet.”

The company plans to use this capital to expand R&D on Aether AI and Chronos, grow the business in key European markets, and build out the company’s Power-to-Compute business.

]]> Europe’s startup ecosystem is home to a growing community of women business angels who back promising founders, support early-stage innovation, and help shape the next generation of successful companies. Beyond providing capital, these investors bring valuable industry expertise, entrepreneurial experience, and networks that help startups grow.

While venture capital often dominates conversations about startup funding, business angels play an important role in Europe’s technology ecosystem, particularly at the earliest stages. It is no surprise therefore that a 2025 report by the European Parliamentary Research Service identifies business angels as a major component of the EU’s innovation ecosystem.

From established investors with extensive portfolios to entrepreneurs-turned-angels backing emerging technologies, this alphabetical list highlights 50 women shaping the European Tech landscape today.

Ana Barjasic is the founder and CEO of Connectology, an angel investor and an ambassador for the European Innovation Council. She supports early-stage companies through investment, fundraising expertise and initiatives connecting European founders with international capital.

 

Andrea Sinclair is a UK-based angel investor, member of the HERmesa investment syndicate and Venture Partner at Ascension. With extensive early-stage investment experience, she was individually named as an investor in women’s health startup PeriPear’s 2026 pre-seed funding round.

Annegien Blokpoel is the founder and Managing Partner of PerspeXo and founder of Catalyst Impact Investment Club, focusing on early-stage impact investing and sustainable technologies. She was named Europe’s Female Angel Investor of the Year in 2024.

 

Bettine Schmitz is the co-founder and General Partner of Auxxo Female Catalyst Fund and a co-founder of the Evangelistas angel network. With her investments, Bettine supports women-led and mixed-gender founding teams across Europe’s technology sector.

 

Céline Lazorthes is a French entrepreneur, angel investor and founder of Leetchi, the FinTech business behind Mangopay. She backs early-stage technology companies, with personally attributed investments in HealthTech startups Lucis and DermaScan during 2026.

 

Christina Caljé is the founder and CEO of TINTT, an independent angel investor and startup adviser. Her historical investment portfolio includes Lalaland, Newcon and Lucky Sweater, reflecting her interest in emerging technology and consumer businesses.

 

Cintia Mano is a Portuguese angel investor, COREangels partner and former CEO of COREangels International. She has personally invested in more than 30 startups and was recognised as Europe’s Female Angel Investor of the Year in 2025.

 

Constanze Buchheim is the founder and Managing Partner of i-potentials, a German leadership advisory firm, and an experienced business angel. Her historical startup investments include Delivery Hero and Empion, alongside her work advising technology companies on leadership and scaling.

Debbie Wosskow is a British entrepreneur, angel investor and co-chair of the Invest in Women Taskforce. A co-founder of WJV and Executive Chair of The Better Menopause, she has backed early-stage businesses including Hybr and advocates for greater access to investment capital for women founders.

Deepali Nangia is a Partner at Speedinvest, co-founder of Alma Angels and an experienced independent angel investor. Her personal investments include PensionBee and Planera, and she works to increase women’s participation in early-stage investing across Europe.

 

Emilie Dellecker is the co-founder of FoodHack, HackGroup and HackCapital, supporting investment and entrepreneurship in the food technology sector. She invests through the FoodHack angel syndicate and was individually named among the angels participating in Bright Biotech’s 2022 funding round.

Fiona Pathiraja is the Managing Partner of Crista Galli Ventures, a former NHS doctor and an experienced HealthTech angel investor. She has backed early-stage healthcare businesses including Skin Analytics and Jude, focusing on technologies that improve healthcare delivery and patient outcomes.

Georgie Smallwood is the Chief Product and Technology Officer at Moonpig Group, founder of Auxilia Global and an early-stage technology investor. Her investment experience includes backing emerging startups such as LiSA, alongside supporting women in technology and entrepreneurship.
