]]> Founded in 2021, AppliedAI builds Opus, the AI transformation platform that rewires how enterprises run and ties every change to the bottom line. 

Many companies have tested AI, but few have scaled it across their workflows and systems. Opus closes this gap. Opus starts with how a process really runs today, and then redesigns it for AI. The result is a workflow built for the real world, which allows AI to scale in daily operations. Every run of the workflow and every decision, whether made by an AI agent or a person, is recorded.

Over time, this creates a digital twin of the organisation’s processes. Companies can always show what happened, why it happened, when, and based on which data. Before a project starts, Opus calculates what the new process will deliver, and it measures the result after go-live. Opus is now launching in the DACH region. The focus is on insurance, healthcare and other regulated industries, where strict rules make reliable and traceable AI especially valuable.

Why is 2026 the right moment for European enterprises to move AI from pilots to production, and why is DACH both a demanding and promising market?

AI models are no longer the bottleneck. When pilots fail, the reasons are usually operational: old systems are hard to connect, results are not measured, and there is no governance. These are exactly the problems we built Opus to solve. Opus takes an existing process, redesigns it for AI, and runs it in production with full governance and a complete audit trail. Today, this works reliably in regulated environments. That is why we are bringing Opus to DACH now.

DACH is a demanding market. Regulation is strict, data must stay in the region, and buyers expect governance from day one. But this is also what makes the market so promising. Banks, insurers and healthcare providers here run large, document-heavy back offices. This is exactly where reliable, well-governed AI creates the most value. 

What most often prevents European companies from scaling AI beyond pilots, and how should they choose the processes and solutions most likely to deliver value?

I see three main reasons why pilots stall. First, they are built on assumptions, not on the real process, so the first exception breaks them. Second, integration and governance come too late. Third, nobody owns a clear target, and often there is no way to measure success at all.

Good starting points share a few traits. The work is high-volume and repetitive. It spans several systems and involves many documents and exceptions. And someone owns the result. But the most important criterion is the return on investment. Not every process that can use AI should use AI.

AI pays off when we redesign the process, not just automate it. That is why, at Opus, we start by mapping how a process really runs today and measuring its baseline: time, cost, quality and error rates. Opus draws on its Work Knowledge Graph, a proprietary model of over a million enterprise processes organised by industry and jurisdiction. Then we calculate the expected return of the redesigned process, ideally before anything is built or changed. Once the new workflow is live, we measure again. This way, the value is clear before the project starts and provable after it goes live.

Then start with one process, prove it on real data within weeks, and expand from there. Choosing well also means knowing where AI does not belong. If an existing system already handles a process end to end, leave it alone.

Beyond cost savings, how should companies measure the success of AI-driven automation?

Cost savings are easy to report, but they are rarely the biggest benefit. I recommend five measures:

  • Capacity: Can the team handle more work without adding people?
  • Quality: How accurate is each field, for each case type? Measure this on test data that was never used for training. A single “97% accurate” number hides too much.
  • Exceptions: A high automation rate is not enough. A wrong result that slips through unnoticed is worse than one that is flagged.
  • Cycle time: How long does a case take from start to finish? Most delays come from waiting for human review, not from the machine.
  • Auditability: In regulated industries, full traceability is a result in itself.

One example from our work: with Opus, a financial regulator cut licensing reviews from weeks to minutes of structured preparation, and every step remained fully traceable.

With the EU AI Act and strict data-protection rules, how can regulated sectors such as insurance and healthcare turn compliance and governance into a competitive advantage?

Many companies see governance as a cost. I see it as the thing that lets you go live. In regulated industries, the key question is not “Can AI do this?” It is “Will this pass risk, legal and security review?”

Governance becomes an advantage when it is built in from the start. That means AI acts within clear limits, humans approve the critical steps, every action is logged, and sensitive data stays in the company’s environment. This is how we built Opus: governance is part of the foundation. Every run and every decision is recorded, and over time this builds a Digital Twin of the organisation: a living model of how the business runs and what each part of it is worth. Companies that add compliance later often cannot use AI in these processes at all.

One more point: credibility with risk teams comes from precision. Be clear about which rules apply to you, from the EU AI Act to BaFin or FINMA. And never claim more than you can prove.

As AI agents take on more complex workflows, how will the relationship between employees and AI evolve, and what role do leadership, trust, and culture play?

Nobody can say how work will look in ten years. But for the next few years, we have a clear view. AI will free up a large share of the time knowledge workers spend today on routine tasks like typing, searching and checking. We should not pretend otherwise.

The real question is what happens with that time. If companies redesign their processes now, they can create meaningful new responsibilities for these people. Employees can then focus on the work where their judgement counts and where they create real value: complex cases, difficult decisions and contact with customers.

But these new roles do not appear on their own. They must be made visible. When we map a process with Opus, we define exactly where AI does the work and where a human needs to decide. This makes the human role clear from the start, instead of leaving it to chance.

This is where leadership matters most. Leaders need to explain openly what will change, and show employees where their future role lies. Trust grows when people can see that AI works within clear limits, and when they help shape the new processes themselves. Culture follows when people experience that AI takes over routine work, not their responsibility.

Over the next three to five years, where can European businesses differentiate from the US and China in enterprise AI, and what should leaders do today to prepare?

Europe will probably not build the biggest AI models. But that is not where most value will come from. Europe’s strength is trusted, well-governed AI in regulated industries, built under its own rules and in its own languages. That is a real advantage, if leaders use it.

There are four things leaders should do now:

  1. Start with reality. Map how your processes really run today, including all the exceptions and workarounds. The process in the handbook is rarely the process people actually follow. With Opus Discover, AI agents interview the people doing the work and map how the process really runs, including the exceptions and workarounds.
  2. Define your KPIs before you start. Decide what should improve, for example cycle time, quality or capacity, and measure where you stand today. Without a baseline, you cannot prove success.
  3. Think in processes, not in tools. Don’t buy a new AI tool for every task. Look for a platform that can run many processes in one place, with one standard for governance.
  4. Plan the new roles early. Decide where people will add value once AI takes over routine work, and communicate it openly.

The winners will not be the companies with the biggest models. They will be the ones that turned AI into part of how they operate, while others were still running pilots.

]]> Kabilio, a Barcelona-based startup building an AI platform for accounting firms and the small businesses they serve, has closed a €10 million funding round. 

The round was led by Picus Capital and Visionaries; they also led Kabilio’s pre-Seed round. CDTI, Spain’s public agency for technological innovation, also participated. 

“Nobody becomes an accountant to chase receipts, and nobody starts a business to do paperwork, yet that is where so much time gets lost. We built Kabilio to let AI handle the repetitive work and the accountant stays in control. This funding takes us from automating isolated tasks, to giving firms an agent that carries out complete workflows under their direction,” said Jose Ojeda, co-founder and Co-CEO of Kabilio.

Founded in 2025 by Jose Ojeda and Álex Valls, Kabilio has developed a platform that uses generative AI to help accounting advisors and their clients modernise the way they collaborate. 

Kabilio began with pre-accounting, collecting and preparing documents and data for bookkeeping, a task typically done manually. The company says that on Kabilio, AI reads invoices and suggests how to book them, matches bank transactions, prepares the reconciliation, and flags what needs a professional’s eye, without changing the tools the firm already uses; the accountant reviews and approves rather than types.

It claims to cut time spent on bookkeeping and reconciliation by around 60%. “The rails were also built for what comes next: every document, transaction and entry is structured data, with the firm’s rules and decisions recorded alongside it, so an agent can take over the work,” the company mentioned in the press release. 

The company also announced that it is now launching its own AI accounting agent, starting with firms’ core internal workflows. The agent can retrieve invoices and statements from client emails, match and reconcile bank transactions, validate entries, and follow up on missing paperwork.

The Spanish startup also notes that in order to streamline data collection, the agent can also communicate directly with clients via email and WhatsApp to request additional documents and information. Accountants give instructions in plain language and decide, client by client, exactly how much autonomy the agent receives. 

The company also launched Kabilio Empresas in September for SMEs, which lets clients invoice, connect their bank accounts, and track cash flow on the same platform their accounting firm uses.

It also notes that information reaches the firm as soon as it’s recorded, so it works with live data year-round, not just at tax deadlines. Kabilio works only through the accounting firm, which decides which clients join the platform and what the agent does for them. Fiscalidad Inteligente and Alemany Assessors already use the technology to manage a large part of their client portfolios, Kabilio revealed. 

In a later phase, the company will extend the agent to its clients. Using the shared platform, it will issue invoices, chase late payments, and request missing receipts on behalf of business owners. It will also answer everyday tax and accounting questions in seconds, not days. 

“An agent is only as good as the data it works on. That is why we are bringing the firm’s clients onto the same platform: the moment a business issues an invoice or a payment hits its bank, the firm has it and the agent will be able to act on it. The firm is freed from busy work, and its clients feel the difference,” said Valls, co-founder and Co-CEO of Kabilio.

The company plans to use this round to fund the next phase of a plan Kabilio has followed since launch: first a system to boost accountants; next introducing an AI workforce to handle repetitive tasks under accountants’ direction; and finally, extending that workforce to the firm’s clients through a shared platform.

Kabilio will close 2026 working with more than 500 accounting firms, with notable customers including Adlanter, as well as Solfico and Gemap, part of the iusTime group. The company has grown to 80 people, more than half in product and engineering.

]]> Sequoia Capital, one of Silicon Valley’s oldest and most prominent venture capital firms, has closed its London office as part of a broader restructuring.

In an announcement titled “The Sequoia of Tomorrow”, the firm outlined several sweeping changes and confirmed that it has raised €8.89 billion ($10 billion) in new funds. The biggest announcement is that it no longer sees the need for a physical European presence. While the firm is exiting Europe, three of its four London-based partners have decided to remain in Europe rather than relocate to California.

“We are closing our London office, which means several people will be leaving Sequoia.  This is not about the team – they are excellent. We simply don’t see the need for a local presence. We believe that Europe will continue to produce outlier founders and companies, and that we can continue to provide world class support from our home base in the Bay Area,” the firm said.

Despite being offered the opportunity to move to San Francisco, three of Sequoia’s four London-based partners – Luciana Lixandru, Julien Bek, and George Robson – have opted to remain in Europe. Anas Biad is the only London-based partner who has confirmed he will relocate to the United States and remain with Sequoia.

Lixandru joined Sequoia in 2020 as its first European partner and has backed companies such as Trade Republic, Pennylane, and Rillet. “My conviction on Europe hasn’t moved, and neither am I; when given the opportunity to move to San Francisco, I chose to stay here and focus on this wonderful, imperfect ecosystem.  Europe is where my family is, and where I want to build,” she wrote on LinkedIn.

She further confirmed that she will remain a Sequoia partner, continue serving on portfolio company boards, and also invest personally in the next generation of European founders.

Bek, who spent a decade investing in European founders through Sequoia, backing companies including Revolut, Miro, Attio, and Dust, added that he is already thinking about what the next decade in European venture could look like.

“My heart is in Europe, and I’ve decided to stay here. I’ll continue supporting the founders I work with and serving on my boards,” he said.

The closure of Sequoia’s London office follows a similar move by fellow US VC giant Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), which shuttered its London office in early 2025, less than two years after opening its first international outpost in the UK.

After roughly 20 years of expansion, during which it built multiple businesses across geographies, Sequoia says it is now pulling back to focus on what it does best: high-conviction, highly selective venture capital investing.

As part of this restructuring, the firm has decided to simplify the structure of the Sequoia Capital Fund, sunset its batch accelerator Arc and Scouts programmes, and streamline both its operational and investing teams. It is also eliminating the distinction between its Early and Growth stages, consolidating into one team under a single mission. The firm is also doing away with its Monday partner meeting cycle.

“Founders operate 24/7, and so do we.  Founders shouldn’t have to adhere to our process – we will do our best to adhere to yours,” the firm added.

European founders have already weathered a16z’s exit and now need to prepare for a phase where Sequoia may be hard to reach, especially without a local partner to back them. While the firm has insisted it can keep backing European companies from its Bay Area base, the attention will be on the UK partners who decided to stay, and the European tech ecosystem will watch their next move closely.

]]> FluoRok, an Oxford-based chemical manufacturing startup that has developed a patented process to produce fluorochemicals without using highly hazardous hydrogen fluoride (HF), has secured a €26.64 million ($30 million) Series A financing round.

The round was led by Orano Ventures Fund/Supernova Invest, with participation from investor Bidra Innovation Ventures. Existing backers Oxford Science Enterprises, BGF, GGF, Volta Energy Technologies, and the University of Oxford also participated in the round.

“We back companies whose technologies support a sovereign, sustainable industrial transition. FluoRok has already shown its process works at pilot scale, and taking hydrogen fluoride out of fluorochemical production tackles a safety and supply problem the whole industry shares. We are pleased to join a strong group of investors supporting the team as it moves to industrial scale,” said Florian de Beauchaine, Investment Manager, Orano Venture Fund/Supernova Invest.

FluoRok says its Series A funding round exceeded its original target and included several angel investors, smaller partners such as EverQuest Capital Partners, CPI Enterprises, and WS Investment, as well as approximately €1.15 million ($1.3 million) in grant funding from Innovate UK through its Investor Partnerships programme.

Founded in 2022, FluoRok is a University of Oxford spin-out developing a patented manufacturing platform that bypasses the conventional HF-based process used to produce fluorochemicals entirely. Conventional fluorochemical production has relied on a 250-year-old process that depends on HF, one of the most hazardous chemicals in industrial use, and high-purity fluorspar predominantly sourced from China, creating safety, supply, and cost risks.

FluoRok bypasses this process by relying on mechanical activation combined with base chemistry to unlock fluorine from lower-grade mineral sources and even fluoride-containing industrial waste streams, under controllable conditions. The process runs on off-the-shelf industrial equipment, which makes it faster and easier to scale.

The company targets critical end markets including pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and lithium-ion battery manufacturing, sectors where fluorochemicals are indispensable but supply remains heavily concentrated and hazard-prone.

Dr. Gabriele Pupo, founder and CEO, FluoRok, said, ”We are thrilled to welcome new investors on our journey to fundamentally change how the world makes fluorochemicals, with safer chemistry and better economics.”

“Closing another oversubscribed round, backed by both new and existing investors from around the world, is a testament to the strength of our technology, the incredible commercial traction and the speed of execution of the FluoRok team. This funding will ensure FluoRok can swiftly move from start-up to scale-up and take a further step towards becoming a large-scale industrial manufacturer,” he added.

FluoRok says it has completed pilot qualifications and established strong commercial traction with key customers, with products being validated by more than ten partners across eight countries and three continents.

The Series A funding round builds on the €12.43 million ($14 million) secured in previous rounds and more than €11.54 million ($13 million) in UK and European public funding to date. It plans to use the new capital to transition from startup to industrial scale, including building demonstrator facilities for its reagents and battery electrolyte salts, expanding its team, and deepening its commercial partnerships.

The company also plans to scale its platform for next-generation battery products such as LiFSI and FEC, and for a waste-to-value stream that transforms fluorinated polymer waste, over 25,000 tonnes of which is incinerated annually in Europe alone, into high-value chemical intermediates.

AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ Aerospace Global News Fri, 06 Nov 2026 15:41:47 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cropped-AGN_Icon_Jet-32x32.png AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ 32 32 Air India and IndiGo bosses reveal why they’re betting big on India’s aviation future https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/indigo-air-india-ceos-india-aviation-growth/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 17:59:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55957 Rising fuel costs, closed airspace and mounting financial pressures are testing India's biggest airlines. But their new CEOs see an opportunity too big to ignore.

The post Air India and IndiGo bosses reveal why they’re betting big on India’s aviation future appeared first on AGN.

]]> Willie Walsh was planning to retire. Instead, the former British Airways and IAG boss found himself taking charge of India’s largest airline, IndiGo.

For Walsh, the opportunity was too good to turn down.

Across the industry, fellow aviation veteran Tewolde Gebremariam has taken on an equally formidable challenge: steering Air India‘s transformation while navigating rising costs, airspace restrictions and mounting pressures on international routes.

Speaking at the Aviation India Summit and Exhibition held in Delhi earlier this week, both underlined the challenges facing India’s aviation industry – and why they believe the country’s potential as a global aviation hub makes the short-term pain worthwhile.

Taking the helm at IndiGo and Air India

Willie Walsh, former chief executive of and IAG and ex-director general of the International Air Transport Association (IATA), took over as CEO of IndiGo in August 2026. Meanwhile, Tewolde Gebremariam, who spent 37 years at Ethiopian Airlines, including 11 as CEO, also took the helm of Air India in August.

Walsh revealed that prior to taking on the role at IndiGo, he had planned to retire. “But when you get an opportunity to participate in India’s aviation story, it’s not an opportunity you turn down,” he said during a keynote interview at Aviation India.

He said the decision to join IndiGo was the “easiest he had made.” He knew the market from his years at British Airways, when the airline ran a large India operation.

Gebremariam left Ethiopian Airlines in March 2022 and moved to the US, where he worked in an advisory capacity for Delta Airlines before accepting the Air India role. He said he has been tasked with leading the airline’s transformation as it progresses through its next stage of rebuilding and growth. He also has a history in the country’s aviation market, having served as Ethiopian’s country director in India in the mid-1990s.

Both agreed that, with a huge and growing domestic catchment, the opportunity in India’s aviation sector is vast.

IndiGo’s fleet renewal

Walsh said IndiGo’s leased Boeing 787 operation to accelerate the airline’s entry into the long-haul market was launched in a very different environment from the one the airline now faces. Higher fuel prices and airspace restrictions made the operation hard to sustain, he said.

The airline is now shifting international growth to the Airbus A321XLR, with five delivered by the end of this year and 14 by the end of 2027. IndiGo has begun flying to Amsterdam on a flight of just over 10 hours and has launched its longest XLR route to date. Walsh said the XLR combines widebody unit costs with narrowbody trip costs and offers range that is “almost unlimited.”

Airbus A350s are due to follow in the second quarter of 2028. Walsh said he hoped that airspace conditions would have eased by then enabling the airline to continue building its codeshare partnerships. IndiGo already has codeshares with 13 airlines. “Our partners want to serve India; they want access to our network,” he said. “In that sense, we hold a lucrative key to the market.”

This week, IndiGo is also launching its first lie-flat seats, and it is reportedly in talks to buy around 100 Embraer jets. The low-cost carrier also signed with Skywise to deploy the Airbus A320 Virtual Procedure Trainer (VPT), becoming the first VPT customer in the South Asia region. Together, the moves signal broader ambitions for an airline built on low-cost short-haul flying.

Walsh said the company must not lose focus on its core. IndiGo holds about 65% of the domestic market and serves more than 300 city pairs. It flies international services from 23 Indian airports. Growth slowed in the second quarter of this financial year, he said, and in response, the airline is reviewing all its costs. Seat factor fell by about two points as the airline took measures to offset rising fuel costs, though he said demand is now where the airline expected it to be.  

The steep rises in fuel prices are “unlike anything [Walsh] has seen to date. Refining capacity has been disrupted, particularly in Europe, and he now expects elevated jet fuel crack spreads to persist even if crude oil prices fall.

By 2030, Walsh said, he expects IndiGo to operate around 600 aircraft with significant international expansion and the A350 in service. He cited Turkish Airlines in Istanbul and the Gulf carriers in Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Doha as examples of what hub airlines can achieve and said the same opportunity exists in India.

IndiGo doubles Airbus A350 commitment as it attempts to crack the low-cost long-haul conundrum IndiGo doubles Airbus A350 commitment as it attempts to crack the low-cost long-haul conundrum

Airport charges

Walsh was direct about airports, which he said are critical to IndiGo’s growth, but must keep charges in check. He said the move to Navi Mumbai is important to the airline and acknowledged that the planned Terminal 1 renovation in Mumbai is needed, but he expressed concern about the timelines and costs of delivering it.

If the work adds capacity, he said, per-passenger costs should fall rather than rise. He argued that airports earn more stable returns than airlines and that regulatory models in Europe have in some cases encouraged wasteful spending, but he also said airlines must be able to earn a return on their capital.

Rebalancing Air India’s network

Gebremariam said Air India faces losses in the short term but a clear route to growth. He also cited the spike in fuel prices as an immediate challenge, along with geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and Pakistan’s airspace closure as headwinds.

Services to Europe and North America have been affected, and the airline has cut frequencies to some US cities, including Chicago, Washington and San Francisco.

In response, Air India is rebalancing its network toward its eastern and southeastern markets, which are not affected by the airspace closures. “Efficiency, efficiency, efficiency” is the guiding principle, he said. The airline is also further integrating its operations with its low-cost arm, Air India Express, so the two share corporate functions, which he expects to lower some costs.

Gebremariam said the right foundations are in place to achieve the growth Air India is targeting. This includes a large maintenance facility in Delhi and training academies in Mumbai and Amritsar. He said Air India’s priority is to win back market share while building international-to-international and domestic-to-international connectivity.

He said the airline’s shareholders, Tata Group and Singapore Airlines, remain committed. “We have their backing 120% with our ambitions,” he said. “I am more impatient than the shareholders,” he added, “to see the airline return to profitability.”

India’s future as a global hub

Gebremariam, who helped grow Ethiopian Airlines into one of Africa’s leading carriers, said India has everything it needs to become a global aviation hub. He pointed to its geographic position, a population of 1.4 billion and a diaspora of more than 30 million. Success would depend on the right infrastructure, network, strategy, and product, and on taking a long-term view, he said.

At Ethiopian, he noted how he extended a five-year plan to a 15-year roadmap and grew the airline’s network from about 60 to 128 destinations before the pandemic. He pointed out that while aviation often looks like a short-term business because of its volatility, it rewards long-term planning, and India is no exception.  

Gebremariam concluded that at the heart of that growth, Air India’s brand remains strong with Indians at home and abroad. “Together, we will make Air India great again,” he said.

]]> How do airlines decide if a bomb threat is credible? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/how-do-airlines-decide-if-a-bomb-threat-is-credible/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:14:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55807 A single warning can disrupt hundreds of journeys, leaving security teams to make difficult decisions with little information and no room for mistakes.

The post How do airlines decide if a bomb threat is credible? appeared first on AGN.

]]> A series of suspected bomb hoaxes affecting passenger flights across Europe has raised questions about how airlines distinguish credible security warnings from malicious hoaxes.

Around 30 flights were affected by bomb threats on 5 November, with seven more security alerts today (6 November). Aircraft were diverted, airports activated security procedures and military jets were scrambled in several countries. No explosives were found.

A bomb threat against an aircraft presents a difficult decision for airline operations teams who are juggling safety priorities with the commercial pressure to minimise disruption.

Here’s how they assess potentially serious warnings when information is limited and decisions need to be made quickly.

What happens when a pilot receives a bomb threat? What happens when a pilot receives a bomb threat?

How are bomb threats typically made to airlines?

Although many bomb threats prove to be hoaxes, each must be assessed on the information available at the time, with the safety of the aircraft, passengers and crew always taking priority.

A bomb threat against a passenger aircraft can be made through telephone calls, emails, social media, written messages left on an aircraft or via third parties. This makes the preservation of the original communication and its associated information important. 

For notes left on an aircraft, it is vital to preserve any fingerprints or other identifying information for police when the investigation begins. 

Information is often incomplete or deliberately vague, and the assessment of whether it is credible or not involves several parties, including the airline’s security department, its operations control centre (OCC), flight crew, airport authorities, air traffic control and police or security agencies. 

UK police guidance notes that most bomb threats are hoaxes, often intended to generate fear and disrupt operations. Still, each threat should be reported and assessed.

What makes an airline bomb threat “credible”?

A central part of the process is establishing how specific the warning is.

FBI documentation says this involves determining whether a threat identifies details such as its intended target, timing, location or method, as well as assessing the source and viability of what is being alleged.

On the part of the airline, this means establishing whether a message refers to a particular flight, aircraft, airport or individual, and whether it contains information that could indicate knowledge of the operation. This is useful in determining how genuine the threat is. 

Security specialists will also consider the circumstances in which the threat was received, whether similar messages have been reported elsewhere and whether intelligence agencies or police hold relevant information.

Assessors also consider the wider security context, including the departure and destination locations, any ongoing security concerns and relevant intelligence reporting.

The UK’s ProtectUK guidance emphasises the importance of considering the wider circumstances rather than relying on the wording of a message alone.

Who decides whether an airline bomb threat is genuine?

Assessing a threat can involve several organisations.

Joji Waites, BALPA’s Director of Flight Safety, Policy and Regulation, explains that the airline industry has “well proved mechanisms” for dealing with bomb threats.

“When a threat to an aircraft has been notified to the airline the threat is passed to a team of assessors. These assessors use standard processes to grade the threat and decide whether the threat is Red (credible), Amber (partially credible) or Green (not credible). Amber is not considered an appropriate assessment if the plane is airborne.

“If the threat is assessed as not credible staff on the plane will not be informed of it. However, when a threat is assessed as credible (red or amber) the flight crew will be informed immediately and they will carry out company procedures for a credible bomb threat.”

What did the Ryanair FR4978 bomb threat reveal about aviation security?

The importance of clear communication was highlighted by the 2021 diversion of Ryanair flight FR4978 from Athens to Vilnius to Minsk, following a bomb threat email. 

The Boeing 737 was flying from Athens to Vilnius with 122 passengers when Belarusian authorities received an email claiming that an explosive device had been planted on board and would detonate over Vilnius.

An International Civil Aviation Organization investigation subsequently found that the threat was deliberately false. Its report also identified significant shortcomings in the transmission of information to the crew and the coordination between the airline and Belarusian authorities.

Although Minsk Airport received the email, the information passed to air traffic control was limited to the claim that a bomb was on board and would explode over Vilnius. 

The investigation found that the threat had not been properly shared with other relevant air traffic control units or the airline in a timely manner.

]]> Turkey tests Bayraktar TB2 as mothership for FPV attack drones https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/bayraktar-tb2-fpv-drone-mothership-test/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 15:39:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55921 Baykar's test highlights an emerging drone warfare concept, combining a long-endurance UAV with operator-guided strike drones launched from standoff distances.

The post Turkey tests Bayraktar TB2 as mothership for FPV attack drones appeared first on AGN.

]]> Turkish drone manufacturer Baykar has demonstrated a new strike capability for its Bayraktar TB2 unmanned aircraft, launching two smaller attack drones from the aircraft during a flight test in northwestern Turkiye.

The TB2 took off from Baykar’s Keşan Flight Training and Test Centre in Edirne province carrying 16 first-person-view (FPV) kamikaze drones developed by Turkish company Skydagger.

Two of the drones were released during the test and struck designated targets, according to a statement issued by Baykar on 4 November.

The demonstration marks a new role for the TB2, which has traditionally been used for surveillance, reconnaissance and precision attacks with guided munitions. It can now carry smaller attack drones to a target area and provide the communications link needed to operate them.

Baykar said the FPV drones were controlled by operators through a connection established via the TB2 rather than through a direct link to a ground station.

The arrangement allows the larger aircraft to act as both a launch platform or mothership, and an airborne communications relay, potentially extending the distance at which the smaller drones can be operated.

How the new system works

FPV drones are typically flown by operators who receive live video from cameras mounted on the aircraft. This allows them to steer towards a selected target and make adjustments during the final approach.

Unlike conventional guided munitions, which follow a programmed or guided trajectory after release, FPV drones can be manoeuvred by an operator throughout their flight, subject to the available communications link.

This could allow the TB2 to remain at a distance while the FPV drones conduct the final attack.

The drones are carried in a system called DAGGER POD, developed by Skydagger for the Bayraktar TB2. According to the company’s Instagram statement, the system can accommodate up to 16 SKYDAGGER FPV drones and has a modular design that allows it to be adapted for other aircraft platforms.

During the November test, the TB2 carried 16 drones and released two, which were guided by operators through a communications link provided by the larger aircraft. Baykar said both drones struck their designated targets.

Baykar has not disclosed the range, speed or warhead specifications of the Skydagger drones used in the demonstration.

The company has also not announced whether the configuration has entered operational service or when it might become available to existing TB2 operators.

A new role for an established combat drone

The Bayraktar TB2 entered service with the Turkish Armed Forces in 2014 and acquired an armed capability in 2015.

It subsequently became one of Turkiye’s best-known military exports, with combat operations in Syria, Libya, Nagorno-Karabakh and Ukraine.

The aircraft gained particular attention during the early stages of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, when Ukrainian forces used TB2 drones against Russian military equipment.

However, the increasing density of air defence systems and electronic warfare equipment has made operations more difficult for relatively slow, non-stealthy unmanned aircraft.

Launching smaller attack drones from a TB2 offers another way of employing the platform, although it does not eliminate the larger aircraft’s vulnerability to enemy air defences.

The new configuration could also allow an operator to attack several targets during a single mission, rather than relying entirely on the TB2’s conventional guided weapons.

Whether this approach proves effective in combat will depend on the range of the FPV drones, the resilience of their communications links and the ability of the carrier aircraft to operate safely.

TB2 endurance and payload

Baykar classifies the TB2 as a medium-altitude, long-endurance unmanned aircraft.

According to the company’s published specifications, the aircraft has a maximum take-off weight of 700kg and a payload capacity of 150kg.

It has a 12-metre wingspan, measures 6.4 metres in length and is powered by a 100hp internal combustion engine.

Baykar lists an endurance of more than 18 hours, an operational altitude of 16,000ft and a service ceiling of 20,000ft. The aircraft has also established a flight endurance record of 27 hours and three minutes.

Its flight control system incorporates three redundant autopilots, while its navigation system can operate without relying entirely on GPS.

The TB2 can conduct autonomous taxiing, take-off, cruising and landing. Its existing weapons integrations include laser-guided and other precision munitions.

The aircraft’s endurance could be useful when carrying FPV drones, allowing it to remain airborne while operators select targets. However, Baykar has not disclosed how carrying 16 drones affects endurance or flight performance.

Baykar’s expanding export market

The latest demonstration comes as Baykar continues to develop additional capabilities for its unmanned aircraft fleet.

The company says it has signed export agreements with 39 countries across its two principal combat drone programmes.

These include agreements with 36 countries for the TB2 and 16 for the larger Bayraktar Akıncı. Some customers have ordered both aircraft.

Baykar reported exports worth $2.2 billion in 2025 and said overseas sales have accounted for approximately 90% of its revenue in recent years.

The company has not identified potential customers for the new FPV drone configuration.

]]> Lufthansa targets faster route profitability as it advances ‘one airline’ strategy https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/lufthansa-route-profitability-tap-airline-routes-world/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 14:42:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55821 Speaking at the Routes World 2026 event in Frankfurt, Dieter Vranckx said the changing geopolitical and economic environment meant airlines could no longer rely on fixed, long-term network strategies.

The post Lufthansa targets faster route profitability as it advances ‘one airline’ strategy appeared first on AGN.

]]> Lufthansa Group expects new routes to reach profitability at least twice as quickly as in the past, as it adopts a more flexible approach to its network by shifting capacity towards growing markets including South America and Asia-Pacific, the group’s chief commercial officer has said. 

Speaking at the Routes World 2026 event in Frankfurt, Dieter Vranckx said the changing geopolitical and economic environment meant airlines could no longer rely on fixed, long-term network strategies.

Lufthansa expects a faster return from its new routes

Instead, he said capacity needed to be deployed more dynamically across the group’s hubs and carriers in response to fast changing market conditions.

Vranckx said Lufthansa had been reallocating some of its North Atlantic capacity towards South America and Asia-Pacific during the first half of 2026, as demand to the US ebbs. 

“We need to go much faster into profitability. We need to see an immediate impact in the market. We need to see that we create value in that market,” he said. The target was for new routes to become profitable “at least double as fast” as previously.

A decade ago, Lufthansa would launch new long-haul destinations and allow at least one year to adjust to the market, another year to build up demand, and then expect to reach profitability. Those expectations have now shifted. 

His comments suggest Lufthansa is pursuing a more disciplined approach to the European airline group’s network expansion, with an emphasis on capacity generating returns more quickly.

TAP acquisition would fit wider group strategy

Vranckx also explained Lufthansa’s interest in acquiring a stake in TAP Air Portugal within its broader strategy of operating as an integrated airline group, rather than treating each carrier and hub as a separate commercial operation.

Perhaps more than any other of Europe’s big airline groups, Lufthansa has employed a tactic of integration rather than celebrating each national carrier’s differences. 

The carrier already operates five airlines across six hubs, and Vranckx said decisions on network development and capacity allocation were increasingly being taken from a group-wide perspective.

“We will always look at the whole concept as if it would be one airline, and we optimise today the five airlines and the six hubs commercially from that perspective,” he said.

The addition of TAP will therefore be assessed in terms of how it adds to the group’s existing network, rather than solely as an individual airline investment. 

Vranckx said Lufthansa had considered several factors in evaluating the Portuguese carrier, including its financial value, geographical position, network fit and the overall contribution to the group.

“TAP should be similar to ITA. Ideally, since we are an ambitious airline group, I always say it should go faster than ITA,” he said of the acquisition and integration. “I think if we manage between one year and one and a half, we should be not only happy but very proud to manage that.”

The outcome is still dependent on the acquisition process and the work required to bring the airline into the group.

Vranckx did not identify a target number of airlines for Lufthansa to operate, saying the priority over the coming years would be to consolidate and strengthen the existing group structure.

Read more from Routes World: How Condor’s post-Lufthansa ‘Plan B’ is paying off Read more from Routes World: How Condor’s post-Lufthansa ‘Plan B’ is paying off

Market conditions call for a more flexible approach to network planning

The strategy also has implications for how Lufthansa allocates routes between its hubs. 

Vranckx said there was not necessarily a commercial case for every destination to be served from every hub, with some short-haul traffic better concentrated through a smaller number of airports.

“We don’t see the need for every hub to serve Oslo,” he said, giving the example of traffic that could be consolidated through two or three hubs rather than all five or six.

Those decisions form part of a wider effort to make better use of the group’s network and aircraft.

Vranckx said the traditional approach of developing a network strategy over the long term and then following it through was becoming less relevant.

“The times of setting up a network strategy for the next five to 10 years and then to follow through are probably over,” he said.

Instead, Vranckx said Lufthansa needs to remain flexible as geopolitical developments and market conditions change, including the ability to move capacity between hubs and regions.

“It’s our job always to find solutions when geopolitics hit, when there are complications in the market, when market dynamics change, and then you have to adjust capacity,” he said.

]]> VietJet moves to settle $250m aircraft leasing dispute after court order https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/vietjet-aircraft-leasing-dispute-uk-court-order/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 13:55:56 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55913 The airline is aiming to make the payment by 13 November, when a further hearing is scheduled in London to consider additional sums it may owe, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Reuters.

The post VietJet moves to settle $250m aircraft leasing dispute after court order appeared first on AGN.

]]> VietJet is preparing to pay approximately $250m to resolve a long-running aircraft leasing dispute with lessor FW Aviation, Reuters reports, after a series of court orders gave the appointed receivers powers over the low cost carrier’s assets outside Vietnam.

The airline is aiming to make the payment by 13 November, when a further hearing is scheduled in London to consider additional sums it may owe, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Reuters. 

The Vietnamese government has reportedly encouraged the airline to reach a quick settlement and instructed the carrier to pay the outstanding amount.

What is behind the VietJet dispute?

The dispute centres on four Airbus A321 aircraft that were grounded in Vietnam during the Covid-19 pandemic. 

FW Aviation, part of London-based investment firm FitzWalter Capital, brought proceedings in 2022 over unpaid lease obligations. 

While all four aircraft had been recovered by December 2022, the two sides remained in dispute over money that FWA said was still owed under the lease agreements.

Read more: VietJet applies to launch new Australian-based low-cost carrier using Boeing 737 MAXs Read more: VietJet applies to launch new Australian-based low-cost carrier using Boeing 737 MAXs

The resulting judgments put the debt at more than $250m, including interest.

VietJet paid $2m towards the amount in 2025, according to the court record.

VietJet said it had not paid more since it was restricted in paying the judgment debt due to Vietnamese foreign currency restrictions, and that the Vietnamese courts had refused to recognise the English judgments on policy grounds.

Latest in a long-running court saga involving VietJet

The latest developments follow a series of enforcement measures secured by FW Aviation in the English Commercial Court. 

In October, the court appointed two professionals from Alvarez & Marsal as joint receivers over VietJet’s assets outside Vietnam.

Their powers extend beyond existing aircraft to include bank accounts, ticket-sales, maintenance reserves, lease deposits and contractual rights associated with aircraft orders. 

The receivers can also take delivery of aircraft and engines on the airline’s behalf, including new aircraft due from manufacturers such as Airbus and Boeing, and arrange for them to be delivered to a third party.

A separate worldwide freezing order restricts VietJet’s ability to deal with certain assets outside Vietnam without court permission. 

These include undelivered aircraft, engines, purchase-contract rights and deposits. The receivership order also permits the receivers to seize and sell existing aircraft and take control of offshore subsidiaries.

The measures are intended to prevent assets from being moved or transferred in a way that could complicate enforcement of the judgment.

]]> Airbus must deliver 249 aircraft in two months to hit record 2026 target https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/airbus-249-deliveries-two-months-2026-target/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 12:23:30 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55941 Airbus delivered 74 commercial aircraft in October, taking its 2026 total to 621. The manufacturer needs 249 deliveries in November and December to reach its target.

The post Airbus must deliver 249 aircraft in two months to hit record 2026 target appeared first on AGN.

]]> Airbus must deliver another 249 commercial aircraft in November and December to meet its 2026 target of around 870, after handing over 74 jets in October.

The planemaker delivered 621 aircraft during the first ten months of the year. That is up 6.2% from the same period in 2025. October’s deliveries went to 45 customers.

October marked the third consecutive month in which Airbus delivered fewer aircraft than a year earlier. The manufacturer handed over 74 jets, down from 78 in October 2025, after smaller year-on-year shortfalls in August and September. Deliveries across the three months totalled 203 aircraft, nine fewer than in the same period last year.

To reach its target, Airbus now needs to average 124.5 deliveries in each of the final two months. That is more than double its January–October monthly average of 62.1 aircraft. The target would also exceed its previous annual record of 863 deliveries, set in 2019.

Airbus delivery target requires a sharp year-end increase

The latest figures narrow the gap from September, when Airbus needed 323 deliveries in the final quarter after delivering 547 aircraft by the end of September.

Airbus handed over 286 aircraft in the final quarter of 2025, including 136 in December. 

Repeating last year’s November–December performance would not be enough to meet the higher 2026 target. However, the manufacturer has historically concentrated a substantial share of deliveries towards year-end.

In its 28 October nine-month results, Airbus reaffirmed its guidance of around 870 commercial aircraft deliveries for 2026. Chief executive Guillaume Faury said the company was focused on meeting its objectives while maintaining quality. The manufacturer also attributed its negative free cash flow before customer financing partly to inventory built up for later deliveries.

A321neo accounts for more than half of October deliveries

By aircraft family, Airbus’ deliveries break down like this:

The A321neo was Airbus’s most-delivered model in October, with 39 aircraft handed over, accounting for more than half of the month’s deliveries. Airbus also delivered 15 A320neos, nine A220-300s and one A319neo, alongside four A330-900s and six A350s.

From January to October, Airbus delivered 77 A220s and 483 A320-family aircraft, along with 17 A330s and 44 A350s. Single-aisle aircraft accounted for 560 of the 621 deliveries, or around 90%.

Airbus continues to face delays involving engines and other suppliers, alongside recent quality issues affecting some A321neo and A330 aircraft. The company said at its nine-month results that its longer-term production plans were unchanged, including a target of 70–75 A320-family aircraft a month by the end of 2027.

Orders rise even as delivery deadline approaches

Airbus recorded 202 gross aircraft orders in October, taking its total for the year to 1,376. After 71 cancellations, net orders stood at 1,305.

The October order tally included major commitments from aircraft lessors Avolon and Aviation Capital Group, each committing to 75 new narrowbody planes. Avolon ordered 40 A320neo and 35 A321neo aircraft, while Aviation Capital ordered 23 A320neos and 52 A321neos. Atlantic Airways ordered two A320neo aircraft. The planemaker also recorded a widebody order for 35 A330 aircraft from CIT Leasing.

Continued strong demand is pitted against immediate pressure to complete and hand over already ordered aircraft. 

The 249 aircraft required in November and December do not all need to be newly assembled during those months; aircraft already in production or awaiting completion and handover can contribute to the total. Still, as the year wraps up, the next monthly figures will show whether Airbus is likely to meet its 2026 target.

The post Breaking: Fresh bomb threats disrupt European flights appeared first on AGN.

]]> Passengers on European flights have faced another morning of security alerts, with a Ryanair flight reportedly targeted by a bomb threat and police investigating threats at Copenhagen Airport and Prague Airport.

The latest incidents follow several days of disruption across Europe, during which passenger planes have been forced to make emergency landings or been diverted due to bomb threats.

Authorities have not established who is behind the threats or whether they are connected.

What happens when a pilot receives a bomb threat? What happens when a pilot receives a bomb threat?

Ryanair flight from Rome targeted by bomb threat at Lisbon airport

A Ryanair flight arriving at Lisbon’s Humberto Delgado Airport from Rome was reportedly the subject of a bomb threat on Friday morning.

Portugese media reported the service as Flight FR8196. According to reports, Portugal’s Public Security Police (PSP) received an alert about a possible explosive on board the aircraft.

According to Portuguese media, the alert was received through a phone call from a law enforcement officer, rather than an email as in Thursday’s incidents.

The flight arrived at Lisbon on Friday morning.

Copenhagen Airport faces renewed threats as police investigate

Police returned to Copenhagen Airport on Friday after receiving further threats.

Copenhagen police confirmed that officers were present at Denmark’s largest airport while investigations continued.

Copenhagen Airport confirmed the police presence but said flight operations were continuing normally.

It’s not yet clear what threats were made.

Prague Airport investigates renewed threats against passenger aircraft

Bomb threats have also been made against planes at Prague airport, according to Czech police.

Posting on X this morning (6 November), Czech police wrote:

“Today, the threat to place an improvised explosive device on board a number of aircraft arriving at and departing from Prague Airport is being repeated.

“In cooperation with Prague Airport, we have taken the necessary security measures with minimal impact on the airport’s normal operations. We continue to investigate the case.”

Prague Airport has confirmed that airport operations are not affected.

European bomb threats trigger flight diversions and fighter jet escorts

The latest alerts follow extensive disruption across Europe on 5 November, when nearly 30 passenger flights were reportedly targeted by bomb threats. All turned out to be hoaxes.

Airlines affected included Ryanair, Aer Lingus, Finnair, Wizz Air, LOT Polish Airlines and Aegean Airlines.

Several aircraft were diverted, while military fighter jets were deployed to escort passenger flights.

]]> Singapore Airlines unveils S$2bn long-haul cabins with new first class double beds https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/singapore-airlines-new-long-haul-cabins-2027/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 11:01:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55895 Singapore Airlines has revealed new long-haul cabins for its Boeing 777-9 and 41 retrofitted Airbus A350 aircraft, including first class double beds and new business class.

The post Singapore Airlines unveils S$2bn long-haul cabins with new first class double beds appeared first on AGN.

]]> Singapore Airlines has unveiled new first class, business class, premium economy and economy class seats as part of an over S$2 billion (US$1.56 billion) investment in its new long-haul passenger experience. 

The new cabin products will enter service progressively from the second half of 2027 on retrofitted Airbus A350-900 aircraft and the airline’s incoming Boeing 777-9 fleet.

The programme includes 41 A350-900 long-haul and ultra-long-range (ULR) aircraft. The Boeing 777-9 will carry all four new cabin products. The A350 retrofit will introduce redesigned business class seats and, on the A350-900ULR, first class for the first time.

The airline announced the new cabin products, accompanied by a refresh of its inflight entertainment, dining, amenities, connectivity and lounges. 

Singapore Airlines’ new cabin designs draw on research involving more than 5,000 frequent travellers, customers, employees and industry specialists.

New first class seats can form double beds

The new Singapore Airlines first class suites have curved sliding privacy doors. The centre pair can be converted into a two-seat sofa or a double bed measuring 80 inches long and 60 inches wide, which the airline describes as the largest double bed in commercial aviation. Each seat converts into an 80-inch fully flat bed. 

Other features include companion dining, electronically adjustable seating, wireless charging, a 32-inch 4K entertainment screen and controls that can remember a passenger’s preferred seat and lighting settings.

The 777-9 will have six first class seats, while the A350-900ULR will have four.

Business class adds privacy doors and companion beds

Singapore Airlines’ new business class seat features sliding privacy doors, adjustable dividers between centre seats and selected pairs that can be arranged as companion beds.

The fully flat bed measures 79 inches long and up to 24 inches wide. The airline has redesigned the dining table stowage to create more foot space when passengers are lying down. The seats also include adjustable support, wireless charging and entertainment screens of up to 22 inches, depending on aircraft type.

The new business class product will be fitted to both the 777-9 and the retrofitted A350 aircraft.

Collins Aerospace is manufacturing the first class, premium economy and economy seats. RECARO Aircraft Seating will supply business class seats.

Singapore Airlines recruited top industry designers to reimagine its passenger experience. The airline said PriestmanGoode designed the new first class, Designworks designed business class, and Factorydesign designed premium economy and economy class. 

“While each cabin has been designed individually, they are united by the same ambition to make the experience more comfortable, flexible, and rewarding for our customers,” said Lee Lik Hsin, Singapore Airlines’ chief commercial officer.

Premium economy, economy and onboard technology

Singapore Airlines said the premium economy and economy products will offer improvements in comfort, space, convenience and entertainment.

Both classes will feature the next-generation KrisWorld system, with 4K touchscreens and more than 2,500 entertainment options across the new offering.

The system will also support Bluetooth headphone pairing, spatial audio, revised navigation and wellness content. The airline plans Starlink-based high-speed connectivity for its A380 and A350-900 long-haul and ULR aircraft.

Singapore Airlines also announced over 100 new or refreshed dishes and expanded beverage choices across all cabin classes. 

The airline will introduce new amenity kits from November 2026, including SISLEY products in Suites and First Class and BYREDO products in business class. Business class passengers will also receive sleeper suits for the first time.

On the ground, the airline said it has invested more than S$130 million (US$101.5 million) to upgrade and expand its SilverKris lounges.

“This launch marks another major milestone in Singapore Airlines’ unwavering commitment to elevating the end-to-end travel experience,” said Mr Goh Choon Phong, Chief Executive Officer of Singapore Airlines, adding that it was “not an endpoint, but another step in our continuous pursuit to earn and retain the trust and loyalty of our customers, and reinforce our leadership in the airline industry.”

The airline has not yet announced the first routes to receive the new seats. Its latest timetable places the rollout to begin in the second half of 2027.

]]> Boeing uses AI-powered drones to speed up C-17 aircraft inspections https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/boeing-ai-drone-c17-aircraft-inspections/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 10:13:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55888 Boeing is advancing autonomous drone inspections of C-17 Globemaster III aircraft at its San Antonio maintenance facility to detect damage shorten inspections.

The post Boeing uses AI-powered drones to speed up C-17 aircraft inspections appeared first on AGN.

]]> Boeing is testing drone inspections of C-17 Globemaster III transport aircraft at its San Antonio maintenance facility in Texas.

Under its Advanced Aircraft Inspection (AAI) programme, camera-equipped drones fly around the aircraft and photograph its exterior.

Boeing’s Automated Damage Detection Software (ADDS) checks the photographs for possible damage. Technicians then review the findings.

Boeing says the approach could shorten inspections and reduce risky work on elevated platforms.

How Boeing’s drone inspections work

Inspectors normally check the fuselage, wings and other external surfaces from platforms or other access equipment.

The drones photograph areas that would otherwise need close-range inspection. The software flags anything that warrants a closer look. The photographs also give maintenance teams a record they can compare with later inspections.

Boeing is training the software to spot damage such as corrosion and lightning strikes. The software does not make the final assessment. Maintenance staff must examine suspected defects and decide what work is needed.

Boeing says it has tested the main inspection procedures and developed guidance for staff training and quality checks.

Boeing aims to improve aircraft availability

A shorter inspection could return a C-17 to service sooner. The US Air Force and other operators use the C-17 to carry troops, vehicles and equipment, so reducing maintenance downtime is critical.

The drones could also improve worker safety by reducing the need for inspectors to climb onto aircraft or use raised work platforms.

“AAI is about turning innovation into operational value,” said Travis Williams, Boeing vice president of Mobility and Surveillance Aircraft Services. “We’re delivering measurable improvements and building a repeatable capability that can be scaled as we validate outcomes.”

The San Antonio team is still refining the process before wider use.

Drone inspection technology already tested on other military aircraft

The latest announcement follows several years of development involving Boeing and autonomous flight specialist Near Earth Autonomy. Boeing invested in the company through its HorizonX Ventures arm in 2017.

As Defence News reported in 2023, the companies tested autonomous inspections at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam in Hawaii. Early trials proved drones could collect images during inspections and transmit them for automated analysis. Each image is linked to a location on the aircraft so inspectors can check the same area again.

The National Centre for Manufacturing Sciences (NCMS) has also published results from the inspection programme.

NCMS reports that the system cut inspection time by at least 40% during C-17 heavy maintenance visits. The C-17 detection model identified more than 95% of anomalies in each scan. 

The technology has also been tested on other military aircraft, including the KC-46 Pegasus, KC-135 Stratotanker, P-8 Poseidon, EA-18G Growler and C-5 Galaxy.

AI becomes part of Boeing’s wider C-17 maintenance strategy

Boeing is also using aircraft data to help plan C-17 maintenance. In April, the company introduced Aircraft Data Reasoner, software that examines aircraft data for signs of component problems.

“With the Aircraft Data Reasoner, operators gain near‑real‑time insight into component health so we can act before failures occur. That predictive visibility not only improves C-17 mission readiness and reduces unscheduled downtime, but it also drives smarter parts positioning and sustainment decisions across the fleet,” said Williams.

Boeing said an analysis of historical service data indicated a 2%–3% increase in aircraft availability.

In July, Boeing announced plans to work with Pelico on maintenance scheduling and parts supply.

Boeing wants to extend the drone inspection process to other maintenance sites and other aircraft. Its military and commercial maintenance teams are sharing what they learn from the trials.

.sie-field-hero{position: relative; 
 left: 50%;
 right: 50%;
 margin-left: -50vw;
 margin-right: -50vw;
 width: 100vw; 
 min-height: 480px;
 max-height: 560px;
 background-size: cover;
 background-position: center 40%;
 background-repeat: no-repeat; 
 background-color: #003B73;
 overflow: hidden;
 margin-bottom: 0;}
.sie-field-hero--no-image{background: linear-gradient(
 135deg,
 var(--field-color, #003B73) 0%,
 color-mix(in srgb, var(--field-color, #003B73) 65%, #000) 100%
 );}
.sie-field-hero__bg-img{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center 40%;
 z-index: 0;
 display: block;}
.sie-field-hero__overlay{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 1;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.90) 0%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.60) 38%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.25) 65%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.12) 100%
 );
 display: flex;
 align-items: flex-end;
 padding-bottom: 52px;}
.sie-field-hero__inner{width: 100%;
 max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-field-hero__label{display: block;
 font-size: 13px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}
.sie-field-category-badge{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 7px;
 padding: 6px 14px;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.18);
 border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.35);
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 12px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 20px;
 margin-bottom: 14px;
 backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-category-badge i{font-size: 11px;
 opacity: 0.9;}
.sie-field-hero__title{font-size: clamp(30px, 5vw, 54px);
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #ffffff;
 margin: 0 0 14px;
 line-height: 1.1;
 letter-spacing: -0.02em;
 max-width: auto;}
.sie-field-hero__tagline{font-size: clamp(15px, 2vw, 18px);
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 margin: 0 0 28px;
 max-width: auto;
 line-height: 1.55;
 font-weight: 400;}
.sie-field-hero__actions{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 12px;
 margin-top: 4px;}
.sie-field-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 8px;
 padding: 12px 24px;
 background: #1E56B0;
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 6px;
 text-decoration: none;
 transition: background 0.2s;
 white-space: nowrap;}
.sie-field-hero__cta:hover{background: #163e82;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary{background: transparent;
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border-color: #fff;}
.sie-field-body{max-width: 1200px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px 80px;}
.sie-field-highlights{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 0;
 background: #f0f4fb;
 border: 1px solid #d4e0f5;
 border-radius: 12px;
 margin: 32px 0 40px;
 overflow: hidden;}
.sie-field-intro-block{margin: 0 0 48px;}
.sie-field-intro-block p{font-size: 17px;
 line-height: 1.78;
 color: #374151;
 margin: 0;
 margin-top:40px;}
.sie-field-section{padding: 64px 0;
 border-bottom: 1px solid #E5E7EB;}
.sie-field-section:last-child{border-bottom: none;}
.sie-field-section-header{margin-bottom: 40px;}
.sie-field-section-header h2{font-size: 32px;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #003B73;
 margin: 0 0 8px;}
.sie-field-section-header p{font-size: 17px;
 color: #003B73;
 margin: 0;}
.sie-breadcrumb{padding: 16px 0 0;}
.sie-breadcrumb__list{display: flex; gap: 8px; list-style: none;
 margin: 0; padding: 0; font-size: 0.85rem; color: #6B7280;
 flex-wrap: wrap;}
.sie-breadcrumb__list li:not(:last-child)::after{content: '/'; margin-left: 8px;}

.sie-dest-panel__globe { font-size:22px; color:#1e66f5; line-height:1; }
.sie-dest-panel__title { font-size:1.5rem; font-weight:800; color:#0b3770; margin:0; line-height:1.2; }
.sie-dest-panel__close { background:transparent; border:0; font-size:22px; color:#0b3770; cursor:pointer; padding:6px 8px; border-radius:8px; line-height:1; opacity:.75; transition:opacity .15s,background .15s; flex-shrink:0; }
.sie-dest-panel__close:hover { opacity:1; background:#f0f4ff; }
.sie-dest-panel__sub { color:#466087; font-size:.94rem; margin:0 0 20px; flex-shrink:0; }
.sie-dest-panel__grid { display:grid; grid-template-columns:repeat(4,1fr); gap:14px; flex:1; align-content:start; }
@media (max-width:620px){ .sie-dest-panel__grid { grid-template-columns:repeat(2,1fr); gap:10px; } }
@media (min-width:621px) and (max-width:860px){ .sie-dest-panel__grid { grid-template-columns:repeat(3,1fr); } }
.sie-dest-panel__card { position:relative; display:block; aspect-ratio:3/2; border-radius:12px; overflow:hidden; text-decoration:none; background:#1d3557; }
/* background-image only applies once the panel is open — browsers don't fetch a
 url() sitting unused in a custom property, so the 24 card images (~170KB) cost
 nothing at page load. They fetch on the first SIEDest.open(). */
.sie-dest-panel__card-bg { position:absolute; inset:0; background-size:cover; background-position:center; transition:transform .4s ease; will-change:transform; }
.sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__card-bg { background-image:var(--card-hero); }
.sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg { transform:scale(1.07); }
.sie-dest-panel__card-body { position:absolute; inset:0; display:flex; flex-direction:column; justify-content:flex-end; padding:10px 12px; background:linear-gradient(to top,rgba(0,0,0,.72) 0%,rgba(0,0,0,.30) 55%,transparent 100%); }
.sie-dest-panel__card-name { color:#fff; font-weight:700; font-size:.92rem; line-height:1.2; text-shadow:0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,.55); display:block; }
.sie-dest-panel__card-arrow { display:block; color:rgba(255,255,255,0); font-size:.75rem; margin-top:2px; transition:color .2s ease,transform .2s ease; line-height:1; }

<span><span>sandoel</span></span>

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
	<li><a class="external-link eac-external-link" href="https://twitter.com/search?q=%23TheFutureIsYours" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">#TheFutureIsYours</a></li>

</ul>

                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>

                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                      </div>

                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on areas of mutual interest</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital that Inter-Institutional Agreements are based on areas of mutual interest. These agreements should identify shared quality requirements specific to the planned exchanges, including concrete proposals as to how these activities will contribute to the development of learning and teaching in participating institutions. The involvement of academic staff is key to ensuring that the selection of partners is based on sufficient knowledge of the area. Each HEI should decide who is responsible for initiating, signing and implementing these agreements and the list of responsible persons should be available on the website for contact and consultation purposes.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on the compatibility of study programmes</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Inter-Institutional Agreements should be based on a comprehensive understanding of the partner HEIs, the compatibility of study programmes, quality levels and standards considered adequate for student and staff mobility activities. For example, selected partners should have learning, teaching and assessment procedures that can be accepted by the sending institution without requiring mobile students to do any additional work or take examinations upon returning from the receiving institution. The compatibility of the programmes should be reflected in the learning outcomes to be achieved.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on shared quality requirements, student and staff selection for mobility and clear timelines at all stages of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>A key role of Inter-Institutional Agreements is to set out agreed, shared quality criteria and clear timelines for all stages of the mobility.<br>Shared quality criteria may include, but are not limited to: selection criteria for the nomination of students and staff, recommended language skills, grading systems, measures for preparing, receiving and integrating Erasmus+ participants. These might be expanded with geographic and subject-specific criteria.<br>In terms of the timelines set out for the mobility activities, particular attention should be paid to:</p><ul><li>The nomination of mobile students by the sending HEI,</li><li>The acceptance of nominees, and</li><li>The issuing of the Transcript of Records after the study period abroad by the receiving HEI. This is normally issued within five weeks after the end date of the mobility period.</li></ul>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are regularly monitored and if necessary adapted.</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Establishing Inter-Institutional Agreements is only the first step in promoting mobility. Once signed, Agreements should be actively honoured and adjusted over time as needed. To ensure that an institution’s Inter-Institutional Agreements continue addressing well-defined needs and opportunities, such agreements should be monitored regularly both in quantitative (e.g. number of mobilities) and qualitative (e.g. shared quality criteria) terms. This can be done in a number of ways for example by a designated responsible individual, office or an established process. Seeking input from across the organisation helps create acceptance at all levels of the institution and reinforces commitment towards mobility.</p>                      </div>
